en: Commentary on the "Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (Including Preface) Compiled by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai Recorded by his Disciple Guanding The text begins with the following preface: I have heard that the Buddha-Dharma is vast and profound, and its principles are subtle and difficult to fathom. It is like the great ocean; though one may enter it, there is no end to its depths. It is like Mount Sumeru; though one may ascend it, there is no limit to its height. If one wishes to grasp the essence of this Dharma, one must first rely upon the Bodhisattva Precepts as the foundation. These precepts are the root of all virtues and the source of all wisdom. Without them, one cannot attain the stage of non-retrogression or achieve the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, I have compiled this commentary to elucidate the meaning of the "Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Chapter," hoping that those who practice will find a clear path and that future generations may follow this light.

May all beings together realize the Way of the Buddhas. [End of Preface] [The main body of the Commentary follows... (Note: This is a structural translation of the title and introductory materials provided. The actual exegesis of the text would require a much more extensive treatment.)
The Bodhisattva precepts are the opening chapter for directing one toward goodness and the vanguard for repelling evil. By returning directly to the Way, the source of birth may be fully exhausted.
Even the minor practices of the Śrāvakas cherish and revere the Prātimokṣa; how much more so should a Mahāsattva, possessing a dual resolve, not maintain them with meticulous care?
Both the internal and external paths are reverently upheld; the royal family and the common people alike offer their persons in devotion.
This is truly the supreme cause for attaining the ultimate fruit and the wondrous practice for establishing the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Nevertheless, regarding the characteristics of the precepts as recorded in the sūtras and śāstras, there are naturally many varieties; and as explained in the biographies and traditions, the methods of receiving them are not without their differences.

This is because the capacities and insights of sentient beings vary between the partial and the perfect, and thus they require detailed or concise expositions accordingly. Since words cannot express both simultaneously and phenomena do not operate in parallel, I now respectfully...
Examining the Dharma characteristics set forth by Master Kumārajīva, they originate from the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, specifically the "Vinaya-piṭaka Section.

Master Kumārajīva arrived within the borders of Han in the third year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty. He brought forth the Great Vehicle, rectified the holy teachings, and translated over three hundred fascicles of sūtras and śāstras.
This single volume of the *Brahmajāla* was the very last he recited and transmitted; he vowed to propagate it extensively, and for this reason, [the Emperor] treated it with profound reverence.
I have diligently repeated these words three times because their literary meaning is profoundly obscure and their significance is deep and mysterious;

thus, I point them out as clearly as one’s palm so that later generations may easily attain awakening. The title *Brahmajāla* (The Brahma’s Net) is intended to clarify that the Buddha-dharma teachings differ from one another, just like the mesh of the net of the Brahma King.
The chapter on the "Mind-Ground" (*Cittabhūmi*) refers to the Bodhisattva Vinaya-piṭaka, which is all-encompassing.

To guard against the three karmas, one must understand that while the mind, consciousness, and mental faculty are one in essence, they differ in name; among these three karmas, the karma of the mind is primary, with those of body and speech following in sequence.
Since this is discussed according to what is most preeminent, it is called the "mind-ground."
Commentary on the *Brahmajāla Bodhisattva-śīla Sūtra*, based on the *Bodhisattva-śīla Sūtra*.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuxian of the White Lotus Society at the Eastern Courtyard. (This includes annotations added to the sūtra text and further sub-commentaries added to the original commentary.)

[Note] Regarding this title, the various masters of antiquity have differed in their additions and deletions. If one follows personal opinion, Master Zang (Zhiyi) states that it is the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" spoken by Rocana Buddha in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
The *Auspicious Commentary* (*Āo shū*) on the *Bodhisattva Precepts Text* (*Pusa jie ben*) agrees with this.

Furthermore, the *Kuang shū* (Commentary by Kuang) shares the same eight characters for the first part, while the latter part reads: "The Bodhisattva Mind-Ground: Ten Grave [Precepts] and Forty [Minor Precepts]."
Chapter Ten: The Eight Light Precepts. In the current circulating edition, the first eight characters are identical to those below;
some call it the "Bodhisattva Ground Heart-Dharma Gate Chapter," while others call it the "Bodhisattva Ground Heart Chapter. Master Xi’s *Commentary* states:

"I have searched through ancient collections, but in the upper scroll, only the general title and the chapter headings are established; furthermore, the one who expounds it—Vairocana—is not listed therein."
The title should be removed; it ought to follow the wording of the scripture.

The scripture states that this was spoken in the Fourth Dhyāna within the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground," and further states that the "Subtle Precepts of the Mind-Ground" were proclaimed by the Buddha himself. The *Qishi Dingshan Ji* says:
"This [title] is also hardly more than a minor error. For now, following our Patriarch’s commentary, we shall simply refer to it as the *Brahmajāla Sūtra Bodhisattva* [Precepts].
The "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" (Xindi-pin) serves as the definitive authority. Furthermore, Master Xi said:
"One must not establish the three characters 'Rocana' [as the title], for this sutra was preached by Śākyamuni; how can those of our school be so mistaken? (and so forth).
Nevertheless, while using this manifest name [Śākyamuni] rather than another carries no great fault, if the name established is incorrect, then the interpretation of its meaning will have no basis.
Since the source of this illness lies herein, how could there not be a great error?
Now, by consulting the indications in the ancient catalogs, I see that the original commentary (*śāstra*) was titled *The Sequence of Name and Substance* (*Mingti youxu*).

Furthermore, the Sui Renshou Catalog records a two-fascicle *Brahmajāla-sūtra* translated by Master Kumārajīva, as well as a one-fascicle *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, also said to be translated by Kumārajīva, both of which are listed among the missing texts.
The *Zhongjing tuji* (Record of the Translation of Scriptures) agrees with the *Sui lu* (Sui Dynasty Catalogue).

The *Dazhou kanding zhongjing mulu* (Great Zhou Catalogue of Authorized Scriptures) also contains one fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, likewise attributed to Kumārajīva; it states that it consists of eighteen sheets.
However, other catalogues list translations by Master Śīlamañju and Master Zangshi, which are not included here. Only the version translated by Master Kumārajīva is the current edition. (2)
Regarding the single fascicle titled *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, Bodhisattva Heart-Mind Ground Chapter, it is simply called the *Bodhisattva Precept Text* (*Bodhisattva-śīla-mūla*).
Examining this, we know that Master Kumārajīva recited out two fascicles on the "Heart-Mind Ground":

the upper fascicle clarifies the stages of the bodhisattva, while the lower fascicle clarifies the bodhisattva precepts. From within these, Kumārajīva separately extracted one fascicle on the precepts.
When people recite and uphold it, they call it either the *Bodhisattva-śīla-mūla* or the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.

In the commentary of my ancestor [Master Zhiyi], this title is explained in such a way that one sees its non-falsity. The commentary states: "The name of the sūtra is the 'Brahmajāla' chapter; the name of the chapter is the 'Bodhisattva Mind-Ground.
This reveals both the general title of the entire sūtra and the general title of this specific chapter within the two fascicles. Thus, the two are combined.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind," begins this volume with a general table of contents for the sūtra and its chapters;

this is to ensure that the fundamental source is not forgotten. What is now explained in this commentary consists of the verses extracted by Master Kumārajīva from within this chapter, comprising one fascicle of the ten grave and numerous light precepts, intended for people to study and recite accordingly.

The *Dānítí Púsà Jìng* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva Precepts) is precisely the text of one fascicle that separately extracts the characteristics of the precepts (*jìxiàng*). Therefore, the commentary states: "Extracted from the Great Text;
both the introduction (*xù*) and the dissemination (*liútōng*) sections are missing. This indicates that it is a separate section referred to as the *Púsà Jìng*.
Based on this commentary, determining the title separately is highly appropriate; thus, in the chapter on explaining the name (*shìmíng zhāng*), only the person and the dharma are explained.

Regarding the "name," it refers to the two characters for "Bodhisattva"; regarding the "dharma," it refers to the character for "precepts. To discuss the meaning and intent at length is simply to explain this name.
At the conclusion of the analytical selection (*viniścaya*), I shall briefly explain the general headings of the sutra chapters as they follow one another;

it need not be said that when opening a chapter, one must know that in our tradition, whenever a primary title is explained, it invariably follows the version established by the translator of the scriptural canon.

Regarding the titles of these chapters, both the *Aoshu* and the *Zangshu* have arbitrarily added characters to the headings based on their own private views, thereby utterly losing the original intent.
Although Kuang’s commentary is by one of our own school, he too was ignorant of this principle.

Although Xi’s copy distinguishes between the two categories—the general and the specific—within the title of the *Śīlasūtra*, he fails to clarify them. Although Dingshan takes the commentaries of our own school as his definitive authority, yet...

The *Shi zong jing pin mu* (General Catalogue of Sūtras) does not distinguish between the various sections; in the *Xianming Dashi Shu* (Commentary by Master Xianming), it is clearly stated that apart from the separate divisions, they are called the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.

Why, then, is this not cited as the definitive authority? To possess [this text] yet fail to follow it, while forcibly employing what one lacks—this is precisely the fault for which one is reproached.
Furthermore, you do not permit the *Xi chao* (Xuanchao’s Commentary) to remove the capacity of Vairocana.
To claim that this scripture is taught by the masters of all three periods is a profound error regarding its essential intent.
As will be shown below, the single fascicle titled *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Pusa jieben) found in the Tripiṭaka, translated by Śikṣānanda and still extant, differs significantly from this [text].
It is feared that the single fascicle translated by Kumārajīva is a different version; why then was it used? Answer: In the translation by Śikṣānanda, [the title] is placed at the beginning.
The four barbarian tribes follow next; the sections clarifying minor auspicious matters differ in number, yet their underlying principles are similar.

Since Kumārajīva’s translation is listed among the missing texts, it is difficult to verify. In the Great Master’s commentary, he himself notes that this is a distinct section titled the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, which serves as the definitive evidence.
Furthermore, the commentary cites Master Paramārtha’s reception of the precepts at Gaochang.
Regarding the ritual protocols and the verification of the translated precepts, it is likewise so. Question:

Now, when one observes the current version, there is a prose introduction (*dīrgha-pada*) at the beginning of the volume, which the *Auspicious Commentary* (*Āo shū*) explains. Why does our Patriarch’s commentary omit the explanation for everything prior to the verses, starting only from the gāthās?
Furthermore, where should this title be placed: at the beginning of the volume or at the beginning of the verses? Answer: The prose introduction is...
Regarding the subsequent section of the preceding scroll, because the text there is extensive, it has been divided and balanced here;
thus, the two scrolls may circulate together, with the prose introduction (*gadya*) placed at the beginning of the scroll.

As for the currently circulating separate record of the precepts (*śīla-dharma*), which is called the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, it should not have the prose introduction placed at the beginning of the scroll, as was done later on.
As for the seal [of the text], it would not be appropriate to proceed by conflating this intention with that;

furthermore, one observes in the Tiantai commentary (*Sūtra Commentary*) that it simply states "Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra" without including chapter titles, which more perfectly captures the profound essence of the text.
Since even those who are obscure regarding this have explained it thus, we know that this title properly belongs before the verses. (The rest of the passage appears to be a fragmentary note.)

One who understands this intent may also provide a topical analysis (*kośa-śāstra*) by selecting what is profound and discarding errors; yet to claim that "the arising and ceasing have their causes" is again to miss the essential point.
Question: Although it has long been understood that the prose passages (*dīrgha-pāṭha*) should belong to the upper fascicle, I do not know upon what authority this is based.
Answer: The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The prose of the upper fascicle mentions the Great Brahmā King’s *Jāla-dhvaja* (Net-Canopy) banner."

Since [the commentators] above have cited the upper fascicle as their proof—and because there is no other such passage within that upper fascicle, this text appearing here in the prose portion being the only instance—it is clear that this text properly belongs to the upper fascicle; this principle is quite evident.

Commentaries such as the *Shibiqi shu* and the *Lü deng cao* are all ignorant of this meaning, treating it as a separate section in their prefaces and commentaries; only our Tiantai school [correctly understands it].
Having skillfully mastered this meaning, I now explain this commentary, which is divided into two parts: first, an explanation of the manifest [meaning], and second, an explanation of the text.
The first part further consists of two sections. First, the headings and enumeration.
[Commentary]: This explains the threefold profound meaning (san-chong xuan-yi) of this Precept Sūtra.
First, the explanation of the title; second, the determination of its essence; third, the critical analysis. [Note:
In our school, whenever a title is explained, one must invariably employ the fivefold profound meaning (pañcavidha-gambhīrārtha). Why does this commentary open only three chapters?
Although there have been many who have explained this according to ancient traditions, those who have sought and understood it with absolute precision are extremely rare.

I have merely used this as a title because the general and specific aspects were not clarified, which led to a misunderstanding of the essential intent of the *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) regarding the "Three and Five.

The *Xi-chao* (Xih’s Sub-commentary) maintains that the "Chapter on the Substance" (*Ti-zhang*) must necessarily encompass the "Principle" (*Zong*) and the "Application" (*Yong*). It holds that taking the precepts of virtuous conduct as the means to attain the supreme fruit is the Principle, while the cessation of evil and the promotion of good is the Application.
This naturally includes the text concerning the classification of teachings (*panjiao*), for the meaning of the five chapters is already complete. [This was stated] by Dingshan based on the person.

The complete integration of doctrine and metaphor constitutes its name; non-conceptual unconditioned form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) constitutes its essence; the immediate conferral of the *prātimokṣa* constitutes its thesis;
the manifestation of virtue by immediately obstructing [transgressions] constitutes its function; and the pure milk of the Sudden School (*tun-bu*) constitutes its teaching.

However, these two masters arbitrarily establish five chapters without fundamentally investigating that our Patriarch did not open such five chapters for a profound reason—a point which other masters have been unable to grasp.
To seek its meaning too deeply and give rise to arbitrary interpretations is most contrary to the principles of the text.

I have long hesitated over this point; however, upon searching through the commentaries, I found that there is a separate section titled *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, and thus I have come to understand this principle.
I shall now attempt to clarify it, noting that three points must be understood: first, the distinction between the general and the specific, as previously cited by our Great Master.
Since the commentary states that it is "separately titled the Bodhisattva Precept Sūtra" (*bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*) outside its own section,

and that this is neither the general title of a single sūtra nor the general title of a single chapter, but rather refers to one fascicle of the precept dharma extracted from Master Kumārajīva’s recitation of one chapter within two fascicles,
which circulated separately in the world under the name *Bodhisattva Precept Sūtra*— if it were [the title] of a single sūtra...
The title should be called the *Brahmajāla* [Sūtra]; if it were the title of a single chapter, it should be called the "Chapter on the Mind-Ground Sūtra.
Regarding the five chapters (*pañca-varga*) and the separate recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, I have personally assigned these titles—what need is there for five chapters?

Tiantai understood this; thus, in his *Shiming* (Explanation of Names), he explained only the two names of person and dharma, and in his explanation of the essence (*tattva*), he discussed only non-action (*avijñapti*).

Having seen deeply and understood its principle, later generations arbitrarily established five chapters; how could this reflect the Great Master’s intention? Second, because phenomena and principle differ:
the essence of the Sūtra is the principle inherent in phenomena, while the essence of the precepts is the phenomenon inherent in principle.

Since the substance of principle is that which is manifested by the宗 (zhōng, "central tenet") and upon which the 用 (yòng, "function") relies, it is necessary to provide both a general and specific treatment, thus requiring all five.

The substance of this chapter focuses exclusively on the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) matter that should be analyzed: the reason why the precept-color (*śīla-rūpa*) is produced by the three masters and seven witnesses.
Regarding the explanation of the name in the commentary, it explains only the person who is a bodhisattva and the dharma which is the precept-method. Based on the name, one analyzes the substance;

this substance is simply the capacity of the person who receives the precepts to produce the unconditioned artificial color-matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*). This substance belongs to the category of phenomena (*dharma*).
The essence of the principle revealed by the five chapters does not employ the three [aspects] because the substance of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is distinct from them;
that is, the essence of the principle is precisely the essence of the sūtra within the five chapters, and it is also the essence upon which the precepts rely.
The "one point" mentioned above in the treatise is what is manifested by the thesis and is the basis for its function; one must discern the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) within the five chapters.
Since the essence is a substantial entity, it belongs to the section on the "Thesis" (*zong*) among the five chapters.

However, as this [treatise] specifically discusses the formal substance (*jiesè*) of the precepts generated through the practice of upholding or violating them—rather than what is revealed by the Thesis itself, rather than being the basis for its function, and rather than being that which clarifies the five chapters—it is not included therein.

Thus, in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), the presence or absence of the unmanifest (*wuzuo*) is discussed in terms of provisional and definitive teachings; this is precisely what constitutes the five chapters.

Within the elucidation of the fundamental principle (*zhong*), one type of preceptual practice is the very essence of that essence; this ontological essence (*ti*) is precisely the foundation upon which practice relies.
Therefore, among the twenty-five expedient means (*fangbian*) of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the purity of upholding the precepts serves to clarify non-action (*wu zuo*).

As the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states, "The latter three [of the expedient means] clarify the fundamental principle. Thus, we know that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* take the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way as their basis.
That the essence of the *asaṃskṛta-śīla* (unconditioned precepts) is precisely the core tenet of this scripture is a profound and subtle meaning rarely understood by people.
If one understands this meaning, the core tenet and its essence will become clear; how then could one discuss the five chapters [of the *Śīlaparivarta*] without this?

Therefore, it is necessary first to understand the general and specific titles and the establishment of their names; only when the correct meaning is established can one return to the single family’s core tenet, which is not easily expounded.
Although the two masters establish their chapters with a desire to forcefully assert their views, they ultimately remain confused regarding the intent of the Patriarch.

If one were to evaluate the relative heights of these two masters, Ding Shan does not equal Xi Chao. Take Ding Shan, for instance: he takes the sudden realization of the *Prātimokṣa* as his primary tenet.

Is this cultivation? Is it nature? Is it cause? Or is it fruit? What grounds are there for such a hierarchy? This is because he fails to realize the essential purport of the sūtra’s doctrine. Furthermore—

In the *Ti* (The Body), it asks: "Is the provisional color (rūpa) a phenomenon (*dharma*) or a principle (*li*)? Since the substance (*ti*) of the five chapters belongs to the principle, why is it made of phenomenal color?

If both the substance and the thesis (*zong*) are lost, the five meanings will all become obscured. Although the *Xiyao chao* takes cause and effect as its thesis, it does not clearly grasp the intent of the substance;
its arbitrary opening of five layers stems entirely from a failure to understand this present commentary’s explanation of the precepts.

Furthermore, regarding the discussion of *wu zuò* (non-action), although it specifically clarifies the ontological substance (*vastu*), it is said to be "identical to nature" (*xing*) and thus identical to the principle (*li*) in its factual aspect.

However, when discussing the side of phenomena (*dharma*), there are distinctions such as arising and non-arising, flourishing and decline. As the commentary states: "In terms of principle, there is no [distinction]; in the gates of teaching, there is.
Is this not precisely because one clarifies *wu zuò* by way of phenomena? Thus, we know that the various masters did not merely differ in their titles.
Furthermore, although there are five chapters in the *Ming*, the essential core of Tiantai’s fundamental tenets is not yet understood within them.

If these are not clarified, how can one extract the relevant scriptures from the Great Canon and thereby discern the relative superiority of their doctrinal essence, or distinguish between the partial and the perfect nature of the teachings?
As for those who study the teachings, if their "eye of the doctrine" is not clear, they will fail to comprehend the Buddha’s intent. This I have often observed.

Examining various ancient expositions, the profound and subtle meaning of these three and five has not been heard of at all; I hope that the worthy and accomplished ones will examine and elaborate upon it.
II. The Exegesis, which is further divided into three parts. First, the Explanation of Names, which is further divided into two parts. First, the Enumeration.
[Commentary] Within the explanation of the names, first the personal name is clarified, next the title of the Dharma is discussed, and finally the stages and ranks are explained.
Regarding the second [section], there are three parts; first, the personal name:
the Sanskrit sound from India is *Mahāsatva*, which is now called "Bodhisattva. This is a translation that abridges the remaining characters.
It is called the "Great Path Mind" because it brings sentient beings to fulfillment; it is also called the "Great Being" (Mahāsattva) and the "Great Courageous Mind.
Furthermore, it is named according to its virtuous and beautiful conduct. Because its mental application is vast and universal, this title is established.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that such a person possesses a Great Path Mind that cannot be destroyed, like a diamond, from the very first moment they resolve their mind upon awakening.
Those who ultimately reach equal enlightenment are all called Bodhisattvas; they are also termed "Sons of the Buddha" (Buddhaputra), with the meaning being that of succession.
All three vehicles arise from the Buddha, and thus the sense of being a "son" applies to them all. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"If one is like my son, the Mahāsattva who succeeds [the lineage] is superior and is called a 'true son'. Furthermore, since those of the three vehicles alike cultivate the Path, they all possess this significance.
The two vehicles proceed from their own path to a small fruit; thus, they are narrow and short. The Great Being’s path is broad and long, as he proceeds through his own path and leads others;
therefore, he receives the title of "Great. As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "From the first aspiration, one is already a teacher for humans and devas, surpassing the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas";
hence, it is called the "Great Mind."

[Note] Regarding the name "Bodhisattva," first the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are distinguished, followed by an explanation of the meaning of the word *suta* (son). In India, the full term is *mahācittī bodhisattva*;
here, the two characters *bodhi* are abbreviated, and the name is established according to its function.

Thus, there are various translations. As for the meaning of "son" (*suta*), it has both general and specific senses. Generally, all three [types of sons] arise from the Buddha’s awakening; thus, they are all equally entitled to the designation.

If we distinguish them by their titles, those of the Two Vehicles—who have attained the extinction of ashes—lack the principle of succession and thus are not called "sons. Bodhisattvas, however, are indeed sons;

yet, within the Tripiṭaka, because they have not yet severed their afflictions, the meaning of "son" is not fully established. If we rely on the revelation of the ultimate truth (the Ekayāna), there is no one who is not a son.
Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, both those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment and those who have first resolved to do so are universally entitled to be called "sons."
Because the great supersedes the small, it is said that it "surpasses" or "excels. **II. The Name of the Dharma.** First, citing sūtras and śāstras to explain the name. [Commentary:

Next, we shall discuss the designation of this dharma, which is the meaning of *śīla*. The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "In the language of Qin, it means 'natural goodness' (*xing shan*), and it is also called 'coolness' (*qing liang*).
It is so named because it can cease the feverish affliction of breaking the precepts; it is also named according to its function. It is also called...

*Prātimokṣa* is translated as "preserving liberation" (*baode jietuo*). It is also called "pure livelihood" (*jingming*), and further termed "accomplishing dignified deportment" (*chengjiu weiyi*) and "having nothing to receive or store" (*wusuoshouchu*).
Regarding future places of rebirth, it ensures one leaves the three evil realms and receives a physical form in a pure land.

It can arrest wrong livelihood, prevent transgressions, and cease evil; thus it is also called "precept" (*jie*). In its etymological sense, it signifies "restraint" (*yueyi*) and "training" (*xunyi*); furthermore, it signifies "diligence" (*qenyi*).

The meaning of "prohibition" (jin) is likewise established according to its etymological sense. A major sūtra states: "If you still speak of impermanence despite the Buddha’s prohibition, you violate the Buddha’s prohibition;
your tongue shall immediately fall away. It further states: "All the precepts possessed by such a person are incomplete;
they cannot even attain the enlightenment of the Two Vehicles, let alone the Unsurpassed Way."

[Note] The commentary on the meaning of this name is self-evident in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*). Regarding the intent of citing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is for the purpose of providing an exegesis that prohibits [the notion of impermanence] while explaining the term "precept" (*śīla*).
Since the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* discusses permanence, one must prohibit impermanence; if one speaks of impermanence, one violates the Buddha’s prohibition.

To extensively employ the three types of cultivation or to equate and cite both [permanence and impermanence] as being in harmony is not the intended meaning of the text. △ Second, distinguishing the characteristics by employing the Great and Small Vehicles.
Furthermore, there are three [categories]. ○ First, an explanation based on the three types of precepts in the Hīnayāna.

【Commentary】 Now, regarding what is called "precepts" (*śīla*), there are the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts of restraint), the *dhyāna-sahabhū-śīla* (precepts co-arising with meditative concentration), and the *mārga-sahabhū-śīla* (precepts co-arising with the Path).

The origin of these names lies in the Tripiṭaka. "Vinaya" (*viniyati*) means restraint; it refers to formal conduct (*vinaya*), which is capable of restraining various evils upon the physical form; therefore, it is so named.
Precepts are also called *vīrya* (dignity) and *īryā* (conduct). *Vīrya* means pure, solemn, and awe-inspiring; *īryā* means a model for practitioners, such that they are reverent and awe-struck.
They are also called "taming and governing," which means making the mental activities harmonious and wholesome. Concentration (*samādhi*) means stillness and withdrawal;

at the time of entering concentration, one naturally becomes harmonious and wholesome, preventing all evils. The Way (*mārga*) is that which enables penetration; after the realization of truth has been awakened, it proceeds spontaneously.

There is no violation [of the precepts] regarding the insects in the soil of the field of the first fruit (srotāpanna) within a path four inches wide; this is due to the power of the "concomitant" (*sādhāraṇa*).
Since these two dharma-precepts are the superior power of the mind, they are able to give rise to the path of the precepts, concentration (*samādhi*), and discipline (*vinaya*) simultaneously;

therefore, they are called "concomitant. The Sarvāstivāda school says that there are three types of precepts: the discipline-precept (*saṃvara-śīla*), the meditative-precept (*dhyāna-śīla*), and the outflow-free-precept (*anāsrava-śīla*); although these names appear in three [categories], [they are subsumed under the aforementioned].
In the present system of Bodhisattva precepts, there are likewise these three types: that which is obtained through a formal vow is called *saṃvara* (restraint);
that which is associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*) all ceases the three types of action and is collectively termed "precept" (*śīla*).
[Note] These three types of precepts pertain to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

Within the Hīnayāna, when one attains the first fruit (*srota-āpanna*) at the time of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) and realizes the Truth, the power of the "Path-concomitant" (*mārga-sahagata*) causes one to spontaneously abandon evil paths; at the moment of this definite arising, the "restraint of discipline" (*saṃvara-śīla*) arises concurrently.

Thus, they are called "concurrent precepts. This refers to their arising precisely upon entering the stages of the Hīnayāna. As for the Mahāyāna, it concerns the contemplation of the mind through the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

When merged with the precepts, one possesses non-action (*avijñapti*), which is not the same as the Small Vehicle’s position that it is only attained upon entering a specific stage, as will be explained below in the section on the two types of non-action.
Here, "meditation" and "outflow-free" refer to the names *samādhi-sāṃvṛta* (concomitant with concentration) and *mārga-sāṃvṛta* (concomitant with the path).
Second, the explanation according to the three precepts of the Mahāyāna.

[Commentary]: Regarding the three categories of precepts—restraint of conduct (*śīla-saṃvara*), gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka*), and benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā*)—the name "threefold aggregate of precepts" (*tri-kaṣāya-śīla*) originates from the *Bhūmivastu* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and does not apply to the three Piṭakas.

The "Great Being’s restraint" (*mahāsattva-saṃvara*) encompasses both cessation and cultivation; it causes the three karmas to manifest through body and speech, and all such manifestations are termed "restraint.
As for "gathering wholesome dharmas," based upon the restraint of conduct, one gives rise to the mind of great enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
To cease all non-cultivation of wholesome deeds and diligently cultivate all virtues so as to fulfill the vow for Bodhi;
regarding the "gathering of beings," there are eleven matters by which a Bodhisattva benefits sentient beings, all of which constitute extensive benefit and vast assistance to living beings.
Having extensively enumerated all the Bodhisattva precepts in the Chapter on Precepts, the nine kinds of precepts are finally summarized as being comprised within the three types of precepts.

The three types of vows encompassed herein—the vow of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), which causes the mind to abide; the vow of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), by which one spontaneously accomplishes the Buddha-dharma;

and the vow of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla*), by which one brings sentient beings to maturity—exhaust all the precepts of a Mahāsattva. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "The vow of restraint refers to the ten *pārājikas*;

the vow of gathering wholesome qualities refers to the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates; and the vow of benefiting sentient beings refers to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity."
The transformation reaches all sentient beings, causing them to attain peace and happiness.
[Note] It should be understood that the Mahāyāna’s three clusters encompass all precepts without exception.

These three are established in opposition to the three paths to manifest the three virtues: the restraint (*saṃvara*) opposes the path of suffering and accomplishes the virtue of the *dharmakāya*; by means of this, sentient beings...
The body of karmic suffering lacks the restraint of the precepts; during its movements and activities, it creates sinful karma that leads to this retribution of suffering.

By receiving the precepts, one restrains body and speech so as not to commit transgressions. Through maintaining the discipline (*vinaya*), this body of karmic suffering becomes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
at the time of fruition, the virtues of the Dharma-body are realized. This [process] subsumes all that is wholesome and destroys [all that is unwholesome].

The path of afflictions becomes the necklace of the virtue of *prajñā*. Since the eighty thousand dharma-gates constitute the precept of gathering wholesome qualities, one should accordingly counteract and destroy the eighty-four thousand dust-like afflictions (*kleśa*) to achieve the virtue of *prajñā*.
Gathering in sentient beings means destroying the path of karma to achieve the virtue of liberation; for by committing various sins, one is bound and attached everywhere, yet through compassion...

Through the teachings of compassion, joy, and equanimity, one brings sentient beings to maturity; because one perceives liberation within every phenomenon (*dharma*), at the time of attaining the fruit, the virtue of liberation is perfected.
Regarding the *Śīla-vyūha* (The Ornament of the Precepts), the underlying intent is a single, continuous thread.

As for the nine kinds of precepts, they are collectively elucidated in the section on the "Precepts of Skillful Means" (*upāya-śīla*): first, the precept of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śīla*); second, the universal precept (*sarva-śīla*); third, the difficult precept (*duṣkara-śīla*).
1. The precept of all four doors; 2. The precept of virtuous persons; 3. The precept of all modes of conduct; 4. The precept of removing affliction; 5.
The precept for this world and other worlds; 6. The pure precept. Regarding the explanation of the nature of these precepts, there are four kinds:

first, receiving them correctly from another—this refers to looking toward others' transgressions and generating a sense of shame within one's own mind; second, receiving them with a well-purified mind internally.

1. To feel shame and remorse upon seeing one's own transgressions; 2. To repent immediately after committing a transgression; 3. To practice with single-minded diligence so as not to commit further transgressions; 4. To maintain mindfulness through diligent application.

Next, the three clusters (*tri-skandha*) and eleven matters that encompass all precepts are explained. Third, regarding the difficulty of the precepts, it is briefly stated that there are three [requirements]:
possessing great wealth, possessing great power, and being able to renounce them all to leave the household life and receive the Bodhisattva precepts. This is the first [point].

First, a bodhisattva who faces difficulty with the precepts: even when encountering urgent peril or facing the loss of life, they do not allow the precepts they have received to become deficient, much less violate them completely.
This is the second [type of] bodhisattva who faces difficulty with the precepts:
throughout all practices, all right concentrations, and all abidings in mindfulness, they remain undistracted, and even unto the end of their lives, they ultimately [uphold] those subtle precepts.
"Not deficient, let alone excessive" is the third difficult precept; the rest can all be clearly seen.
The summary at the end of the nine precepts states that they are all subsumed within the three precepts. Regarding the eleven matters: first, to act as a companion for the benefit of sentient beings;
second, to act as a companion for sentient beings who have already experienced or have not yet experienced various sufferings such as illness, as well as for those who tend to the sick.
1. Accompanying others, he preaches the mundane and supramundane teachings for them, or uses skillful means to enable them to attain wisdom;
2. He knows gratitude and repays kindness; 3. When sentient beings are terrified by lions, tigers, wolves, kings, thieves, water, or fire, he is able to rescue and protect them;
or when they have lost their relatives or wealth, he can provide consolation and explanation to free them from suffering and distress; 4. Seeing... [the sixth point].
1. To provide all that is needed to those who are poor and destitute; 2. To be fully endowed with the seven virtues and to rely upon right reception (*samyak-samādāna*);

3. To maintain [disciples] in accordance with the Dharma; 4. To first speak words of comfort, to visit them at appropriate times, and to provide them with food and drink while speaking virtuous words concerning the world;
5. To praise those who possess genuine virtue; 6. To reprove and subdue those who have faults or evil deeds with a heart of loving-kindness.

Eleventh, by means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one manifests the miserable realms (*durgati*) to cause others to feel dread and revulsion toward all evils, leading them to reverently practice the Buddha-dharma;
although this final type occurs at the stage of the fruit (*phala*), it must necessarily rely on the power of the causal mind (*hetu-citta*) for its operation.
III. Explanation according to the ten precepts of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

[Commentary]: In the "Chapter on Precepts" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, ten types of precepts are enumerated: first, unimpaired; second, unbroken; third, unpierced; fourth, unmixed; fifth, conforming to the Path;
sixth, unattached; seventh, praised by the wise; eighth, sovereign; ninth, conforming to meditative concentration;

and tenth, complete. Inferring the meaning of these ten: "unimpaired" refers to upholding the natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*); their nature is so grave and pure that they are guarded as if protecting one's very life.
If the bright pearl is violated, one is like a vessel that has already been cracked—a marginal person to the Buddha-dharma.

If it is not broken, one maintains the thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣa] precepts without impairment. If it is not pierced, then regarding offenses such as pāyattika (pāyantika), if there is a transgression, one is like a vessel with holes and leaks, incapable of receiving the Way.
"Not mixed" means maintaining the *dhyāna-saṃvara* (meditative restraint); although one maintains the Vinaya...

To mindfully contemplate matters of broken precepts is called "mixed concentration" (*vyavakīrṇa-samādhi*); it is the maintenance of the mind such that sensual desires do not arise. A Great Sūtra states:
"Mocking speech, the sound of bracelets heard outside a wall, and men and women pursuing one another—all these defile the pure precepts.

"Following the Path" means to accord with the principle of the Truths (*satya*), thereby being able to destroy the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*). "Non-attachment" refers to seeing the Truth and becoming a noble one (*ārya*). At this point—
Contemplating that there is no defilement or attachment within the afflictions—these two refer to the observance of the precepts according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The "precepts praised by wisdom" and the "precepts of mastery" refer to the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others; they are praised by the Buddha as attaining self-mastery within the world, and these concern the observance of the precepts according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
When the two sets of precepts are fully endowed with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are then called "following the head."

In the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, one does not arise from the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) yet manifests all dignified postures (*īryāpatha*), displaying the forms of the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) to guide and benefit sentient beings.
Although these postures are active and mobile, they are spontaneously and eternally pure; therefore, it is called the "precept that accords with concentration" (*samādhi-anuvartaka-śīla*).

The various precepts and disciplines mentioned previously involve prevention and restraint, and thus are termed "incomplete" as they do not encompass the Middle Way. Because there is no precept that is not fully prepared here, it is called "complete."
Because one universally enters into all phenomena by means of the wisdom of the Middle Way, it is called "complete"; this is the upholding of the precept of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way.

[Note] A comprehensive explanation of the ten precepts is provided in the *Fuxing Zhuan* (Commentary on the Practice of Samatha and Vipaśyanā), the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), and the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary), which extensively cite and analyze various sutras and śāstras.

The similarities and differences have been examined in detail in the *Bejian Tushi* (Illustrations for Comprehensive Inspection), so they will not be recorded here again. However, regarding the meaning herein:

while the first four belong to the precepts (*śīla*), the latter six—since they are discussed in terms of upholding [the precepts] through the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*)—belong to the vehicle (*yāna*).

Thus, these ten precepts are fully equipped with both the vehicle and the precepts. These Mahayana Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*) of the Bodhisattva, as previously stated, constitute a direct counter-action to [the opposing faults].
The completion of the three paths into the three virtues is precisely the simultaneous cultivation of the vehicle and the precepts, which collectively return to the treasury of principle;
thus, it is only by means of the tenfold assembly for entering the dharma-gate of the three aggregates that one attains the wondrous practice of non-action of the Mahāyāna.
△ Third, clarifying the stages and positions, which has two parts. ○ First, the heading and basis.

[Commentary] Next, the stages and positions are explained. By inferring the meaning of the various teaching gates (dharma-gates) taught throughout Śākyamuni Buddha’s single career of transformation, it is clearly established that there are four teachings:
namely, the Tripitaka, the Shared, the Distinct, and the Perfect. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites Kātyāyanīputra regarding the limits of the six perfections:

the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) was fulfilled when [the Bodhisattva] sacrificed himself to replace the dove; the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) was fulfilled when King Sumati did not speak falsely; and the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*)... [is fulfilled].

When the Rishi Kāliṅga King cut out his heart and he remained unmoved, this was the fulfillment of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). When he drained the ocean through great giving, this was the fulfillment of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

When the bird’s nest was left intact at the hermitage of Śāṇakavāsin, this was the fulfillment of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). When the minister Gopaka divided the land to settle a dispute, this was the fulfillment of equal wisdom (*samatājñāna-pāramitā*).

This refers specifically to the Bodhisattva. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that there are Bodhisattvas who resolve their minds toward awakening in conjunction with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

There are bodhisattvas who have attained mastery; there are also bodhisattvas who, having resolved their minds on enlightenment, sport with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), purify buddha-fields, and attain inconceivable liberation as described in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, yet who, upon transforming their bodies and ascending the throne, are nonetheless humbled and rebuked by others—these are distinct bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, upon resolving their minds, immediately sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), achieve perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*), and turn the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*).
Saving sentient beings is the perfection of the Bodhisattva. Among the four types of Bodhisattvas, the varying depths of their stages and positions shall now be explained.
[Note: First, the four teachings are generally indicated; next, the four distinctions are established based on realization.
The meaning of these four types of Bodhisattvas cannot be fully exhausted here. Ancient masters failed to understand this and merely claimed that a Bodhisattva belongs exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
Because the interpretation of the meaning in the sūtras and śāstras would otherwise become obstructed, the *Miaoxuan* states: "Others say that the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is the Bodhisattva precepts.

Now we ask: what kind of Bodhisattva precepts are these? If they were to answer, 'They are the Bodhisattva precepts of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) or *Tong* (Shared) vehicles,' then there should be a separate assembly of Bodhisattvas;
since no such assembly exists separately, how could the precepts be different? Furthermore, if they were explained separately..."

Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, what distinguishes them from the Pratyekabuddha precepts? Herein it is clarified that within the Three Piṭakas and the Three Vehicles there is no distinction among the assemblies;
thus, there cannot be separate Pratyekabuddha precepts. If one were to interpret this as referring to the distinct and perfect Bodhisattvas, that would be acceptable. Why?
Because outside of the common assembly of the Three Vehicles, there are distinct Bodhisattvas, and therefore they have distinct precepts. Now, as for our own school...

It is not that the capacities [of sentient beings] are not subsumed within the four teachings; yet, since there are four different versions of the *Bodhisattva Sūtra* (or *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*), how can they be clearly distinguished?

Since other schools do not understand this, how can they explain the sūtras? △ Second, the detailed explanation, which is further divided into four parts. First, the Tripiṭaka Teaching, which is further divided into two.
○ First, the stage of the Śrāvaka. [Commentary]:

Regarding the first three baskets (*piṭaka*), they are primarily intended for the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) Śrāvakas. Among the seven types of noble ones and sages, there are three stages of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*):

1. the five stabilizing practices (*pañcavasthāpana*); 2. the distinct-characteristics mindfulness foundations (*svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*); and 3. the general-characteristics mindfulness foundations (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*). Next, one enters the internal ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*), which consists of four stages.

The roots of goodness consist of: fourth, the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*); fifth, the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*); sixth, the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*); and seventh, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Beyond these, one enters the stage of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), which comprises:

first, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); second, the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*); third, the one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); fourth, the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*);

fifth, the one who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*); sixth, the one liberated by time (*samayavimukta*); and seventh, the one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*). Such are the stages of the Śrāvaka.

[Note] Regarding the stages of the Tripiṭaka, there are the seven stages of the *pṛthagjana* (ordinary beings) and the seven stages of the noble ones (*ārya*). The stage of the ordinary beings belongs to the mundane; they are divided into external and internal.
The first three belong to the external, as they have not yet attained the water of principle (*tattva-jala*); the latter four belong to the internal, namely the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

Following these, one enters the stage of the noble ones, beginning with the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). The reason for dividing them into seven is that spiritual capacities (*indriya*) are either sharp or dull, and practices consist of either faith or the Dharma, just as in the case of the *Miao* [Sutra].
First, the stage of "following through faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) refers to those of dull faculties entering the path of seeing;

it means that they do not rely on their own intellectual power, but rather depend upon others to generate understanding. Second, the stage of "following through the Dharma" (*dharmānusārin*) is the name for those of sharp faculties entering the path.
"Sharp" means that by means of their own intellectual power, they perceive the principle and sever the fetters while still in the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Using contemplation to contemplate the Four Noble Truths (and so forth). Third, regarding the stage of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*):

this refers to those who practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita*) entering the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), at which point they are renamed "those of faith and understanding. Such persons have three types of realization (*adhigama*), up to eight kinds of *parinirvāṇa* (and so forth).
Fourth, clarifying the stage of vision and attainment: those who practice through the Dharma (*dharma-carita*) enter the path of cultivation and are termed "those of vision" (*darśana*).
Those who possess these sharp faculties (tīkṣṇendriya) perceive the Dharma and attain the principle through their own wisdom; therefore, they are called "attainers by vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

There are also various other [categories]... [as explained at length]. Regarding the stage of bodily realization (kāyasākṣin), it refers to those two types—the one resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and the attainer by vision—who enter the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), employ untainted wisdom (anāsravajñāna) to sever the fetters of the upper and lower realms (ūrdhvam-adhaḥ-bhāga-vidhāna-saṃyojana), and give rise to the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti).

(As stated above... One who attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is called an Anāgāmin who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*). 6. Regarding the Arhat liberated by time (*samayavimukta*):
this refers to one of faith-practice (*śraddhānusārin*) with dull faculties, who attains liberation only when waiting for the proper time and when all necessary conditions are assembled.

(As stated above... 7. Regarding the Arhat liberated not by time (*asamayavimukta*): this refers to one of dharma-practice (*dharmānusārin*) with sharp faculties, known as the Arhat of immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*).

Furthermore, because this person cultivates the path during the causal stage, they are able at all times to advance in the cultivation of wholesome karma according to their desires without depending on external requisites;
therefore, they are called "one liberated at any time" (*asamaya-vimukta*). There are also two types of such persons:

those who have not attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and are thus called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukta*), and those who have attained the attainment of cessation and are called "doubly liberated" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*). (And so forth. The faculties and capacities of the *śrāvaka* are great.

Approximately seven types [of practitioners] are established; if one follows the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, twenty-seven stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) are elucidated, as fully detailed in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text).

Within these stages, one should examine the various practices of the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*), the reduction of conditions for practice, and the differing characteristics of Arhats who regress or waver.

These matters are somewhat touched upon here, but they are treated extensively in the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary), the *Sìjiàoyì* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), the *Fēnxuán* (Analysis of the Profound), and other works.
The details are so comprehensive that I have no leisure to explain them here. ○ Second, the stage of the Bodhisattva. [Commentary:
Regarding Bodhisattvas, one does not discuss their formal stages nor do they sever afflictions; they simply cultivate the six perfections.

If one were to discuss their sequential stages, one could only estimate their depth and shallowness by comparing them to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle. From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, they give rise to compassion and vows.

Observing the Four Noble Truths with the Truth of the Path as the primary gateway, he single-mindedly cultivated the Six Perfections: through *dāna* (generosity), he broke the fetters of hungry ghosts;

through *kṣānti* (patience), he rescued those in the hells; through *vīrya* (diligence), he delivered the animals; through *dhyāna* (meditation), he uprooted the asuras; and through *prajñā* (wisdom), he illumined the celestial hosts among men.
From the time of the first Śākya until Kanaśi-Kāśyapa, this is called the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, in which one attains five kinds of merit.
1. Not being born in the three evil realms; 2. not being born in a borderland; 3. having complete sense faculties; 4. not receiving a female body; 5.

constantly knowing past lives while not yet knowing that one will become a Buddha—this provisional position is within the five cessations and the specific and general foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
From Śikhin to Dīpaṃkara is called the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*; at that time, although one knows for oneself [that one will become a Buddha],...
Having become a Buddha, he does not speak of it with his mouth; his position is estimated to be within the stage of the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) of the Dharma-nature.
Since he possesses faith that realizes the Dharma, he must know he will become a Buddha; yet, while practicing the six perfections, his mind is not yet clear, so he does not speak of it to others.
From the time of Dīpaṃkara until Vipaśyin, when the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are fulfilled, at that time he clearly knows it within his own mind.
When one acts as a Buddha and speaks with one's own mouth, it corresponds to being in the stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*) within the Dharma-position;
there, one practices the six perfections and clearly understands the Four Noble Truths, just as one sees all four directions clearly from the peak of a mountain when speaking to others.

If one has passed through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and planted the karma for the thirty-two marks, this corresponds to the stage of Lower Patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*); if one sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), [it corresponds to the stage of Supreme Patience].
Abiding in the stage immediately following "Ultimate Patience" (kṣānty-anantaram), one enters the true path in the thirty-four moments of mind;
by severing the fetters and attaining *traya-sambodhi*, one becomes a Buddha.
[Note: The stages, practices, cultivation, and realization of the Tripiṭaka Bodhisattva differ from those of other teachings, being based on three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Regarding the practice of the six pāramitās and the cultivation of the marks and characteristics of Buddhahood until the attainment of enlightenment: from the perspective of stages, these marks are cultivated over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

These three *kalpas* correspond to the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*). Upon sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one enters "middle and upper patience" (*madhya-adhimātra-kṣānti*) within a single *kṣaṇa*.

This sequence of entry into realization corresponds to the various stages; while this commentary merely provides a brief outline of the stages, they are fully detailed in the *Sìjiàoyì* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings).

The textual passages concerning the stage of "clarity in conduct" (*vidyā-caryā-bhūmi*) are extremely detailed; however, regarding this bodhisattva’s claim that "afflictions are not severed," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn) rebukes it, calling it a "great error.
The intention of the *Śāstra*’s author is to refute the provisional [teachings] by means of practice (*caryā*) in order to overcome the Lesser Vehicle, and thus he makes this statement.
If one adheres to those teachings as a concealed provisional expression, it does not mean that there is no sense of non-severance at all; rather, it refers only to what is severed.

There are two kinds of delusion: that which is severed by the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and that which is severed by the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). If it is severed by the contaminated, it is not yet called "severed";

only when severed by the uncontaminated, true severance, is it called "severed. Therefore, in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), two treatises are cited and harmonized to provide a detailed and thorough explanation of the text;
students should consult them. As for what is called the "ground of nature" (*gotrabhūmi*) in the *Dīrgha Āgama*: since...

The meaning of the non-practice gate is the same as that of the *śrāvaka* stage in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*), in that [defilements] have not yet been severed. **2. The Shared Teaching.** [Commentary:

The Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching share the ten stages common to the three vehicles. The first, the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*), is identical in name to that in the Tripiṭaka Teaching regarding its phenomenal characteristics;

however, the mental state of its contemplative practice differs. While it takes the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*) as its substance, it views them as being like illusions and transformations, thereby comprehensively destroying both views and attachments.

The eight inversions are called the application of mindfulness to the body; the same applies to the mind, feelings, and dharmas. Abiding within this contemplation, one cultivates right effort, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the awakening factor of investigation, and the path factor of right view.

Although one has not yet attained the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), because the water-like principle of the general-characteristic wisdom is profound and sharp, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*).
As for the Second Stage (*gotra-bhūmi*), one attains the Dharma of Heat after having transcended the Stage of Dry Wisdom.

Having been able to progress through the initial, middle, and final stages of mind, one enters the "Summit Dharma" (*mūrdha-dharma*) and continues up to the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*);

these are all termed the "Stage of Nature" (*dharmatā-bhūmi*). Because one attains the water of the untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharmatā*), it is called the "Stage of Nature. (38) Regarding the "Stages of Persons":

for those of the three vehicles who practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita*) or through the Dharma (*dharma-carita*), their realization of the provisional gives rise to the true, and they sever delusions within the "Uninterrupted Samādhi" (*ānantarya-samādhi*), wherein the eight patiences (*aṣṭa-kṣānti*) are fully possessed.
Lacking one part of the perfection of wisdom is called the Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*). Regarding the Stage of Vision (*darśana-bhūmi*):

the three vehicles equally perceive the ultimate principle of the Four Noble Truths of non-arising; they equally sever the delusions of vision, exhausting all eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The Stage of Thinness (*tanu-bhūmi*) refers to the essence of attenuating attachment; by manifesting the true path, one severs the afflictions of the desire realm and realizes the sixth liberation, wherein the afflictions are thinned.
Sixth, the Stage of Freedom from Desire (*vītarāgabhūmi*): This refers to those of the Three Vehicles who realize that the essence of attachment to desire is itself the Truth;

by severing the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), and anger (*pratigha*)—it is called the Stage of Freedom from Desire. Seventh, the Stage of Having Accomplished What Was to Be Done (*kṛtāvibhūmi*):

This refers to those of the Three Vehicles who realize that the essence of attachment to the realms of form and formlessness is itself the Truth; they give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and sever the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

The Stage of Having Accomplished (Kṛtāvī-bhūmi) is so called because one has exhausted the seventy-two categories of afflictions—including restlessness, pride, doubt, and the defilements of the form and formless realms—thereby bringing to ultimate completion all matters concerning the three realms.

The Stage of the Pratyekabuddha (Pratyekabuddha-bhūmi) refers to the stage of the *pratyekabuddha*, who has awakened to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and possesses great power of merit to eliminate even habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The Ninth, the Stage of the Bodhisattva (Bodhisattva-bhūmi), is that from which one enters the provisional through emptiness, wherein the path and contemplation flow as a dual stream.

Through profound contemplation of the two truths, one advances to sever the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). When form and mind are devoid of cognition, one attains the Dharma-eye and the knowledge of the modes of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-mārga-jñāna*).
One sports with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), purifies Buddha-fields, and brings sentient beings to maturity.

By training in the ten powers (*bala*) and four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) of a Buddha, the habitual tendencies are nearly exhausted. Regarding the ten Buddha-stages (*daśa-bhūmi*): by means of the power of great merit, one supports wisdom in a single thought-moment.
When the wisdom of correspondence contemplates the ultimate truth, even the residual habits are exhausted without remainder, like wood consumed by the kalpa-fire leaving no ash or charcoal;

or like a fragrant elephant crossing a river until it reaches the very bottom. Although the names "Buddha" and "Bodhisattva" differ from those of the Two Vehicles, they all universally contemplate non-arising;

their realization of the essence of dharmas is identical as that of the Aśaikṣa, and they all return to the same place of fruit-realization where all is reduced to ashes. This is called [the One Vehicle].
The Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).
[Note: Regarding the characteristics of the stages of practice, the severance and suppression of afflictions, and the shared stages of the Three Vehicles, the various texts are identical.

In the *Mysterious Text* (*Xuanyu*) and the *Meaning of the Four Teachings* (*Sijiaoyi*), whenever the shared stages are explained, one must distinguish that while the names are distinct, the meaning is shared; this is because such is the case across all sutras and treatises.

Because the explanations differ, two intentions are established to reconcile them into one: first, using the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*) as a standard of comparison, the Bodhisattva’s distinct stages are established under the name of "patience" (*kṣānti*);

second, using the fifty positions of the Distinct Teaching (*viśeṣa-yāna*) to correspond to the names of the common stages of the three vehicles in the Shared Teaching, the Bodhisattva’s positions are thereby defined. Thus, the establishment of the stages of patience employs the Shared Teaching.
The teaching on the ten stages establishes ten types of patience (*kṣānti*) specifically for Bodhisattvas.

Although both [Bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles] equally contemplate the truth and sever delusions to realize non-arising (*anutpāda*), the followers of the two vehicles abide in non-arising to discipline and liberate themselves, whereas Bodhisattvas do not abide in such patience toward suffering but instead benefit others and can give rise to transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-karman*).
Therefore, this name "patience" is established separately for Bodhisattvas; thus it is said that it belongs exclusively to Bodhisattvas.
The details regarding the stage of the Bodhisattva (*bodhisattvabhūmi*) are extremely thorough in the *Myōgen* (Wondrous Profundity) and the *Shikyōgi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings).

If one uses the stages of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*) as a standard for comparison with the common stages of the Bodhisattvas, then within the commonality of the Three Vehicles, one takes the Bodhisattva’s perspective;

this also carries the sense that distinct names are applied to the universal [teachings]. Furthermore, various texts state that "common to the Three Vehicles" refers to... [the stage] where the Two Vehicles do not speak [of these matters].

If a bodhisattva employs names such as "the stage of dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) and so forth, these names are shared with those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), because the ten stages practiced by those of the two vehicles are also called "dry wisdom" and so on.
When people do not perceive this, they claim that [these terms] are merely metaphorical expressions used across the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
This is truly because they have not seen the various texts that distinguish the bodhisattva path specifically; some even say this regarding it.
Regarding these two meanings, both generally borrow the stages of the Distinct Teaching (Bie-jiao) to name the stages of the Shared Teaching (Tong-jiao).

Furthermore, it is because one does not see in various texts that the "Establishment of Patience" (Li-ren) employs the ten stages of the Shared Teaching; rather, it is only within the context of borrowing from the Distinct Teaching that the names of the Distinct stages are used.

Thus, one meaning involves borrowing the names of the Distinct Teaching for the Shared Teaching, while the other meaning involves employing the establishment of patience according to the Shared Teaching—it is not as some might claim.
Both meanings are borrowed from the specific [terminology] used by the reader; when these names are applied correctly, the various texts harmonize and their meanings are unobstructed.
Only in the *Sijiaoyi* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings) are the titles of these two sections established most appropriately.

It states: "First, using the stages of the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching) to establish the names of the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching) stages—though the names are distinct, the meaning is shared. Second, clarifying the application."
The distinct teaching and distinct stages are so named because while the names are distinct, their meanings are pervasive; only when these names are established does their meaning become manifest.

Herein, the clarification of the stages is based solely on the common stages shared by the three vehicles, as the sequence of abandoning and suppressing [afflictions] is easier to understand in this context.

Furthermore, within the practice and stages of this teaching, there are those who abandon delusions at the first stage (*bhūmi*), because the capacity of beings subsumed within the Shared Teaching is broad, and thus its meaning is [varied].

One must understand that "inclusivity" (含容) refers to the threefold penetration (三通); thus, the meaning is naturally correct. Since it benefits others, one is able to sever afflictions within the first stage (初地). Question:
Regarding the three instances of the "burning wick" (燋炷) mentioned in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, is this also the first flame of the Shared Teaching (通教) at the first stage?

What practice and position does this refer to? Answer: There are many differing explanations regarding the meaning of the "burning wick," all of which stem from a failure to understand the Shared Teaching.
The threefold penetration clarifies this meaning: just as a burning wick illuminates its position, all things are made transparently clear.

This is because within the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), there are those of sharp faculties who possess the capacity for the inclusion of the path while severing delusions; their capacities are shared, and thus the teaching is shared. Through the clarity of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the teachings of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect are mutually penetrating.
The Buddha’s contemplation of these three types of capacities occurs within a single seat, wherein they are all established as the tenth stage.
The teaching is explained through these three types of persons: for those who understand the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), it is the initial flame of the stage of Dry Wisdom;
for those of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), it is the initial flame of the first bhūmi; and for those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), it is the initial flame of the first abode.

For the Distinct and Perfect teachings, the "initial flame" consists of the destruction of ignorance; for the Shared Teaching, it consists of the destruction of views. Thus, the Tathāgata speaks while encompassing all three teachings.

Those who possess the nature of the three roots enter the stages of the Distinct and Perfect teachings from within the Shared Teaching; this is further illustrated by the three metaphors of walking, horse-riding, and supernatural power.
"Walking" symbolizes the Shared Teaching, "horse-riding" symbolizes the Shared-Distinct, and "supernatural power" symbolizes the Shared-Perfect.

These are all clarified at the first stage (*bhūmi*). Because those at the initial stage of the flames do not see their existence, they rely on the Shared Teaching for guidance to explain the profound meaning of the "burning wick."

To lose the essential meaning: for instance, if one relies on the principle of "penetration" (*tong*) without considering the "destruction of delusions," then those who interpret this as referring to a person at the first stage (*bhūmi*) who has already been "received" [into the higher path] are all missing the intended meaning of the text.
This precisely accords with the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, which states that it refers to the meaning of a sharp-facultied Bodhisattva perceiving the Truth (*satya*) at the first stage.
As for the statement that "seventy-two [delusions] are exhausted," it is because of the seven... [text fragment].

Within the stages (*bhūmi*), one progressively abandons the afflictions of the two upper realms; since there are nine grades in each of the eight dhyāna-stages, it is said that there are seventy-two [afflictions to be abandoned].
This is because the nine grades of the desire realm are excluded, as they are abandoned within the six [lower] stages. △ Third, the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) also has three parts.
○ First, showing the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*).
[Commentary]: The stages of the Separate Teaching consist of fifty-two grounds. First, the ten stages of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*):
1. Faith; 2. Mindfulness; 3. Progress; 4. Wisdom; 5. Concentration; 6. Non-retrogression; 7. Dedication; 8. Protection of the Dharma; 9. Precepts; 10. Vows.

Second, the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) of the nature of the cultivated seeds (*śikṣamāṇagotra*), which constitute the internal ordinary person: 1. Arousing the mind; 2. Maintaining the ground; 3. Practice; 4. Birth.
The fifth is the perfection of the five skillful means; the sixth is the six right mentalities; the seventh is non-retrogression; the eighth is the stage of the youthful prince;

the ninth is the stage of the Dharma-son; and the tenth is the stage of consecration. All thirty minds up to this point are termed the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); they are all internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and are collectively termed the "nature-ground" (*gotra-bhūmi*).
Third is the nature-seed-nature (*gotra-gotra*), which consists of ten practices: first, joy; second, benefit; third, freedom from resentment; fourth... [and so forth].
1. Exhaustless; 2. Free from delusion and confusion; 3. Well-manifested; 4. Unattached; 5. Honorable; 6. Wholesome Dharma; 7. Reality; 8.
The fourth lineage of the path; 9. The tenth dedication: Saving and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings;
10. Indestructible; 11. Equal to all Buddhas; 12. Pervading all places; 13. Non-existent.
1. The treasury of all merit; 2. The sixfold conformity to all firm and equal roots of goodness; 3. The conformity to the impartial contemplation of all sentient beings;
4. The characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*); 5. Unbound and unattached liberation; 6. The immeasurability of the Dharma-realm.
The fifth noble lineage consists of the ten stages (*bhūmi*): 1. Joy (*pramuditā*); 2. Purity (*vimalā*); 3. Radiance (*prabhākārī*); 4. Blazing (*arciṣmatī*).

The fifth is the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjaya*), the sixth is the Manifest (*Abhimukhī*), the seventh is the Far-Reaching (*Dūraṅgamā*), the eighth is the Immovable (*Acalā*), the ninth is the Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī*), and the tenth is the Cloud of Dharma (*Dharmameghā*).
The sixth stage, Equal Enlightenment (*Samyaksambodhi*), is called the Vajra-Mind Bodhisattva stage and is also named the Stainless Stage (*Vimalā*);

it is the pinnacle of the realization of all Buddhas, bordering upon ultimate reality. The seventh stage, Sublime Enlightenment (*Pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), is the ultimate Buddha-enlightenment (*bodhi*) of seeing one's true nature.
When the fruit is clearly realized as the nature of reality, it is called "Sublime Enlightenment" (*miao-jue*).

[Note] The provisional teachings regarding the stages of practice in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) and their realization of the ultimate truth are somewhat difficult to understand. First, the doctrinal intent is clarified, followed by an analysis of the characteristics of practice.

The Separate Teaching and the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) equally expound the Middle Principle (*zhongli*); for example, the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings equally expound the True Principle (*zhentili*), yet they are considered "clumsy."

Because the skillful conceal their cleverness, they are termed "contemplation of integration" (*zhèguān*); because the direct [approach] penetrates skillfulness, it is termed "contemplation of essence" (*tǐguān*). The same applies to the Separate and Complete teachings.
Although they equally expound the Middle Principle, because the teaching is clumsy, one produces sequential interpretations, thereby resulting in the Separate Teaching.

If the teaching is skillful, although there are stages of practice with varying degrees of depth, by means of the three contemplations within one mind (*sānguān yīxīn*), it is based on the inconceivable (*bùsīyì*).

Within that which lacks sequential order, the discussion of sequence naturally fulfills the meaning of perfection; it is simply that within a single principle of understanding there are levels of depth and shallowness, resulting in both the incomplete and the complete.

This is most difficult to comprehend. For example, when the two types of capacities are seated together at the Avataṃsaka assembly, the Tathāgata speaks with a single voice and the Bodhisattvas hear with a single ear;
