yet those of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jian) provide separate interpretations, while those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jian) provide a unified interpretation of the stages of dwelling, practice, and direction.

Those who hold a partial understanding also hear the teaching on the inconceivable matters of perfect interfusion—how the one contains the many and the many contain the one, and how lands as numerous as atoms mutually enter and merge with one another. Yet, although they hear of this perfect interfusion, they point it out as belonging only to the stage of fruition;
they do not realize that this very fusion at the stage of fruition is entirely the original mind’s inherent perfection from the very beginning.
Although the names of the stages are fully explained, their meanings are not yet present; thus, even though the understanding is perfectly interfused, it still results in a sequential progression.

Therefore, it is said that those at the initial stage look up with faith toward this principle, which consequently becomes the "Only-Middle" (but-madhya). This purport is profound and subtle, rarely understood by people.

Those who fail to grasp this meaning when explaining the Separate Teaching (pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana) have utterly missed its essential point. I frequently observe students discussing the Separate Teaching [in such a manner].

The Dharma is like the moon beyond the clouds; it resembles a lotus flower emerging from the water. It is rare to encounter this teaching, and as for those who receive its instruction, how can their internal realization ever become a sequential understanding?

When explained through the method of "separated and distinct" (kalāsa), the practitioners of the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha/śrāvaka) often fail to reach the insight into the reality of the universal principle found in the Shared Teaching (sambhoga).
This is truly lamentable. Even those of the Shared Teaching still perceive all phenomena [as distinct].

One immediately understands that [all things] are like illusions and transformations; since one speaks of emptiness within form itself, how could those who know this through separate teachings be so obstructed and deluded?
Therefore, it is known that what is called "expounding the same Middle Principle" takes non-bias as the meaning of the Middle and the transcendence of grasping as its function;
this is identical to the person of the Perfect Teaching in both their seat and their vision.
Fang said: "Since they share the same interpretation, we know that this person’s mind can understand the principle of perfect fusion (*yuanrong*) and their mouth can speak words of perfect fusion;
yet there is but one point of non-comprehension, such that although they are 'perfectly fused' all day long, it still results in a sequential process.

Jingxi specifically stated: "They only know the interpenetration at the level of the fruition, but do not know the fundamental nature of the principle within the capacities of sentient beings. This is what he meant.
The two phrases exhaustively clarify the purport of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao). This is because while the fruit is integrated (*rong*), the cause is not integrated;

thus, when the *xuánwén* (Profound Meaning) discusses integration and non-integration by contrasting the stages (*di*) and the directions (*xiang*), it establishes the meaning of the Separate Teaching.

Only when contrasting the abidings (*zhu*) and the faiths (*xin*) to discuss integration and non-integration does it establish the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*Yuan*). Regarding the "vertical" (*zong*) and "horizontal" (*heng*) meanings cited from ancient commentaries in the *Zhiguan*, if one relies upon...
Regarding the Dharma-gates taught by the ancients, why are those that surpass this in terms of perfection and subtlety all judged by the Great Master to be "separate" (distinct)?
It is solely because the ancient masters did not recognize the meaning of "completeness" (*ju*); though they spoke of perfection and subtlety, their explanations remained fragmented and disjointed.

That our present school has attained the essential principle is precisely due to its discourse on completeness; therefore, it excels the hundred schools of those who study the teachings. This is the core principle.

It is unclear why the Perfect and Distinct teachings are distinguished here; if one were to thoroughly understand the doctrines and meanings of the Distinct Teaching, they would be clear and unobstructed.
Next, the stages of practice (*xingwei*) are discussed. This commentary merely lists the names of the various stages without explaining the intended meaning of what is severed or subdued (*duanfu*).
The *Xuanyan* states: "Since there are such immeasurable gradations, for this reason the sutras and treatises provide their designations."
Regarding the various methods for enumerating, severing, subduing, and reconciling the higher and lower stages among the various Dharma-gates, there are many differences:
the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies forty-one stages (*bhūmi*); the *Ratnakūṭa-śiṅkhala-sūtra* clarifies fifty-two positions; the *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra* clarifies fifty-one positions;

the new *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* merely mentions the ten stages; the *Śrīmaladevī-bhadrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies fourteen patiences (*kṣānti*); and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* merely... [text ends]
It clarifies the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and *nirvāṇa*, and elucidates the five practices and ten merits (and so forth).

Furthermore, treatises such as the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* all explain the number and presence or absence of the bodhisattva stages differently; their rankings regarding the severance and suppression of afflictions also vary (and so forth).
How could one definitively assert [a single view] without extensively investigating the sūtras and śāstras? It would be like being without eyes.
Regarding the present day, if one wishes to clarify the numerical positions, one must rely on the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò) and the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi-sūtra* (Rénwáng);

if one wishes to clarify the hierarchy of severance and subduing, one must rely on the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dàpǐn); and if one is to correlate these with the gates of the Dharma, one must rely on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

By employing the intent of these various sutras together, the two gates of the teaching and the contemplation for the beginner are made clear. (As stated above... This is explained in detail as found in the *Xuánwén*.

Regarding the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), this should be discussed in conjunction with the nature of cultivation (*bhāvanā-svabhāva*), whether vertical or horizontal, the study of the perfect cultivation (*pūrṇa-bhāvanā*), the emergence from the provisional (*niryāṇa-kuśala*), and so forth;

these are not elaborated here as the intent of the teaching is such that if one clarifies these various meanings, they will be easily understood. 2. The Sequence of Innate Nature (*prakṛti*) and Habitual Tendencies (*vāsanā*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the two natures—the innate (*prakṛti*) and the cultivated (*bhāvanā*)—if distinguished according to their stages, the cultivated seeds precede and the innate seeds follow.

However, if discussed according to their activity, the innate and cultivated natures are simultaneous; thus, their sequence is not fixed. When arising from the essence to manifest function, the innate seeds are explained first and the cultivated seeds second.

Conversely, when seeking the essence by means of its function, the cultivated comes first and the innate second. This corresponds to the two paths of scriptural teaching (*āgama-mārga*) and realization (*adhigama-mārga*).

If discussed according to their positions, the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*) comes first and the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*) comes later; if discussed according to practice, realization and teaching are simultaneous, and their sequence is not fixed.
If one proceeds from essence to function, realization comes first and teaching later; if one seeks the essence through its function, teaching comes first and realization later.
Within the context of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*), there are further four types: first, understanding and practice; second, the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).

The third is dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and the fourth is the lineage of the path (*mārgajātīya*). Because one understands the supramundane path and exerts oneself in its practice, it is called "conduct through understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*).

Because one generates the aspiration for great enlightenment and seeks it, it is called "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*). Because one directs the wholesome dharmas already employed toward enlightenment, it is called "dedication.

Since these are established according to the stages of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), they are termed "the lineage of the path" (*mārgajātīya*). This is in anticipation of [the subsequent stages].

The subsequent fruit of Buddhahood is called the "seed" because it is capable of producing [the result]. The nature of the practice-seed (*śikṣā-bīja*) is capable of producing the *saṃbhoga-kāya* Buddha, and the nature of the essence-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) is capable of producing the *dharma-kāya* Buddha.

[Note: Regarding the distinct stages elucidated in conventional teachings, there is rarely discussion of this; as for its essence and function, the scriptural evidence does not establish that they are simultaneous.

Regarding this meaning, since it has been clarified herein that the two natures—innate (*prakṛti*) and acquired (*vāsanā*)—are not necessarily simultaneous, there is this example. The general purport is as follows:

from the perspective of stages and positions (*pada*), one discusses them in terms of sequence; from the perspective of those who have attained the essential meaning, one distinguishes them as simultaneous;

and based on the manifestation of the acquired nature, one argues they are not fixed. This is evident in the text. Regarding the two paths—the path of teaching (*āgama*) and the path of realization (*adhigama*)—the commentators of old have spoken extensively.

Most do not say that the beginning and end of the single teaching are explained as the "teaching path" (jiaodao), while the exposition of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) is explained as the "realization path" (zhendao).
Regarding this realization path, some explain it as sequential (gelie) and others as perfectly integrated (yuanrong);

thus, conflicting theories have long been prevalent, and even the former masters were collectively confused about this meaning. Now, by examining the specific intent of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), one sees [the truth].

The two paths of teaching and realization, along with their fruits, have a definitive point of reference. Regarding what has been explained previously: first, there was the fault of delimiting stages without merit; second, there was the fault of stages belonging to two categories.

Now, I shall briefly distinguish the stages of the teachings through four methods so that no confusion arises. One should take the stage prior to the *bhūmis* (the *pṛthagjana* stage) as the scope for the path of teaching (*śikṣā-mārga*), and the entry into the *bhūmis* as the scope for the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*).

As for the ten *bhūmis*: [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Buddhist stages (likely related to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* or similar treatises). The translation reflects the technical terminology of the original.*
To speak briefly, the "wondrous enlightenment" (*miao-jue*) refers to the path of teaching (*jiao-dao*), whereas the "realization" (*zheng*) refers to the path of realization (*zheng-dao*).

When various scriptures explain the practices of both teaching and realization, they clearly point toward them so that people have no cause for doubt; yet, regarding these explanations of teaching and realization, most people are confused. This is entirely due to their failure to understand what is meant by "speaking briefly.
One must not refer to the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma as "speaking briefly"; rather, it should be understood as referring to the existence of the teachings.
No one has vainly proposed this interpretation, claiming it is a "conventional explanation" (*yōsetsu*) of names and meanings;

rather, it is precisely for those prior to the [first] stage that the beginning and end of the ten stages are explained as the "path of teaching" (*kyōdō*), not as the beginning and end of a single teaching.

Were one to treat it as the beginning and end of a single teaching, the fault would immediately arise that each stage would belong to two categories simultaneously. This "conventional explanation" of the path of realization (*shōdō*) points toward the state of *myōkaku* (wondrous enlightenment).

Since it has already been stated that if one speaks of the dharmas realized at the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), then according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), for which person could one point to as having realized the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*)—is it present or absent?
Setting this aside as not to be discussed, one should instead point to the Sublime Enlightenment (*miaojué*) as the person who has realized them.
Furthermore, since it says "the dharma obtained at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), we know that this refers specifically to the Sublime Enlightenment.
The exposition of the path of realization is clear; yet because past masters failed to investigate it thoroughly, it has resulted in erroneous transmissions.
I urge diligent students to examine this in detail, for only then will they see that what I have now stated accords with the Patriarchs and leaves no room for doubt.
This is merely a brief indication; in my *Fuzong ji* (Collection on Restoring the School), there are chapters on the meaning that extensively cite scriptural treatises.
The commentary and sub-commentary clarify that this interpretation is extremely appropriate. ○ Third, the explanation of the regressive mind in the sixth stage. [Commentary]:
Formerly it was said that Prince Dharmatā regressed from the sixth mind; however, this refers to the sixth mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). An objection is raised:

if a person has planted deep roots in the past, or encounters a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), or hears the wondrous principle in its entirety from a scripture—that all dharmas are one dharma, that one dharma is all dharmas, and that they are neither one nor all—this inconceivable [truth] gives rise to perfect faith and understanding, believing within the single mind.

Possessing the ten dharma-realms within a single minute speck of dust, there exists a great thousand-fold scripture; desiring to open this mind, one cultivates the perfect practice (*pariṇata-caryā*).
The perfect practitioner practices all deeds through a single deed, which, briefly stated, consists of ten aspects:

namely, recognizing that a single thought-moment is equally endowed with inconceivable qualities; grieving over one’s own mental dullness and extending compassion to all beings; and further knowing this very mind.
Constantly quiescent and constantly illuminating, one employs this mind of quiescence and illumination to shatter all phenomena as being simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle.
Furthermore, one recognizes that within the One Mind, all minds—whether unimpeded or obstructed—are fully endowed with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) upon the path toward Bodhi.
Moreover, one understands the primary and auxiliary methods of this mind, and recognizes both one’s own mind and the minds of ordinary beings and sages, thereby abiding in peace.
The mind is unmoving, does not fall away, does not regress, and does not disperse; although it perceives the immeasurable merits of the one mind, it gives rise to no defiled attachment.
When these ten minds are accomplished, every thought-moment of that mind is in perfect correspondence with all the pāramitās.

Second, as for recitation: when the initial arising of perfect faith is nurtured and sustained, it allows the sprout of the Way to emerge even amidst the distractions of involvement with worldly affairs.

Third, regarding the teacher: when internal contemplation grows strong and external resources further augment it, perfect understanding dwells within the breast, and one propagates [the Dharma].

Although the objective phenomena are few, the movement of the intention is vast. Taking this contemplation as primary and the practice of deeds as secondary—this is called practicing the six perfections concurrently.

II. The Inner Worldlings.

The first stage of the inner ordinary person consists of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Through perfect hearing and perfect faith, one cultivates perfect practice (*caryā*), which is skillfully augmented fivefold and thereby becomes profoundly clear.
By virtue of this perfect practice, one enters the perfect stages (*avasthā*). Cultivating the equality of the *dharmadhātu* well, one enters the stage of faith (*śraddhā-citta*);
cultivating compassion well, one enters the stage of mindfulness (*smṛti-citta*); and cultivating tranquil illumination well, one enters the stage of progress (*vīrya-citta*).
Cultivating the destruction of dharmas is entry into the mind of wisdom; skillfully cultivating penetration and obstruction is entry into the mind of concentration;
skillfully cultivating the factors of the path is entry into the mind of non-retrogression; skillfully cultivating the primary and auxiliary practices is entry into the mind of dedication;

skillfully cultivating the mundane and the sacred is entry into the mind of protecting the Dharma; skillfully cultivating immovability is entry into the mind of precepts; skillfully cultivating non-attachment is entry into the mind of vows.

The mind is what is called the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Iron Wheel in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); it is the semblance-understanding (*sijie*) of the Perfect Teaching wherein the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are purified.

The seventh stage, the stage of Sublime Enlightenment, is the ultimate liberation and the unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom; therefore, it is said that there is nothing further to be severed.

This is called the Unsurpassed Being (*anuttarapuruṣa*); it is precisely the Great Nirvāṇa of the ultimate final mind, wherein the three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor distinct.

It is the Great Principle, the Great Vow, the Great Adornment, the Great Wisdom-Abandonment, the Great Universal Knowledge, the Great Path, the Great Function, the Great Expedient Means and Reality, the Great Benefit, and the Great Non-abiding—these are the ten.

One should know that the essence of the precepts (śīla-svabhāva) pervades both matter and mind. This is because, upon receiving the precepts, one receives and maintains them through the three karmas;

When this essence arises, there must be that which causes it to arise and that which is caused to arise: the mind is that which causes it to arise, and matter is that which is caused to arise. This is because the dharma of the precepts is received [through the three karmas].
At the time of receiving [the precepts], if the mind is not distracted, the body is uplifted and diligent, and the mouth provides responses;

Thus we know that if one lacks a sense of reverent diligence, one cannot receive the precepts within the mind. From the perspective of the act of receiving, the precepts are the agent of reception and the mind is the object of reception.
If one proceeds from the perspective of the meaning of "arousing," the mind that initiates [the vow] is the arouser and the precept is that which is aroused.
This aroused precept is a type of noble dharma and wholesome karma; this wholesome karma is unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and can be seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
It is no different in its essential substance from the karma of the Śrāvaka precepts, yet it is distinguished by being defined and measured within the perfect and ultimate teachings of the Mahāyāna.

The distinctions within the Hīnayāna apply to both [precepts and concentration]. From the perspective of that which initiates them, they belong to the mind; from the perspective of that which is initiated, they belong to form.
The *Sub-commentary on the Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* (Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue) takes the mind as their essence, speaking from the perspective of that which initiates them.

The *Commentary on the Vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* takes form as their essence, speaking from the perspective of that which is initiated. Thus we know that without the mind there would be nothing to initiate them, and without form there would be nothing to manifest them.
Therefore, various texts speak of this either from the perspective of the mind or from the perspective of form; such is the reason why these texts are not in vain.
This form and this mind both pertain to the substance itself and both pertain to phenomena.

Their arising and their ceasing, their presence in the teaching and their reliance on skillful means, all result from the three masters receiving, practicing, maintaining with diligence, and restraining themselves, thereby attaining this precept.

Regarding the statement that "the matter derived from grasping (upātta-rūpa) is of the same nature as being induced and also arises, yet it is specifically said that it does not arise," this remark is merely intended to caution against the possibility that the three karmas might not be diligent and thus fail to trigger the arousal of this precept.

Because it is the color of precepts, it is said that they simply do not arise; this is like being without mind. Yet, as soon as there is even a momentary thought, the three thousand [dharmas] are fully present.

It is lamentable indeed that for so long past, various masters have failed to see this meaning, allowing it to remain buried in obscurity.

Regarding the statements that "the principle is not appropriate" and "the teaching is not appropriate," or that "the teaching is appropriate" and "the principle is not appropriate"—since both assertions have scriptural evidence, one must judge between them after careful consideration.

"From the perspective of *upāya* (expedient means), one relies on the teachings to discuss non-action; from the perspective of reality (*tattva*), one relies on principle.

I ask students to seek this through the meaning; the principle is indeed thus. It is simply like, for instance, when one arouses the thought of desire...
For one who receives the precepts, although this mind may be reverent and diligent, it must rely upon the performance of body and speech to give rise to that mind.
If such a mind is unreasonable or does not accord with one's nature, then the actions performed will all be deluded practices rather than practices of the nature-virtue (*xingde*).
Now, the Mahāyāna observance of the precepts—ceasing evil and practicing good—is entirely conducted in reliance upon the nature; only such practice is [true].
The practice of the nature-virtues is precisely the mind of upholding the precepts arising entirely from the nature;

since the nature is fundamentally without action, even if one upholds the precepts all day long, there is no appearance of "upholding" in that which is upheld. Because the mind capable of generating [the precepts] follows the aspect of illuminating principle, the self-centered mind is naturally empty.
Thus, neither sin nor merit has a master; there is neither a person who can uphold, nor is there anything to be upheld.
Regarding these precepts, what characteristic of "form" (rūpa) exists such that one could speak of the dharma of non-action (avijñapti)?

Therefore, it is clear that when one illuminates the principle upon which they rely, there is no such thing as non-action. However, when it comes to the time of illuminating phenomena, what prevents one from using this mind capable of arousal to maintain the precepts one has received?
Let every precept be without flaw and not transgressed even by a hair’s breadth; thus, one spontaneously maintains goodness.
Because non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) manifests when one ceases evil, it is said that within the gate of teaching there is non-informative matter.
Thus, the commentary states that there is non-informative matter, citing the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*:

"It is like having a face and a mirror, whereupon a reflection arises. The mirror is a metaphor for the fundamental nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which is originally without non-informative matter; the reflection is a metaphor for the provisional form (*rūpa*) of non-informative matter.
There is an unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma) that serves as a metaphor for the mind capable of generating [virtue];

because one establishes sublime conduct through the mind’s accord with principle, the unconditioned dharma of the color-form of precepts (śīla-rūpa) is thereby accomplished. Seeking this through metaphor, the principle is very clear;

thus we know that the essence of the precepts (śīla-tattva) pervades both form and mind. As a sutra says: "All Mahāyāna precepts take the mind as their essence," following from the capacity [of the mind].
Speaking from the perspective of its manifestation, it is said that the precepts are an aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Speaking from the perspective of what gives rise to them, both the producer and the produced are the substance itself, as they exist within phenomena; because they arise based on the principle of reality (*dharmatā*), one points to that principle as their basis.
This has been explained in detail as previously argued. By synthesizing these points in this manner, one will see how the commentary addresses the views of the ancients.

The textual principles of these two schools have their respective foundations; yet, as seen in various commentaries (*chao*), they do not clarify the essence [of the text], and their words do not reach this point.

However, the phrasing of this commentary is峻 (jùn—stern/severe) and its meaning is hidden, making it truly difficult to interpret and synthesize. Let the reader examine this in detail. ○ Second, that which is currently employed.
[Commentary] What is employed here consists of both the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
[Note] Having observed that past disputes were based on one-sided perspectives, and being unaware of what is appropriate or inappropriate, we shall now discuss both principle and teaching.
While there is nothing in terms of ultimate principle, the gates of teaching do exist. Now, following the established precepts, we desire to prevent transgressions and cease evil.

When a person advances in their practice, they summarize the matters and summarize the cultivation; they establish conduct based on provisional means and provisional teachings, and establish the Dharma.

It is precisely in discussing "non-action" (*anabhisamskāra*) that the true essence of this school is clarified: it takes the "unmanifested form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*) produced by non-action as its substance. Question:
If this is so, regarding the two previous masters, do they discard the "non-existence of non-action" and adopt the "existence of non-action"? Answer: No.

However, when we examine the two preceding masters each of whom grasped one meaning, they both fall into partial error: the first claims there is no error in the teaching while failing to grasp the principle;
the second claims there is error in the principle while grasping the teaching. Although there is now the "non-arising dharma," one does not discard the principle upon which it relies;
since the principle is fundamentally non-existent, the present claim of "non-existence" regarding the non-arising dharma does not abandon [that principle].
The teaching on practice must rely upon form; to examine this meaning in detail is precisely the non-dual nature of cultivation, which avoids the partial errors of the two masters.
○ Second, the concentration of the Path is non-action.
[Commentary] Next, it is clarified that the concentrations of the Path all take non-action as their essence; within the state of meditative concentration, they give rise to non-action.

Regarding the statement that "the unmanifest (avijñapti) produced within the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga) is called 'concomitant with the path' because it arises together with the superior path of the mind," the masters of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* explain that this does not necessarily mean the unmanifest produced in the path of seeing is the "path-concomitant precept" (*mārgānvaya-śīla*). Rather,
they maintain that one should simply take the unmanifest produced within the mind of the Middle Way’s correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) as that which possesses the power of restraint.

It is not merely in the sense of ceasing evil that it is called "concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahabhū*). As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "First is the precept of the True Dharma; second is the precept received through worldly instruction.
When a Bodhisattva attains the precept of the True Dharma, this refers to the precept concomitant with the Path. One who attains this precept never commits evil;
because it is not obtained through formal transmission from a teacher, it is called "attained. This precept is generated and attained within the mind of the Middle Way. [One] receives the worldly...

The "instructional precepts" (*śikṣāpada*) refer to those obtained after the *jñapticaturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of one motion and three proclamations); because they necessarily rely upon a teacher, they are called "receiving.

They are termed "worldly instruction" (*laukika-śāsana*) because they are distinguished by being demonstrated [to others]. Regarding the "precepts co-arising with meditative concentration" (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*), they are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;

however, according to the Mahāyāna path, meditative concentration is subsumed within the "precept for gathering wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). Some teachers state that only when entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samādhi*) can one give rise to the "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) [precept].

The meditative concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) that is not fixed does not give rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*); only the provisional understanding of emptiness can give rise to non-informative action.

Although there are words [to the contrary], they merely mean that once this concentration and path are realized, one is able to suppress coarse categories [of afflictions] according to one's capacity, and upon their accomplishment, non-informative action arises.
Prior to the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) of the desire realm concentration, all are capable of giving rise to the precepts (*śīla*).

[Note]: Regarding "concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahagata*) and "concomitant with meditative concentration" (*samādhi-sahagata*): if one were to claim that these non-informative acts (*avijñapti*) exist only upon attaining meditative concentration and the Path at the moment of entry, this would be excessively profound.
Therefore, following the Master of *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, we take it that these non-informative acts arise within the mind of right contemplation of the Middle Way;

thus they are called "concomitant with the Path. Since this is the case for "concomitant with the Path," "concomitant with meditative concentration" simply refers to the mind entering concentration being conjoined with the precepts.
In the *Fada* (Introduction), it says: "Regarding the two precepts in the Great Sūtra, the True Dharma is the Path-concentration (*mārga-samādhi*), while the worldly teaching is the Vinaya-restraint.
The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) quotes this, stating: "The precept of the True Dharma applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the three aggregates of morality, concentration, and wisdom;

the 'Path-concentration' belongs to the precept of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-śīla*). Although these words of the Master contain no explicit rejection or selection, their intent is explained in the subsequent commentary.
This is correct. ○ Second, explaining the rise and fall [of the precepts].
[Commentary]: Next, regarding the discussion of rise and fall: first, if one seeks to receive the essence of the bodhisattva vows through skillful means, its substance arises;
if one abandons the vow for enlightenment or commits the ten grave offenses due to predominant afflictions, its substance falls away. If [these conditions] are absent...

These two conditions are abandoned only upon attaining Buddhahood; the two precepts of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*) take the attainment of concentration and the attainment of the Path as their causes.

In the first moment, concentration and the Path have not yet been conjoined with the precepts. With the preceding mind serving as the cause, it is only in the second moment that the mind is conjoined with the precepts;
at that time, one emerges from concentration and the Path. At the very last moment, the two [conditions] are then abandoned. Thus ends the explanation of the two terms.

When entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or the Path, the precepts arise together with the mind; this is called their "arising. When emerging from absorption or the Path, the precepts perish together with the mind;

this is called their "cessation. Therefore, they are termed "precepts that arise together with the mind" (*cittānuparivartin*). Once they have been initiated, they are constantly present during both entry and emergence.
Subsequently, when one enters a superior absorption or a superior Path, they follow along with that superior restraint (*saṃvara*); thus, at those times, they are said to be constantly present.

When the three collections—the arising, the withdrawal from meditative concentration, and the withdrawal from the path—are exhausted for one who has attained the bodhisattva stage for the duration of their life, at that time, the practices of gathering virtue and gathering sentient beings are abandoned;
they are identical to the ritual vows (*vinaya*), being activated upon receiving them and abandoned when those two conditions cease.

[Note] First, regarding the restraint (*saṃvara*), it is distinguished from the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*); subsequently, regarding the two aggregates (*rāśi-dvaya*), it is distinguished from the restraint itself.
Restraint prevents and governs the body and speech: when it is practiced, it arises; when it is transgressed, it is abandoned.

If these two conditions do not exist, they are spontaneously abandoned upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood. This is because ultimate quiescence leaves no dust to be cleansed, and the original nature returns to its source.

The underlying meaning should be stated as follows: the refutation of the three schools' doctrines is established by first summarizing the three minds, secondly summarizing the entry and exit, and thirdly summarizing cause and effect;
this is evident in the text. [Section on] the Second and Third Aggregates (skandhas).

[Commentary] Next, regarding the essence of the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*): *Vinaya* (discipline) refers to the methods, rules, and regulations that lead the practitioner into the Path.

It is also said that "vinaya" means "to level" (*lè*). Just as a worldly horse-race track (*mà-luò*) levels and straightens a horse, so too does vinaya level and straighten the practitioner, preventing them from committing evil.
The Bodhisattva’s vow of mind does not go beyond the cessation of evil and the promotion of good.
If one is good and does not move body or speech, this is the cessation of evil and the arousal of the precepts; to prevent movement and remain unmoving is the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precept).
If it is appropriate to move body or speech, this is the promotion of goodness and the arousal of these precepts;

to prevent non-movement while encompassing goodness and benefiting sentient beings is what is meant by "appropriate movement. Because such activity involves worldly affairs, it is opened up into two categories to encourage and exert oneself in all that is wholesome.

Based on the gateway of the six perfections, it is called "gathering wholesome dharmas" (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*); based on the gateway of the four great vows, it is called "gathering sentient beings" (*sattvaparigraha-śīla*), which is for the sake of others.
Thus, while practicing the myriad virtues to transform sentient beings below, one also aspires to the fruit of Buddhahood above.

Since the *prātimokṣa* discipline primarily governs internal virtue, gathering sentient beings constitutes external transformation, and gathering wholesome dharmas encompasses both the internal and external; therefore, these [three types of precepts] are established.

The Threefold Pure Precepts (Tri-śikṣā-saṃvara). [Note] This passage consists of two sections: first, an explanation based on movement and stillness; second, an explanation based on the internal and external.

Within the section on movement and stillness, the term *vinaya* (律儀) is first explained. *Lü* (埒) is pronounced *lüe*. A *lüe* is a boundary fence that encloses a path; one trains horses between two such fences.
To act without stumbling or leaping is the meaning of restraint: the discipline (*vinaya*) that governs body and speech so as not to commit various non-virtues is precisely the cessation of evil.
This "non-movement" constitutes the observance of the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*); movement therein constitutes a transgression of the precepts.

As for the gathering of virtues and the gathering of sentient beings, one should move through the three karmas; this is precisely the practice of goodness. To personally engage in the practice of the six perfections is the dharma of goodness.

The precept of benefiting others consists of giving rise to the intention to rescue sentient beings; this is the precept for gathering living beings. These two [precepts] should be active, for when they are active, there is benefit;
those who do not act are said to be transgressing the precepts. Next, regarding the internal and external explanation of the *vinaya* (discipline):

internally examining oneself is the gathering of living beings, while externally transforming others is the gathering of others. Gathering wholesome qualities encompasses both the internal and external. Such is the nature of the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*). Therefore...

By explaining it through the two meanings of movement and stillness, as well as internal and external, the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla*) become manifest. △ Second, clarifying stillness and practice, which is further divided into two parts.
○ First, explaining the two names. [Commentary]:

Next, we discuss the two virtues of stillness (*śamatha*) and practice (*vipaśyanā*). As stated in the *Śata-śāstra*, ceasing evil and not committing it is termed "stillness" (*śamatha*), while having faith...
The practice of receiving and cultivating [the teachings] is called "conduct" (*caryā*). Although the Buddha's teachings are numerous, they are all subsumed within conduct:
"Commit no evil" is the gate of prohibition, while "Practice all that is good" is the gate of exhortation.
[Note] To reprimand them, they cease; to exhort them, they act. What evil words are there that do not cause them to desist? What virtuous words are there that do not cause them to practice?
Through these two gates of reprimand and exhortation, the two virtues are fully realized. △ Second, the analysis of non-action (avijñapti), which is further divided into two parts.
○ First, the heading and enumeration.

[Commentary] The meaning of "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome; the meaning of the unmanifest of both the wholesome and the unwholesome generally refers to the cessation and the performance [of action].
△ Second, the explanation of their characteristics has two parts: first, the wholesome precepts; second, the unwholesome precepts. Regarding the first, there are three sections.
First, the explanation based on the two types of wholesome [precepts], which has two parts. ○ First, the two wholesome [precepts] of restraint (*saṃvara*).

Now, first, let us clarify that wholesome non-arising precepts consist simply in not giving rise [to unwholesome states]; once they have arisen, they eliminate evil, which is all the meaning of *śamatha* (cessation).
All possess the quality of progress, which is the meaning of *bhāvanā* (cultivation). The distinction between cessation and cultivation exists because they follow the strength [of the mind]:

following the arising of the mind to cease evil through non-action is the cessation of evil; following the arising of the mind to cultivate good through non-action is the cultivation of good. As it is said:

Constructing wells and bridges, making offerings to the Buddha, and practicing charity constitute non-informative action (avijñapti) that is wholesome; conversely, constructing nets for fishing and hunting constitutes non-informative action that is unwholesome. [Note:

Both wholesome and unwholesome actions, whether they are abstentions or performances, give rise to non-informative action. First, regarding wholesome non-informative action, it arises from acts such as constructing wells and bridges.

Because the discourse follows from that [previous point], it responds by discussing how non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) is like fishing or hunting as examples of evil, whereas virtuous precepts are designated as restraint (*saṃvara*).
○ Second, the two virtues of the concentration of the path (*mārga-samādhi*).

[Commentary]: Next, regarding the discussion of the two types of non-manifestation within the concentration of the path—those involving activity and those involving cessation—the meaning of the two precepts of the concentration of the path is determined as follows:

Regarding the doctrinal classification of the two mental states of the path of cessation (*śamatha*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*): non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) arises from the cessation of discursive thought (*vitarka*) through causal conditions;

because it ceases by relying on cessation, the non-manifest action that subsequently arises is called "wholesome through cessation" (*śamathakuśala*). Wholesome action that arises after the cessation of activity through causal conditions is named "wholesome through activity" (*pragrahakuśala*).

Furthermore, the gate of admonition (*vinītakāraṇa*) belongs to wholesome through cessation, while the gate of encouragement (*samuttejanakāraṇa*) entirely pertains to wholesome through activity. Moreover, some explain that activity consists solely of manifest action (*vijñapti*).
It is said that "stopping" (śamatha) alone constitutes non-manifest action (*avijñapti*); yet it is also stated that both the virtues of stopping and practicing possess non-manifest action.

[Note: "Precept" (*śīla*) is named for its function of restraining; "stopping" is named for the virtue of the mind ceasing [evil]; "practicing" is named for the virtue of the mind initiating wholesome karma.
These five explanations preserved in the text are all clearly evident in their meaning. II. Explanation according to the Three Vehicles.
[Commentary: The precepts of the seven classes of Śrāvakas all constitute the essence of the restraint of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*), yet they merely cease the two evils of body and speech.
The Bodhisattva restraint, however, fully guards the three karmas. Furthermore, extending this up to the Buddha, there are differences in length, brevity, breadth, and narrowness.

Regarding the meaning of non-informative action (*avijñapti*): it arises from conditions and a superior mind; an inferior [mind] does not produce it, and an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind, being deficient, does not produce it.

Just as the afflictions of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in the desire realm consist of nine grades— whereby the first six grades give rise to non-informative action (avijñapti) while the final three do not—
it is said that the Sakṛdāgāmin emerges from non-informative informative action (vijñapti), the Anāgāmin emerges from unwholesome (akuśala) informative action,
and the Arhat emerges from neutral (avyākṛta) informative action.
[Note] Regarding the "seven assemblies": the five assemblies of those who have left the household life (*pravrajita*) are the bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, and śrāmaṇerī;
the two assemblies of those remaining in the household life (*gṛhastha*) are the upāsaka and upāsikā. *Śikṣamāṇā* means "female student of the Dharma";
having already received the ten precepts, she ranks above the *śrāmaṇera*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the Buddha was..."
At one time in the world, there was the wife of a householder who, unaware that she was pregnant, went forth and received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Subsequently, her body became large, and the other householders criticized and disparaged her. Because of this, the Bhikṣuṇīs established a rule:

for two years one must undergo training in the precepts and receive the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*), after which one may receive full ordination. There are two types of these six rules: the first is for a girl of eighteen years to receive them.

Regarding the six dharmas: the householders receive the six precepts, which are: sexual misconduct with a defiled mind, touching [with lust], stealing less than five *kārsāpaṇa*, taking the life of an animal, false speech, and eating at improper times or drinking alcohol.
The followers of the Two Vehicles merely restrain body and speech, whereas Bodhisattvas fully guard the three karmas.
[The former] is short because it seeks only rebirth as a human or deva; [the latter] is long because it aims for the fruit of Buddhahood. These define the ten realms.

Therefore, it is broad in relation to the six ordinary realms and narrow in relation to the True Middle (zhēnzhōng), where length and shortness are further distinguished. ○ Third, the explanation by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
[Commentary]:
Good and evil non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) are discussed in relation to the mind, each having four propositions. Regarding the four propositions of good, the first is:
1. That which is precept (*śīla*) but not non-manifest action (*avijñapti*): this refers to the mind that ceases evil; because it can stop [evil], it is called "precept. 2.

That which is non-manifest action but not precept: this refers to such things as digging wells or building bridges; although there is non-manifest action according to the specific act and its subsequent use, it cannot stop evil, and thus it is not precept.
3. That which is both precept and non-manifest action: this refers to wholesome restraints (*kuśala-saṃvara*) and the like. 4. That which is neither precept nor non-manifest action.

The "agent" refers to other wholesome states of mind. Regarding the four permutations concerning the unwholesome: first, that which is a precept but not non-informative action (*avijñapti*), namely the cessation of a wholesome mind;
second, that which is non-informative action but not a precept, namely the non-informative action arising from acts such as killing or stealing according to their application;

third, that which is both a precept and non-informative action, namely the unwholesome vows (*akuśala-saṃvara*) and so forth; fourth, that which is neither a precept nor non-informative action, namely the remainder.
This refers to an evil mind.
[Note] Although acts such as digging a well possess the non-informative (avijñapti) merit of following utility, they cannot arrest the evils of the three karmas;
therefore, it is said that "non-precepts" are not [merely] evil. These four propositions regarding evil arise according to the circumstances. ○ Second, the non-precept (duḥśīla).
[Commentary] There are two kinds of unwholesome precepts: first, the sixteen types of evil *vinaya* (non-restraint); second, the heterodox and false precepts of non-Buddhists.
Regarding the evil *vinaya* of non-Buddhists, as stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, there are ninety-five kinds, each with its own system of precepts.

Some take ascetic practices as their precepts, such as tending to cattle and horses, worshipping fire, wearing feathers, constantly standing on one leg, leaping into fire, or throwing oneself from cliffs.
This constitutes precept-breaking; that is, any movement of the mind, whether long or short, is all unwholesome precepting. [Note:
In other transcribed records, it is claimed that these four phrases are derived from the "four phrases of evil," but this is incorrect.
In the preceding text of the *Shu* (Commentary), it says: "Now, first clarify that wholesome precepts merely consist in non-arising. This refers precisely to the present section.
This clarifies the precepts against evil conduct. Regarding the sixteen types of evil, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (Dà jīng), fascicle 29, states:

1. For the sake of profit, fattening lambs by feeding them grain and then selling them; 2. For the sake of profit, slaughtering them oneself; 3. and 4. [The same applies to] pigs and hogs; 5. and 6. [the same applies to] oxen and calves;

7. and 8. [the same applies to] raising chickens (*note: 3, 5, and 7 follow the first phrase regarding selling; 4, 6, and 8 follow the second phrase regarding slaughtering*). 9. Fishing with hooks; 10. ... [and so forth].
1. Hunters; 2. Robbers; 3. Executioners; 4. Fishermen; 5. Those who engage in double-tongued speech; 6. Jailers; 7.
Those who curse dragons—those who can forever sever these sixteen kinds of evil for the sake of sentient beings are said to be practicing the precepts (*sīla*).
Regarding the heterodox and false precepts of external paths, such as worshipping fire or throwing oneself from cliffs, these are like the case of Aṅgulimāla.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Do you wish to hear about the causes for the establishment of non-Buddhist paths in the world?
I shall explain it for you. Long ago, in a past age during the time of the Buddha Kuṇḍadhāna, there was a bhikṣu named Buddhajñāna.
A certain virtuous person offered him a priceless robe, which the bhikṣu accepted and showed to some hunters. When the hunters saw it, they conceived the intent to rob and steal it."
That very night, the mind [of the king] led that bhikṣu into the deep mountains, where he mutilated his body, stripped him naked, and hung him by his hands from a tree.
At that time, a flower-gathering brāhmaṇa arrived at the mountain and saw the bhikṣu with his body mutilated, naked, and hanging by his hands from a tree;
he cried out in astonishment, "Alas! This śramaṇa formerly wore the kashaya robe, yet now he is naked."
He must have believed that the *kāṣāya* robe was not the cause for liberation, and that by voluntarily undertaking asceticism he was truly practicing the Way.
How could such a person ever abandon wholesome dharmas? Because he corrupted the True Dharma, he discarded his robes and plucked out his hair, becoming a naked ascetic (*nagna-śramaṇa*).
It was from this that nakedness originated. At that time, the bhikṣu, having attained liberation from his bonds, took tree bark [for clothing].
He coats himself with red ochre to conceal his person and fashions a broom from grass to sweep away mosquitoes and gnats.
When a Brahmin who was gathering flowers saw him, he thought to himself: "This bhikṣu has discarded fine, beautiful robes to wear such garments and carry such a broom.
Could this man ever abandon the wholesome Dharma? It is clear that he is one who has attained liberation."
The Way consists in studying those dharmas; thus did the brahmin who had gone forth emerge from that state.

At that time, a bhikṣu entered the water in the evening to bathe; while washing his head, he had a sore, so he took some water-weeds to cover the sore and took a discarded, worn-out garment left by a cowherd to clothe himself.
A woodcutter saw this and thought to himself: "He must surely know the *kāṣāya*."
Since the *saṃghāṭī* robe is not the cause of liberation, he wore tattered rags and let his hair grow, bathing three times every day and night to practice asceticism.
Eventually, a monk developed a sore on his body; he then lit a fire to cauterize the sore, which only increased its pain.
He even went so far as to throw himself from a cliff to take his own life. Those who witnessed this thought to themselves: "This monk formerly wore fine robes, yet now..."
In this way, how could that person ever abandon wholesome dharmas? One should know that throwing oneself from a cliff is the path to liberation;
the practices of throwing oneself from cliffs and entering fire originated from this. Thus, all ninety-six types [of heterodox paths] arose because of this bhikṣu.
(From the *Sūtra Text*)—The commentator [Daoxuan] considers the account of Sudhana throwing himself from a cliff in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to be incorrect; for in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is the fifth...
The correct practice taught by the thirteen spiritual friends cannot be equated with the methods of the non-Buddhists; how can there be such a great error?
One should apply the account from the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* regarding the act of throwing oneself off a cliff as being precisely the very root of the non-Buddhist path.
△ Third, the threefold selection (*viniścaya*) is further divided into two. ○ First, the heading and enumeration.
【Commentary】 The third section on selection is further divided into three: 1. the necessity of faith; 2. the absence of the three obstructions (*āvaraṇa*);
3. persons and dharmas as conditions.
△ Second, the explanation, which further has three parts. First, the necessity of faith. This further has two parts; first, the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) and the three types of faith.

Regarding "faith," based on the gateway of the Three Baskets, three kinds are briefly enumerated: first, faith that cause and effect are such that good and evil inevitably bring their respective retributions;

second, faith that by contemplating the Truths one attains the Path; third, faith that there is the Precepts, which are the initial gateway for entering the Path through the contemplation of the Truths.
II. Three Faiths of the Vaipulya:
Because one relies on the Vaipulya precepts, one should be prepared with these three faiths, further augmented by three types:

first, the faith that the mind-consciousness of both self and others all possesses Buddha-nature; second, the faith that diligent practice of superior goodness will necessarily result in the attainment of the fruit; third, the faith in that which is attained.
The fruit is permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
[Note] To believe in cause and effect is wisdom; to believe in contemplating the truths is concentration; to believe in the existence of precepts is morality.

This refers to first using wisdom to thoroughly understand the truths, thereby being able to believe in concentration, and subsequently upholding the precepts; or alternatively, following the sequence of first morality, then concentration, and finally wisdom.
The *Śāsanānuśāsanī-sūtra* states: "By relying on this precept, one attains all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.

If one maintains [the precept] such that it gives rise to stillness, then stability constitutes the beginning; this is also according to what is appropriate, and the Vaipulya [sūtras] may be understood accordingly.
II. The Absence of the Three Obstructions, in three parts: First, the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

[Commentary]: Next, regarding "there being no three obstructions": sentient beings have three kinds of obstructions; because afflictions (*kleśa*) are ever-present, they are not explicitly termed "obstructions. [Note]:

This [Name], a Bodhisattva, desires to request and receive the Bodhisattva precepts from the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Sangha.
This [Name] is already a true Bodhisattva; he has already made the vow for Bodhicitta and is capable of generating profound faith."
"I am able to relinquish all that I possess and do not begrudge even my own body or life;
I only pray that the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Saṃgha, out of compassion, will bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon me, [Name] (recite this three times)."
V. Bestowing the Precepts.
Next, ask the candidate for ordination: "Listen, [Name], to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Saṃgha.

You shall receive the Bodhisattva’s code of discipline (*vinaya-śīla*), the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*). These are [the precepts] of the past, future, and present..."

"Regarding the precepts in which all Bodhisattvas dwell—those already studied by past Bodhisattvas, those to be studied by future Bodhisattvas, and those currently being studied by present Bodhisattvas—you should know these as the training. Are you able to uphold them? (Answer: "I am able," three times.)
The sixth announcement is concluded.

Next, following the conclusion of the announcement, it is said: "This bodhisattva [Name], before all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, has already received the bodhisattva precepts from me, the bodhisattva [Name], having recited them for the second and third time; the bodhisattva [Name] has now completed the reception of the bodhisattva precepts."
I bear witness to this. This bodhisattva who has received the precepts is named [Name].
Furthermore, he addresses the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions—the supreme teachers, the gentle ones, and those with soft perceptions toward all sentient beings—saying:
"This bodhisattva [Name] has already three times declared before the bodhisattva [Name] that he receives the entire bodhisattva ethical discipline."
The precepts are concluded (recited three times).

[Commentary]: According to the *Sūtra of the Four Necklaces*, before receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, one first pays homage to the Triple Gem of the three periods (recited three times).
Next, one receives the four indestructible refuges: taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, taking refuge in the Saṃgha, and taking refuge in the Precepts (recited three times).

Next, one performs repentance for the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, and so forth (recited three times). Finally, the ten grave precepts are recited; it is stated that those who violate them lose the forty-two marks of a worthy person (*bhadra-puruṣa*).

The Noble Dharma Questions the Recipient (who answers "I can"), whereupon the Three Refuges are summarized and the ten heavy precepts mentioned above are reiterated, followed by praise and the making of vows.

Regarding the "receiving of precepts": it means to transcend the four māras and cross beyond the suffering of the three realms, never failing to maintain the constant practice throughout successive lives until the attainment of Buddhahood.
If one does not receive the precepts, they are not called a sentient being with consciousness;

they are no different from animals, constantly alienated from the ocean of the Triple Gem, not Bodhisattvas, and practitioners of false views and external paths who do not accord with human sentiment. [Such a person] should be exhorted to receive the precepts.

The merit of the precepts surpasses that of constructing eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas. One who possesses the precepts, even if they commit transgressions, is superior to one who lacks the precepts and does not commit transgressions.
If one receives them in the true presence of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, it is called the superior grade of precepts.

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, within a distance of one thousand li there is no Dharma master, and one receives them before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva by making a self-vow, it is called the inferior grade of precepts.

○ First, the general title of the sutra.
[Commentary] Regarding the title of this sutra, the text of the first fascicle of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* states that the Buddha beheld Mahābrahmādeva and Indra...
A thousandfold net of diverse colors does not obstruct one another; for this reason, it is taught that immeasurable worlds are like the meshes of a net, each world being distinct from the others.
The various gateways of the Buddhas' teachings are likewise so.

Adorning the Brahma-body without obstruction, the name is established based on this analogy as a general metaphor for the entire section of the treatise, which harmonizes excellently with the subject matter.
It is like the net of the Brahma King.
[Note] "Indra" should be called the "Net-Canopy Banner" (*jāla-vitāna-dhvaja*), for while Indra’s net is in the palace, the Brahma King’s net is atop the banner.
As stated in the preceding fascicle, the "canopy banner" is not the Indra-net; this was an error made by the scribe.
This error arises because when the Brahmā King arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, the Buddha perceived that the meshes of his net were distinct and did not obstruct one another;
thus, it was taken as a metaphor for the fact that the worlds of the Buddhas are each different yet mutually fused and mutually encompassed, from which the name is established.
Furthermore, "Brahmā" means "purity"; by using this pure net to fish people out from the ocean of birth and death—
The celestial fish can ferry one across to the other shore; it is for this reason that the name was established, and the intent lies therein.
To argue that the various Brahmā heavens are not the meaning of the present text is incorrect. II. General Title of the Chapter.
[Commentary: The title of the chapter, "Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind," is likewise a metaphorical name for the essential principles of the Great Being elucidated within this chapter.

Just as a human body possesses a mind that can coordinate all affairs and produce superior fruits, serving as the basis for a Great Being (mahāsattva), it is said that [the mind] is like the earth. [Note:

The character "mind" (citta) applies to both the Dharma and the analogy. While the preceding text spoke directly of the three—mind (citta), thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna)—here, "mind" is derived from...
This is the explanation according to the Dharma. The present text uses the analogy of a human body possessing a heart to convey the general meaning.

The character "ground" (di) is taken from its metaphorical sense to signify that which can produce what is created; it may also be understood according to the Dharma as the ground of the principle of the true aspect (dharmatā).

Although this meaning is not explicitly stated in the text, it can be inferred. Alternatively, if one adds the term "Dharma-gate," since the Tripitaka itself lacks [an explicit definition], [the meaning is established through implication].
The *Shu* (Commentary) does not establish a *Chao* (Excerpts), stating: "The mind is a metaphor for that which can encompass [all], while the ground is a metaphor for that which can produce [them].

[Commentary]: *Vairocana* is translated in the *Yao liang jing* as "Pure and Full" (*jingman*):

it is called "pure" because all afflictions have been completely exhausted, and it is called "full" because all virtues are perfectly complete. *Śākyamuni* is translated in the *Ruixing jing* as "Capable Sage" (*nengru*);
it is also called "Capable Benevolent One" (*nengren*), "Capable Enduring One" (*nengren*), or simply "Forest Sage. *Muni* refers to body, speech, and mind.
Some say he crossed the Vojiao (Wojiao) [Sea]; this is a divergent interpretation. In the "Chapter on Names" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he is called Rocana or Śākyamuni;
we now clarify that these are neither identical nor different, appearing according to what is appropriate for the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.

[Note] The two names have already been clearly explained in the *Fanyi chao* (Explanations of Translations): the name Śākyamuni is established based on the *saṃbhogakāya*, while the name Śākyamuni is established based on the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Regarding "Munī" (the Sage), the *Benxing jing* (Sūtra of Past Deeds) translates it as "Silent Stillness" (*jìmò*);
this refers to the fact that his three karmas—body, speech, and mind—are all in a state of silent stillness. As for "crossing the Wójiao," the wandering of sentient beings is like parched [sand].
The five desires drench the stone, yet it remains insatiable; only a Buddha can deliver it, which is why it is said that he "crosses over the Wòjiāo (Wojiao).

This is based on the ninth fascicle of the *Miaoji* (Record of the Sublime), which explains this according to the old *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Regarding the new translation of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Vairocana* and the *Śākyamuni* [sections] are not distinguished;
the *Bianji* (Discriminating Record) states: "In recent translations, the Dharma-body and Reward-body are not differentiated, and the three and two [bodies] cannot be discerned."
II. Specifically identifying the Teacher.
[Commentary]: Śākyamuni preached this "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" (Cittabhūmi-paṭala) from within the palace of Maheśvara in the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven.

Examining the beginning and end of the text, there are one thousand Śākyamunis and hundreds of thousands of billions of Śākyamunis, each connecting with those for whom they have an affinity, all of whom arrive at the Śākya [palace].

Having received that treasury of the Bodhisattva precepts, they each sat at their respective sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to manifest the attainment of perfect awakening and preach the Dharma in succession. [Note:
Regarding the teacher of the *Avataṃsaka*, the interpretations of former masters have not been uniform; some say he is the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), while others say...

Regarding the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), I have previously relied upon this [text] to conclude that the *Avataṃsaka* represents the Honored One in his manifested body of birth (*janmakāya*) as the Teacher.

Now, I shall briefly demonstrate this by distinguishing it through three meanings: first, discussing the fundamental [body] in relation to the physical form; second, determining the body in relation to the land;

and third, distinguishing the response in relation to the capacity of the audience. First, regarding the term "fundamental," there are two senses: first, the fundamental basis for the manifestation of traces (*chui-ji zhi ben*).
Regarding the two aspects of the manifestation of the original and the descent of the trace: the trace-body of Śākyamuni descends from the original body of Vairocana;

thus, Vairocana is pointed to as the original. Although there are two layers of original and trace between the thousand Śākyamunis and the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis, here we speak from the ultimate perspective, pointing only to Vairocana upon the dais as the original; hence it is called "Lu."
Regarding the manifestation of Vairocana himself as the "original source," this actually refers to Śākyamuni as that source;
for how could the body of Vairocana residing upon his lotus throne in the *sambhogakāya* realm be perceived?

It is because, through the radiance and auspicious omens manifested when Śākyamuni attained enlightenment beneath the tree, one beholds the *sambhogakāya* state and thus comes to see this Buddha, as described in the preceding fascicle.

It is said that the body of Śākyamuni emits rays of wisdom-light that illuminate this celestial palace and reach as far as the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), such that all worlds therein are able to see one another;
furthermore, Śākyamuni personally lifts up the great assembly of this world and brings them to the Lotus Treasury World, where they behold the Buddha Vairocana and others.
By examining this, we know that [the manifestation] descends from the fundamental source.

The trace (the manifested form) is indeed Śākyamuni, who views from below toward the high; it is precisely because of Śākyamuni that [Vairocana] is pointed out as the fundamental source of the manifested appearance.

Thus, when the sutra says, "Returning to the original source world, beneath the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa," the Śākyamuni beneath the tree is also considered the source, for he is the very basis of the manifested appearance. Second, regarding...

Regarding the body established in this land: the body currently manifesting transformation through teaching during the five periods in the Sahā world—born in the palace of King Śuddhodana in the kingdom of Central India—namely, Prince Siddhārtha, who left home and attained the Way, first expounded the Great Dharma.
As clearly stated in the sutras, Śākyamuni first attained the Way beneath the Bodhi tree and first bound the *bodhisattva-pātimokkha*.
The *Loutimucha Huayan Jing* (Ratnakūṭa Avataṃsaka Sūtra) also states at its beginning that this sūtra was preached at the very moment of attaining enlightenment within the Sahā world;
specifically, it was preached beneath the Bodhi tree with this very body as the master of the teaching.
Since it is thus for one world, so it is for a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred billion worlds; therefore, [the text] points to the bodhi trees beneath the thousand-billion Śākyamunis.

It is clear that the birth-body (janma-kāya) is the teaching master of the *Avataṃsaka*. The Śākyamuni on the [Vulture] Peak is the teaching master who expounds the Dharma within the land of true recompense (*sambhoga-kāya*).

Now, when distinguishing the five periods of transformational teaching within this Sahā world of common residence (*sahā-loka*), how could the body that expounds the *Avataṃsaka* be identified as the teaching master of the Sahā world? Furthermore, this *Śīla-śāstra* clearly demonstrates this.

Examining the beginning and end of this passage, it states that there are a thousand Śākyamunis, each connecting with those with whom they have a karmic affinity, all of whom receive the Bodhisattva Precept-piṭaka from Vairocana;
subsequently, each sits at a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and manifests the attainment of perfect awakening, reiterating and expounding the Dharma across ten locations.
This section of text is the explicit scriptural evidence demonstrating the Lord of the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra. Since...

It is said that there are ten locations where the Dharma was preached as recounted here; these correspond to the "Seven Locations and Eight Assemblies" described in the commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This commentary harmonizes the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, asserting that both share the same Teacher.
Specifically, this refers to one of the thousands of millions of manifestations of the Buddha appearing here in this Sahā world to preach the *Avataṃsaka*. That is to say:

Regarding this body as the principal teacher of the Jingjue (Pure Enlightenment) school, those who do not understand this profound intent mistake the body manifesting upon the high seat for the teacher of ultimate retribution;
yet, it is precisely this body that serves as the master preaching the sutras in this land—this is the subject of our discussion.
Third, regarding the adaptation to capacities and eloquence: at the very beginning of the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Way, those of great capacity gathered universally in the assembly;
all present were practitioners of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings]. Since their capacities were purely great, the response should have been the Honored One with the Distinctive Features (Zhunté).

This refers precisely to the body described in the sixth section of the "Under the Tree" chapter. Because the great capacity perceives according to its own karmic consciousness, the Buddha manifests through a response from within the Middle Way. Therefore...
This physical body is itself the *vairocana-kāya* (the majestic form) acting as the Teacher.

Although the sutras speak of the "ocean of marks" numbering as many as the atoms in ten lotus-treasury worlds, it is this very [body] that Śākyamuni of this land emits light and manifests auspicious signs, taking the great assembly of this gathering by hand to the platform where Vairocana resides;
it is from him that the precepts have been transmitted, and he has now come beneath this tree to provide shelter for the multitude.
This describes the vast Dharma-gate of the ocean of marks; one must not mistake the described marks for the teaching master who speaks them.
Since it is said that this is a reiteration of the teaching, there is a source from which it was transmitted, and those who possess the eye of the teachings should skillfully discern this.
Some may argue: "Since the *Sūtra of the Brahma’s Net* mentions 'wondrous phrases' (*mi-āo jù*) as a distinct occasion, how can this [text] be identified with it?"
Regarding the fact that [the author] is the master of the *Avataṃsaka*, there are two pieces of evidence. First, according to the commentary (*śāstra*), it states:

"The text of the *Avataṃsaka* has not yet been fully transmitted; the preceding and succeeding sections may differ, all due to the inconceivable nature of the sacred traces and the diverse explanations given according to the capacities of beings.

Within this commentary, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* are brought together, and the textual consistency is clearly evident. Second, [there is the evidence of the title of the work itself].
