[Note] This clarifies the two layers of the fundamental and the manifested (*honji-suijaku*). First, Vairocana is established as the fundamental, manifesting the thousand Śākyamunis as the manifested;

next, the thousand Śākyamunis are established as the fundamental—the fundamental within the manifested—while the hundreds of thousands of millions [of Śākyamunis] are the manifested—the manifested within the manifested.
Thus, the fundamental and the manifested are shown to manifest in infinite, overlapping layers. This is based on the thirteenth fascicle of the sutra.
The world-realm is named Sahā, which translates as "Endurance.

It receives this name because the sentient beings within its current sphere of transformation are able to endure the various sufferings of the three poisons and so forth. To specify it further, the *Yipie zangshu* (Commentary on the One-Leaf Treasury) states:

"Among the various holy teachings, there are five general explanations; the first concerns the various schools of the Hīnayāna regarding this Great Thousandfold World-system (*mahāsāhasralokadhātu*)."
Among the ten billion Jambudvīpas, this Jambudvīpa alone is the place where Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood through true retribution (*vipākaphala*);
in the other continents, he merely manifests as a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This does not refer to Vairocana Buddha.

Furthermore, according to the *Mahāyānāvatāra-śāstra* and other texts, there is one who attains Buddhahood through true retribution on the level of Maheśvara, taking one great trichiliocosm as his domain.
The entire realm is transformed into ten billion Śākyamunis who simultaneously attain Buddhahood.
Third, according to this sutra, the Real Body that attains Buddhahood while seated upon the lotus pedestal in the Lotus-Pedestal Treasury World is named Vairocana;
the Śākyamuni atop each of its thousand petals is a Śākyamuni residing on each of the thousand Mahesvara heavens. These thousand [Śākyamunis]...
Each Śākyamuni manifests one hundred billion Śākyamunis;
thus, there are one thousand billion Śākyamunis who simultaneously attain Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi trees in one thousand billion lands.
According to this principle, when the single true body attains Buddhahood, it takes one thousand three-thousandfold world systems as its sphere of transformation, totaling one thousand [such bodies].
The thousand *śākyamunis* of each billion-fold world system are the bodies of true recompense (*sambhogakāya*), while the hundred billion *śākyamunis* are transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
According to the *Catuḥpratisaraṇa-śāstra* and other treatises, there are two kinds of enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*): first, the self-enjoyment body, which is the true body;

it is the fulfillment of Buddhahood in accordance with the Dharma-realm, where the Buddha-land and the Buddha-body correspond to one another, and the environment and its inhabitants are non-obstructive. This is inhabited by the Buddha alone, and no other bodhisattvas [dwell therein].
The second is the Body for the Enjoyment of Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), which manifests and preaches the Dharma within pure lands for Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*).

For those with the capacities prior to the stages, it manifests as the Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*). The realm over which this body presides is even more vast than the previous five supports.
Because, according to the *Avataṃsaka*, there is neither attainment nor non-attainment, Vairocana attains Buddhahood as a true body in all places.

Furthermore, Vairocana is none other than Śākyamuni, for there is no distinction between the two bodies—the retributive (vipāka) and the transformational (nirmāṇa)—and it is simply by expounding the ten bodies that his inexhaustibility is revealed (*Commentary on that*).

Although the commentaries of other schools cite sutras and śāstras to explain the meaning in great detail, which I have preserved here for comprehensive knowledge, they lack a unifying doctrinal principle;
consequently, they are largely diffuse. Moreover, [they treat] these as being substantially existent...

If one were to regard the body as the true recompense body (*sambhogakāya*), there would be no place for the classification of our own family’s bodies and lands into the environment and its inhabitants; thus, there would be nowhere to turn.
If we compare this with the present commentary on the "Original and Traced" (*honjaku*) aspects, the difference in quality is evident. Jingxi said:

"Even if the ten directions were to act as mutual hosts and companions, they would still not depart from a single mote of dust; that single mote of dust resides only within this platform and upon this leaf. One should know that it is precisely thus.

Because these are the "trace" (the phenomenal) and the "basis" (the noumenal), we know that the discourse of our current school regarding the attainment of the ultimate meaning, though infinite and inexhaustible, does not depart from the present moment of thought.
Jingxi said: "Each and every particle of dust is a body; all bodies are one body. Each and every particle of dust is a land;
all lands are one land. The *Xiyi Chao* cites Yongjia as saying: "The single moon universally contains all waters; the moon in all waters is one."
The Moon [Commentary] states that those who have not studied Tiantai find it difficult to clarify this principle.

○ Third, the three points on how both the Original and the Traced attain the Buddha-way, each sitting beneath the Bodhi tree and simultaneously attaining the Buddha-way. ○ Third, the half-verse summary of the Original and the Traced.
"Thus, the thousands, hundreds, and ten-thousands of millions [of bodies] / Are the original body of Vairocana.

[Commentary]: The first phrase, "thousands, hundreds, and ten-thousands of millions," concludes the discussion of the manifested bodies (*traces*); the subsequent phrase, "the original body of Vairocana," concludes the discussion of the fundamental body.
This clarifies that all thousands, hundreds, and ten-thousands of millions have Vairocana as their source.

[Note] The *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Store) assigns the phrase "the body of Śākyamuni" to the subsequent section and the phrase "thus [there are] thousands of billions" to the preceding section, concluding with the remark:

"In this way, there are a thousand sets of billions. However, if one follows the Tiantai *Shu* (Commentary), which treats these two phrases as a concluding summary of both the "original" (*hon*) and the "traced" (*jaku*), only then will the intent of the sutra be clearly understood. If it were otherwise...
His previous commentary already concluded with "ten billion lands"; what purpose is served by reiterating the numerical total?
Furthermore, leaving the phrase "in his original body" within the subsequent section is entirely without justification; thus, his interpretation of the sutra does not equal that of Tiantai.

△ From "thousand, ten thousand, and hundred million" onwards, the second part clarifies the person and the dharma: first, the person is clarified; next, the dharma is clarified. ○ First, the person is clarified.
The billions of Śākyamunis, each receiving hosts as numerous as motes of dust, have all come together to my abode.
[Commentary]: Among these, there are three phrases: first, it clarifies the persons who receive [the followers], namely the billions of Śākyamunis;
second, it clarifies the persons being received, which signifies those with whom there is a karmic affinity. "Motes of dust" indicates that the number of listeners is vast. First...
The Three Clarities (trividyā) enable both the one who receives and the one who is received to arrive together at the abode of Śākyamuni Buddha.
[Note] The *Xīchāo* states: "One takes those with whom there is a karmic affinity; if it were not for such affinity, how could one hear the sublime precepts?

Therefore, the various devas attached to pleasure in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* do not participate in the Dharma assembly because their vehicle is lax. This refers to the four propositions regarding the Vehicle and the Precepts (*yāna-śīla-catuṣkoṭi*) as explained by Mount Ding.

The Record states: "As for what is called 'receiving,' others say it does not necessarily mean physically holding with the hands, but rather sustaining [the object] through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
According to the explanation in the first fascicle, when Śākyamuni received Vimalakīrti, he 'held up the great trichiliocosm with his hand';
in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he 'received the assembly through supernatural powers'—both of these encompass all such meanings. **Second, the clarification of the Dharma.**
Listen as I recite the Buddha’s precepts; the gate of ambrosia shall then open.
[Commentary] The first phrase clarifies the proclamation of the precepts; the second phrase is a formal praise of the precepts. The initial admonition instructs the Bodhisattvas to listen.

Regarding the phrase "reciting the Buddha’s precepts," one may ask: why is it called "reciting" rather than "proclaiming"? The answer is that these are the precepts of all Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions.
Because this Dharma does not originate from one's own initial creation, it can only be called "recitation" and cannot be termed "expounding. Regarding the "Gate of Ambrosia":

praising the precepts is likened to consuming ambrosia, which causes one to live long and remain immortal. It is essential to rely on these precepts to attain Nirvana—eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
The teaching that enables one to penetrate principle is likened to a gate; furthermore, the precepts can rescue and deliver one from [suffering].
To transcend birth and death is like ingesting the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*) to attain long life. A sutra states:
"If mountains were to come from the four directions, one should simply maintain the precepts and practice giving.
[Note: Tiwei regarded the precepts as the talisman for longevity and the seal of immortality; thus, although there are the five precepts...
Tiantai explains this through the four teachings; in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), it is the talisman for long life and the seal of immortality—namely, the four virtues of Nirvana:
permanence, bliss, self, and purity. In the present text, the "ambrosia" (amṛta) is taken as the dharma of longevity and immortality.
Regarding what is called "opening," there should be four aspects in its full manifestation. The *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Light) explains the "opening of the gate of ambrosia" as follows:
Regarding the first stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), it is called "opening" because it opens the noble path (*āryamārga*) by warding off the two extremes.

Furthermore, it is like showing the vessel [the practitioner], the city, the location, and the chamber, in contrast to the stages of practice, the stages of advancement (*pratipannaka-bhūmi*), and the stages of realization (*phala-bhūmi*). Now, since the precepts are the initial gateway for entering the Path, they are called "opening.
As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "When the four mountains press down from all sides, if one wishes to be rescued and delivered, one should cultivate giving and the precepts."

The *Jishenglaobingdie chao* (Excerpts on Birth, Old Age, Sickness, and Death) quotes a verse by the Great Being (Mahāsattva): "Seek the Unsurpassed Way early; you should thus avoid the mountains of the four quarters. **Part Two:
The Transmission from Śākyamuni, the Trace-Buddha, to the Bodhisattvas, and from the Bodhisattvas to Sentient Beings.** This section is further divided into three parts:

1. An explanation by the scriptural masters regarding the causes and conditions for Śākyamuni’s transmission of the teachings; 2. An explanation of Śākyamuni [himself]; 3. [The subsequent transmission].
The exposition of the precepts and the transmission [of them] to the bodhisattvas consists of three exhortations for bodhisattvas to transmit [the precepts] to all sentient beings.
First, the author of the sutra describes the origins of Śākyamuni’s transmission.
At that time, the thousands of billions [of Buddhas] returned to their original places of enlightenment; each sat beneath a Bodhi tree and recited the precepts of my original teacher.

[Commentary]: These three lines clarify that the thousands of billions of Buddhas each returned to their respective original locations. Now, first, regarding the fact that the Dharma-body is without location: [text follows].
The *Mingji zhuan* (Biographies of Traces) states that the fundamental [precepts] serve as the teachers of the traces, because the traces recite the fundamental.

△ The transmission and bestowal of these precepts to the various bodhisattvas consists of three parts: first, clarifying the essence of the precepts; second, clarifying the function of the precepts; third, exhorting bodhisattvas to receive and uphold them.
○ Now, for the first part, there are the ten grave and forty-eight minor precepts.
[Commentary]: Thus, the ten grave precepts and so forth constitute the essence of the precepts. 2. Praising the Function of the Precepts:
The precepts are like the bright sun and moon, And also like jeweled necklaces.
[Commentary]: Upholding these precepts can eliminate the mist of transgressions; this is likened to the sun. It brings about clarity and coolness, which is compared to [the moon].
The month of Puṣya possesses wholesome dharmas like a necklace of pearls; likewise, the precepts can cause the myriad things to grow.
Furthermore, just as a necklace can dispel poverty, so too can the precepts dispel the poverty of sentient beings and increase the wealth of wholesome dharmas.
Moreover, just as the sun and moon adorn the heavens and there is none who does not look up to them, so it is with those who uphold the precepts.

The essence has nowhere it does not return; the *kaṇṭhaka-śīrṣa* (necklace) adorns the body as the foremost ornament. Upholding the precepts removes ugliness, just as physical beauty brings forth elegance.

[Note] The Master Zang’s commentary states: "The first is the adornment of wisdom (*prajñā-śobhana*), and the second is the adornment of merit (*puṇya-śobhana*). Furthermore, the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint)...
It is like the sun because it destroys all dark evils; it is like the moon because the precept of gathering sentient beings has great compassion as its cooling characteristic;
and it is like a necklace because the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas can gather and cultivate supreme wholesome dharmas which one then wears upon oneself.
○ Third, the exhortation for bodhisattvas to accept and uphold [the precepts].
The multitude of subtle-dust Bodhisattvas attained perfect enlightenment thereby; as Rocana recited this, so too do I recite it.
You, newly initiated Bodhisattvas, must receive and uphold these precepts with the highest reverence.
[Commentary]: Just as one crossing the ocean must rely on a ship, so too must one cross over birth and death by relying on the holding of the precepts. (From the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*)
It is said that [the teachings] are like relying on a boat or raft, and are further likened to a floating life-preserver. Furthermore, there are two types:

those such as Vairocana, who are the ones capable of bestowing [the teachings], and those who are newly learning, who are the recipients. Third, the exhortation for Bodhisattvas to transmit [the teachings] to sentient beings.
Having received and upheld these precepts, one transmits them to all sentient beings.
[Commentary: The Bodhisattvas of the thirty stages transmit [them] to those outside the stages of the ordinary person who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind.

[Note] The commentary (*shū*) states: "Regarding 'three exhortations for the transmission to sentient beings,' the character *fā* (發) is an error; it should be as previously categorized under the section on 'exhorting the Bodhisattvas.

The *Xīchāo* does not explain this clearly, treating it as if it were 'exhorting for the arousal of the aspiration' (*quàn fā*). △ Third, the exhortation to believe, accept, and uphold, which is further divided into three parts:
first, presenting the Dharma to be recited; second, exhorting others to believe and accept it; third, concluding the exhortation. ○ First, presenting [the Dharma]."
The Dharma that is recited:
Listen attentively as I correctly recite the treasury of precepts within the Buddha-dharma, the *Prātimokṣa*.

[Commentary: These precepts distinguish [the Buddhist path] from the "chicken and dog" precepts of the non-Buddhists; pure morality (*śīla*) serves as the cause, and liberation (*mokṣa*) serves as the fruit.
[Note] The *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Treasury) states: *Prātimokṣa* means "individual" (*bie*); *vinaya* means "liberation" (*jie-tuo*).
This refers to the fact that by upholding these precepts, one is individually liberated from all objects of transgression. The *Xihao* (Explanatory Notes) states:
It is called a "Treasury" (*zang*) because it encompasses all precepts; it is also the treasury of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature (*foxing*). △ Second, exhorting others.
Receiving and upholding [the precepts] is further divided into two parts: first, exhorting faith; second, exhorting acceptance. Now, for the first:
The great assembly should believe with a sincere mind: "You shall become a Buddha," "And I am one who has already become a Buddha.
Always maintain such faith, And the category of precepts will be fully perfected.
[Commentary: The reason for this is that faith is the initial gateway for entering the Way. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Faith is that which enables entry;
by upholding these precepts, I have attained perfect enlightenment, and you should do likewise. 2. Exhortation to Receive [the Precepts].
All those who possess a mind Should all receive the Buddha’s precepts. When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of the Buddhas.
Their status being identical to that of Great Enlightenment, They are truly the children of the Buddhas.
[Commentary]: This clarifies that all who possess a mind are capable of receiving the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna precepts of permanence, bliss, and so forth; it elucidates the nature of sentient beings.
Those who possess the Buddha-nature inherent in the mind must receive the two precepts in order to attain Buddhahood. ○ Third, the conclusion and exhortation.

[Note] In the commentary, the division of sections differs between the earlier and later parts. Previously, it was stated that the general meaning of the verses consists of four precepts and three exhortations;

as for the three exhortations: first, the exhortation to believe; second, the exhortation to receive; and third, the exhortation to recite—these correspond to the three exhortations beginning from the section "Listen attentively" (*diǎntīng*) below.

The commentary now formally explains the three exhortations and reopens their topical divisions, stating: "The third exhortation, the text on faith, acceptance, and upholding, is divided into three parts:
first, the dharma to be recited; second, the exhortation for others to accept and uphold it; and third, the conclusion of the exhortation.

Within the section on the exhortation for others to accept and uphold it, the topical division is further opened as: "First, the exhortation to believe; second, the exhortation to accept. What is the difference between these preceding and succeeding [divisions]? Now, let us examine this in detail.

In Master Kōi’s commentary on the sutra, there are many such instances where he occasionally provides this kind of explanation—for example, from the passage beginning "Listen attentively as I recite correctly," the meaning may be divided into two sections, or it may be directly treated as three exhortations.
This is just like the preceding text on the exhortation to recite: by saying "because I recite," it is shown that everyone recites.
Alternatively, the section on "Exhortation" (quàn) may be categorized as follows; although there are slight differences in the details, the general meaning remains the same. Question:

Previously it was said that one is exhorted to receive [the precepts] and exhorted to uphold them; yet now it says one is exhorted to believe and exhorted to receive. Why is this? Answer: One receives because one has expressed faith;

one upholds because one has received. These are explained interchangeably without contradiction. Therefore, the previous commentary stated: "Since you have received them, you must uphold them; since you uphold them, you must recite them."
This is intended so that the transmission may continue without interruption.
The great assembly all listened with reverence and a sincere heart as I recited it.

[Commentary] The first phrase concludes the preceding section, while the second phrase exhorts the listeners; together they clarify the introductory sequence for the transmission of the precepts by all Buddhas.

[End of section]. △ Second, the Introduction of Śākyamuni’s Exhortation, which is divided into two parts: first, the words of the sūtra-author; second, what Śākyamuni himself spoke. The first part has three stages:
first, describing the Buddha’s intent to establish the precepts; second, emitting light as an auspicious omen; third, the great assembly’s desire to hear [the teaching].
The first of these [three] further has four sections. ○ First, identifying the Teacher of Transformation.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha.
[Commentary] First, he identifies the Great Sage, the Honored One Śākyamuni, as the master of transformation.
[Note] Previously, it was established that the birth-body of Śākyamuni is the teaching master of this Flower Garland Sūtra, who now reiterates and expounds it beneath the tree.
The Dharma is established through teaching, and the body is thereby produced; this very body is the *vairocana-kāya* (the majestic, special body), as in the three meanings previously mentioned.
Since the one designated here as the principal is none other than Śākyamuni Buddha, how could this not accord with the intent of the Patriarchs? 2. Designating the Location.
Initially, he sat beneath the Bodhi tree.
[Commentary]: Because he attained the Way beneath this tree, it is called the "Tree of the Way" (*bodhidruma*); it is also called *pippala* in the Sanskrit language, meaning "contemplation.
○ He attained the Way through the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*).
[He] attains unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
[Commentary: This means that attaining perfect enlightenment is the title of "Right Universal Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). △ Fourth, the exposition of the dharma thus established:
namely, the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa, which consists of four further sets of four phrases. ○ First, the designation of the name of what is established.
First, the formulation of the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa. [Note:
The *Zangshu* states that these are fundamental precepts (*mūla-śīla*) rather than those formulated by the Śrāvakas only in response to specific transgressions;
because they were established at the very moment of his initial attainment of Buddhahood, it is so called. Second, their capacity to constitute the supreme cause.
Be filial and obedient toward your parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem.
[Commentary] The *Ratnagarbha Sūtra* states: "The Lord of Heaven, Śakra Devendra, dwells within your home and yet practices filial piety;
the Great Brahmā, the Honored Heaven, dwells within your home and yet fulfills filial duty; Śākyamuni Buddha dwells within..."
In your family, the Bodhisattva Śyāma’s eye ailment was cured by his own eyesight, and the fire-wheel of the girl Maitrī was swiftly extinguished;
these were immediate manifestations of spiritual efficacy. The *Erya* states: "To serve one's parents well is filial piety (*xiao*); filial piety is obedience (*shun*).
Taisi Shuming used "obedience" to explain filial piety. The *Xiaojing Gouming jue* states: "The character for 'filial' (*xiao*) is glossed as 'thorough' (*jiu*); thoroughness is understanding."

This refers entirely to the beginning and end of filial care (*se-yang*). It may also be explained as "crossing over" (*duo*); this "crossing over" refers to ritual propriety (*yi-fa*), wherein the maintenance of warmth and purity accords with ritual.
[Note] Filial piety (*xiao-shun*) is the mind capable of practicing; parents and so forth are the objects of that practice.

When the mind practices wholesome dharmas, it constitutes both the virtues of cessation (*zhi*) and application (*xing*). Filial piety is the virtue of cessation, while compliance (*shun*) is the virtue of application. Therefore, through filial piety, one prevents and restrains...
Because it accords with what is contrary and what is compliant, one serves and honors its countenance. This is as explained in the section on the observance of precepts within *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*:

the two precepts of "conforming to the requisites of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-saṃbhāra*) prevent the two extremes and skillfully accord with the Middle Way. Regarding the maintenance of these two precepts as being identical to the Middle Way, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"The name 'precept' is called the Mahāyāna; it is the name for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It is not blue, yellow, red, or white."

Filial piety is called "xiao"; filial piety is called "shun. Filial piety is the cessation of evil; filial piety is the practice of good. The *Fuxing shu* (Commentary on the Practice of the Path) explains:

"One should take the mutual illumination of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and quiescent appearance as a means of prevention. Being good and compliant is the essence of the precepts. 'Xiao' means to store.
The way to serve one's parents is that one should constantly store [this principle] within the mind; because it is stored within the mind, one can comply with their countenance."
Because it accords with form, it is called "conformity"; now, observing the inconceivable in this same way, it constantly illuminates within the mind and skillfully conforms to principle.
Because it conforms, one contemplates the Three Truths; because it is filial, one rests within the three delusions.

Even such observance of the precepts does not share the same meaning as the observance of precepts for emerging into the provisional in the Separate Teaching; how much less could it be compared to the practice of filial piety by princes, ministers, or commoners?
Since they are of the same essence, one knows that the two characters "filial" (孝) and "obedient" (順) cannot be explained in a superficial or mundane manner.

Because it is called "obedience," one contemplates the Three Truths; because it is "filial," one ceases the three delusions. Furthermore, let us speak of this in relation to the ten stages of filial piety (*shizhong xiaoshun*):

the rational nature (*lixing*) is not evil or rebellious, for it is in accordance with this nature that one upholds the precept against killing; the rational nature is not greed or grasping, for it is in accordance with this nature [that one does so].
The nature of upholding the precept against stealing is non-defiled; because it accords with this nature, one upholds the precept against sexual misconduct. The nature is fundamentally true;
because it accords with this nature, one upholds the precept against lying. The nature is not deluded;

because it accords with this nature, one upholds the precept against intoxicants. Furthermore, the nature is fundamentally sincere and trustworthy; because it accords with this nature, one upholds the precept against slander.
The ten precepts being thus, all other precepts follow this example. For a Bodhisattva, all practices proceed from accord with the nature (*dharmatā*) through non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*);
therefore, it is called "accord. This means that by realizing the nature as practice, such conduct becomes wondrous. Only by understanding it in this way can one properly uphold the precepts.
Stopping the three delusions and acceding to the three truths—from cause to fruit—employing this filial accord reaches its ultimate limit.
Because the three delusions reach their ultimate source in the three truths, only the Buddha alone is said to have perfected the observance of the precepts;

this is what is called filial piety. There are three objects of such filial piety: first, the kindness of parents who gave one birth and nurtured one; second, the kindness of teachers and monks who instructed and guided one;
and third, the kindness of the Triple Gem that protects and saves one. Since these three have bestowed kindness upon me, how could I not be filial?
Regarding the term "parents," there are the parents of the Dharma-gate and the worldly parents. The parents of the Dharma-gate give birth to my Dharma-body;
thus, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem are all included therein, and one should practice filial piety toward them. Worldly parents give birth to my physical body;
this includes both past and present parents who have given birth to this body. Past [parents]... [present parents give birth to this body].
Since all sentient beings of my previous lives were my parents, it is said that there is no life in which I have not been born from them. Now,
by maintaining the precepts and practicing filial piety through this single arousal of the bodhicitta—
a mind that is universally vast— I cause not only my biological parents to attain liberation, but also [all others].
"All sentient beings have been my parents in past lives; together we enter the ocean of requiting their kindness and shall equally attain the fruit of Bodhi—is this not magnificent?
Such words of filial piety must be well understood and interpreted. The commentary states that the Śyāmaka Bodhisattva personally witnessed his father's eyes being healed.
The *Śyāmaka Sūtra* says: "When the Tathāgata was a common person in the past, he served..."
The blind parents had practiced the Way in the mountains for over twenty years; they gathered fruit and drew water, serving him with unwearied devotion.
Their son, clad in a deer-skin garment, encountered a king out hunting and was struck in the chest by a poisoned arrow; he was near death and difficult to save.

Remembering their son’s profound filial piety, the parents resolved to sacrifice their own lives for him; they then sucked the poison from his mouth with their mouths and pulled the arrowhead from his chest with their hands.
He was able to escape [death] and become the King Śakra-Brahmā; by pouring divine medicine into Śyama’s mouth, all his poisoned arrows were removed and he returned to life as before.
His parents were filled with joy and surprise, and both their eyes opened. The King vowed not to kill and observed the five precepts with a virtuous and compassionate heart.
Regarding the boy, the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* states: "The daughter of the Elder Maitrī, wishing to take leave of her mother, went deep into the sea."
While gathering jewels, the Mother would not permit her departure; she plucked out one of her hairs and went to a sea-island.
There she saw a wheel of glowing iron descend from the sky toward the crown of her head. She immediately made this vow: "May the suffering of the entire Dharma-realm be gathered into my own body.
By the power of this vow, the fiery wheel fell away. From that point on, she relinquished her life and was reborn in the sixth heaven, *Uṣṇīṣa*.
The clouds of the mountain stream obstructed his mother and damaged her hair, resulting in a hellish state of mind; he then gave rise to a vow to dedicate himself to the goodness of the Buddha-realm.

[Commentary] Regarding the three phrases concerning the attainment of the fruit: first, it is not a mind of blue or yellow; second, it is neither existent nor non-existent; third, it is not a phenomenon of cause and effect.
[Note] The *Zangshu* (Treasury Commentary) reads "gu gu" (because light) as "gu gu fei qing huang" (because light is not blue or yellow), joining the two characters together; Dingshan also does so.
However, the *Xihui Chao* states: "The sutra says 'there is a cause,' for it is not without a reason; thus, 'light' (*guang*) signifies the beginning of an event.

Its intention is to take "for this reason" (*gu guang*) as a single phrase. I now follow the *Xihui Chao*. This is because each translator has their own stylistic conventions, as seen in the previous fascicle where it says:

First, regarding its being neither form nor mind: the nature of the precepts is not obstructive matter (*rūpa*), nor is it a cognizing mind (*citta*);

furthermore, since they are established upon the seeds of volition (*cetanā-bīja*) and take those seeds as their essence, they are not blue or other such forms; and because they are conventionally designated as "form" upon the seeds of volition, they are not the mind.
Second, regarding its being neither existent nor non-existent: this means that the precepts of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) absolutely lack any self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
It is eternally not existent, and thus it is non-existent; yet it is not non-existent because this precept of non-existence is unlike a rabbit’s horn, and thus it is not non-existent.

According to this interpretation, the analysis of the text is extremely subtle, yet the explanation of its meaning lacks a definitive conclusion.

Since others cannot grasp the core intent of the teaching, it is stated directly: the essence of the precepts is the profound true nature; as for the essence of the precepts, in contrast to the three phrases concerning the causes below, it says: [the essence of the precepts is...]
If the application of the precepts is vast and expansive, then regarding the preceding three phrases as the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*): what kind of essence is this?

If the essence that is produced belongs to unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), it is an essence of phenomena (*dharma-tattva*). If one says it is the true nature (*tathatā*), it is an essence of principle (*li-tattva*), which would still belong to the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that serves as its basis, thereby losing the intended meaning.
If one attains the present school’s tenet, the "nature" (*prakṛti*) indicated in the preceding text is taken as the basis.

Form (*rūpa*) is the wondrous light of the Middle Way in its essential substance; it fully possesses the principle-nature (*li-xing*) and properly belongs to the substance of the supported basis (*āśraya*).

Its substance transcends the ten realms and is free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). All three [form, mind, and existence] are doubly negated, because it is neither the mind of deliberative cognition belonging to the six paths of rebirth nor the segmented form of matter;
thus it is called "neither form nor mind. Furthermore, it is not the partial truth of the conditioned existence of the Two Vehicles.
Because it is empty, it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent;
furthermore, because it is not the cause of a bodhisattva’s activity nor the fruit of attaining realization in the Buddha-realm, it is said to be neither cause nor effect.

Thus, one knows that the true essence does not fall within the realm of ordinary beings, nor is it the domain of the two vehicles, and it transcends all grounds of cultivation and realization. At the conclusion of the following verse, it says: "To calculate a self..."
Those who cling to marks cannot give rise to this Dharma; those who seek realization by extinguishing their lifespan are likewise not the place for planting seeds.
If one wishes to nurture the sprouts of Bodhi so that its radiance illuminates the world, one should calmly observe the true nature of all phenomena.
The light of this true nature universally shines upon everything; this is precisely what is meant by the "Eight Negations," which share the same essential meaning as the present "Three Pairs."

This is the Middle Way and the true mark (*dharmatā*); when discussing the wondrous light, it is the substance upon which the precepts rely, and both belong to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
In the subsequent passage, the three phrases concerning the causal practice are the source and foundation;

these belong to the essential nature itself, while the manifested form of the precepts is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Thus we know that cultivation arises from the nature, and the conventional is established based on the ultimate. Although...

Those who die and return [to this world] mostly harbor fear; the inferior and weak lack supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), while those possessing merit are endowed with them.
