[Note] Regarding the explanation according to the dharma-gate, this follows the previous example of the precept on killing; however, I have now compiled the commentaries and sub-commentaries to explain the specific characteristics of the case.

The meaning is fully detailed herein, categorized into four sections: first, regarding the object; second, regarding the mind; third, regarding the dharma; and fourth, regarding the fruit. Regarding the first:

there are eleven types of objects for sexual misconduct: (1) a corpse that has not yet decayed; (2) intercourse with a ghost; (3) an animal; (4) a human being; (5) various relatives; (6) a prostitute;
(7) members of the two assemblies living at home who observe the five precepts, the eight precepts, and so forth; (8) those who have left the home life...

Regarding the two types of householders, those who have received the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), and so forth—up to the nine categories of parents and the ten types of noble ones (such as those who have committed offenses against an Arhat or a *bhikṣuṇī*)—the offenses committed against these individuals are all light at first and become progressively heavier. Second, regarding the mind: first, the greedy mind;
this refers to when a greedy mind is so intense that one feels no shame before one's parents, or even if shame is present, one’s attachment remains extremely deep.
Second, the mind of hatred refers to intentionally committing sexual acts to humiliate another person.

Third, the mind of delusion refers to the thought that desire does not obstruct the Path and thus acting accordingly. Regarding the third point, there are two aspects of the Dharma: the Dharma of transgression and the Dharma of treatment.
As for transgressions, they may be extremely private or involve avoiding people slightly; they may be committed openly or through the use of forceful coercion.
Some, seeking to curry favor through greed, engage in various forms of sexual misconduct and thereby commit grave offenses (*pārājika*).

Others, though fearing the prohibitions of the precepts, have not yet been able to forget their desires; they claim that touching [the body], emission of semen, coarse speech, acting as a matchmaker, verbal jesting, and playful flirtation regarding the sense bases and objects constitute minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*).
Or, when one is forcibly coerced by another, even if one engages in sexual union with a woman—such as the case of biting a finger—it is likewise considered a minor offense.

If one restrains the mind so that it does not experience pleasure, one does not commit an offense. For example, even if one is forcibly coerced, if the mind experiences pleasure, it is equivalent to a formal transgression.
As for the method of treatment, a Bodhisattva should first regard any object of attachment as urine, excrement, impurity, and so forth;

by employing such contemplations as the visualization of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and the decomposition of corpses, there is no [affliction] that cannot be removed from the mind through this treatment.
One should conceive of [women] as venomous snakes and as rākṣasīs, just as one would place one's own male organ into the mouth of a venomous snake. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"It would be better to place the male organ into the mouth of a venomous snake than to approach a woman;

for while a venomous snake harms but a single lifetime, a woman brings harm across many lifetimes. Furthermore, the harm from a snake does not lead to rebirth in hell, whereas the harm from a woman leads to rebirth in hell."

Snakes harm the physical body, while women harm the Dharma-body; therefore, all who possess wisdom should exercise profound self-restraint. Fourth, regarding the results, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* identifies three kinds of results:

first, the ripening result (*vipākaphala*), which is falling into the three evil destinies and undergoing extreme suffering and affliction; second, the result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), which refers to being born among humans with two wives competing for one's favor or having a wife who is unchaste; and third— Output: Snakes harm the physical body, while women harm the Dharma-body; therefore, all who possess wisdom should exercise profound self-restraint. Fourth, regarding the results, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* identifies three kinds of results: first, the ripening result (*vipākaphala*), which is falling into the three evil destinies and undergoing extreme suffering and affliction;
second, the result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), which refers to being born among humans with two wives competing for one's favor or having a wife who is unchaste; and third—
The dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) refers to being reborn among humans where one encounters much resentment and contention. Furthermore, the fourth fascicle of the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states:
"If there is a person who delights in and clings to sexual misconduct, that person will be unable to protect the bodies of themselves or others;
they will give rise to suspicion regarding all their actions, and because false speech precedes them, they will constantly experience suffering and mental distress at all times."

Constantly distracted, one is unable to cultivate wholesome deeds; one loses wealth and property, feels no affection for one's wife and children, and has a short lifespan—these are called the present evil fruits of sexual misconduct.
After casting off this body, one dwells in hell, receiving an ugly physical form and enduring immeasurable suffering of hunger, thirst, and long life—this is called the evil karma of future lives.
As for the retribution: if one obtains a human body, due to evil karma and harsh speech, people will not take pleasure in seeing him;
he will be unable to protect his wife, concubines, sons, or daughters, and by the power of the causes and conditions of being such an evil person, he will have no mastery over any external objects.
Furthermore, the *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "If there are sentient beings who are addicted to and attached to men, women, wives, concubines, and various female attendants..."

One should know that sensual desire is like licking the edge of a sharp sword, licking a large, glowing iron ball, licking a bed of raw-hot iron, or licking a ladder of hot iron. Furthermore, one should know that women destroy the noble eye of wisdom.
Also, the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (The Discourse on the True and False Ascetics) states: "A bhikṣu falls [into ruin] due to two things."
Regarding those in the cauldron of boiling water, there are two types: first, those who constantly harbor thoughts of sensual desire; second, those who delight in forming intimate bonds with friends.

Such is the sacred teaching: if harboring such thoughts leads one to fall into the cauldron of boiling water, how much more so for those who physically engage in various acts of lust, or even through speech—jesting, laughing, mocking, or physical contact? How can one not be cautious! How can one not be cautious! Indeed.
In this precept-sūtra, it is not asked whether the bodhisattva is a layperson or a monastic; rather, for both, sexual desire is utterly severed.
Therefore, the text does not distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, as all such acts are to be abandoned. Question: If this is so, why do lay bodhisattvas have wives and children?
Answer: There are two types of laypeople. For those who are beginners and have not yet produced offspring, [the possession of a wife] is permitted.

Regarding those who have wives and children: if they have already attained their station and subsequently manifest as having wives and children for the sake of transforming sentient beings, this is due to the power of skillful means.
Thus, when the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* maintain the pure precepts, immeasurable demonesses may come to disturb them;
yet the Bodhisattvas do not give rise to even a single thought of desire, for their minds are as pure as a Buddha’s, except in the case of such skillful means.

Regarding the conversion of sentient beings, as stated in the *Yogācāra-śīla-sūtra*, it is permitted for a lay bodhisattva to follow their desires as a skillful means for the sake of converting others;
that is, with a mind as pure as a Buddha, they employ skillful means. △ Fourth, the precept against false speech.
[Commentary]: "Falsehood" (*mṛṣā*) is a term for that which is unreal. It deceives ordinary people, deludes the sages, and causes confusion in the human mind; therefore, it constitutes an offense.

This precept is violated by all seven classes of practitioners, and it is regulated by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Regarding its similarities and differences with the Śrāvaka vehicle, the general outline is largely the same as in the preceding precept on killing, which is divided into three parts.
First, the identification of the person.

If you are a Buddha’s disciple: △ Second, the section on the sequence of events; within the three parts [of this section], there are three distinct divisions. First, the initial three phrases clarify matters such as false speech;
next, the four phrases clarify the formation of karma; finally, the three phrases cite light matters to illustrate heavy ones. ○ Now, the first [division].
[This refers to] lying oneself, teaching others to lie, and the expedient means of lying.

[Commentary: Lying oneself by claiming to have attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*); teaching another [to lie] means instructing them to speak it or instructing them to speak for oneself;
the expedient means of lying is like honey smeared on a tree, causing all the bees to come.
[Note] Dingshan said: "He secretly smeared honey on a tree and covered it with an object; when the swarms of bees gathered there, he falsely claimed to have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

Others asked him about the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and because he did not understand, he falsely claimed, 'Today I did not enter meditative concentration, therefore I cannot answer.
These are all characteristics of expedient falsehoods; in principle, such [deceptive] states should indeed exist."
The text for rejoicing and praising is omitted where none exists; in such cases, it should be supplied according to the preceding examples. Next, the four phrases establish the karma:
the cause of false speech, the condition of false speech, the dharma of false speech, and the karma of false speech.
[Commentary]: This precept is established as a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) when five conditions are met: first, the sentient being; second, the perception of that being as such;

third, the intention to deceive; fourth, the utterance of the grave matter; and fifth, the understanding by the other party. Regarding "the sentient being," this refers to the objects of the three aforementioned categories.
Within the category of superior objects, if one speaks falsely toward one's parents, teachers, or the Sangha, it constitutes a grave offense; likewise toward the Buddhas or noble beings (*ārya*).

Regarding the two interpretations: first, it is said that one has entered into the profound interior; second, it is said that this person is free from delusion and can further use supernatural powers to shield others so they do not hear [the transgression].
However, among the noble ones (āryas), there are those who are great and those who are small; some possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), while others do not.
Following the majority of cases, the offenses are considered light for Arhats and those above the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), as previously stated. Exclusions apply.

Whether one attains knowledge of another's mind or not, the principle is the same as previously explained regarding the middle-grade object—humans, devas, and so forth—which is precisely the limit for delusion, understanding, and the prevention of the Path.
Regarding the lower-grade object—the four realms of existence—it is said that they are likewise grave;
however, my current explanation is that the two perceptions of sentient beings involve cases of certainty, doubt, and perversion, which are roughly similar [to the previous case].

Regarding what was previously stated—that speaking falsely with a mind directed toward this [truth] while not hearing it oneself, yet hearing it spoken by another, constitutes a grave offense—this is now explained as not being grave, because in that case there is no intentional mind.
Regarding the three types of deceitful minds, these constitute the primary factor (*karmapada*).

If one speaks out of necessity to avoid danger or due to overweening pride (*abhimāna*), there is no offense. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "The Bodhisattva’s attachment to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is called defiled."

Regarding the offense, one should know that when a Bodhisattva gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), it constitutes a secondary transgression (*laghu-āpatti*). There are two interpretations regarding the act of sending a messenger:

first, some say that instructing another to say, "I am a holy person (*ārya*)," is also a grave offense; however, since there are no jade vessels or precious gems in this land, those who speak of such things do so for the sake of profit.

If others praise one's excellence based on what one has taught, and one claims, "The path I have taught is the holy path," yet the fame and profit do not enter into oneself, this is not a grave offense.
Second, it is said that the noble Dharma is realized through profound and subtle inner verification; thus, one must speak of it oneself, for to rely on the testimony of others is deemed slight.
Fourth, "grave equipment" refers to bodily realization and visual witness. If one speaks of attaining the four fruits, the ten stages, the eight dhyānas, or supernormal powers;

or if one says they have seen devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits—all these constitute grave equipment. If one speaks of attaining the stage of nature (gotrabhūmi), this likewise constitutes grave equipment.

One interpretation states that since this is an ordinary dharma, the offense is light and the defilement is fivefold; there are two explanations regarding the duration of the time for the person to understand and the formation of the offense.
One interpretation says it follows the person; the second says it follows the speech.

Since this precept is established as a restraint on vocal karma, it should logically follow the speech, as it causes harm over a long duration. It must necessarily apply to all persons. Regarding the precept against minor false speech, it should follow the person.

Furthermore, if one commits an offense due to predominant afflictions (*kleśa*) as previously described, one loses the precepts; however, it is later stated that this applies only when one commits a fundamental transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

If one does not understand [the offense] face-to-face and merely incurs a preliminary effort (*prayoga*), yet later reflects upon the previous words and suddenly understands them, then a light offense is sublated by a heavy one.
All ten grave offenses (*daśātyaya*) have their specific causes and conditions; for now, I shall explain the four grave offenses, while the others may be understood by analogy.

[Note]: Regarding the phrase "there may be certainty, doubt, perversion, and so forth," Mount Ding (Dingshan) says: "Certainty" means it is clearly evident that [the offense] belongs to sentient beings.
"Doubt" means either doubting whether it is [an offense] or not, or doubting whether it is [a case of] perversion. "Perversion" means clinging;

either clinging to what is not as being right, or clinging to what is right as being wrong, without any further change of mind—these all constitute violations of the ten grave precepts and all have their causes.

Regarding the present explanation of only four [causes], the *Xīchāo* states: "I fear that when the Great Master was lecturing, he did not explain the remaining six causes and conditions, but merely took them as understood by analogy.
However, since they are subsequently listed and explained again, it is likely that they were fully elucidated at another time.
Alternatively, it may be that after the other six constitute karma, their relative gravity is no longer separately indicated; yet here, it is said again, "if increased... and so forth.

Since committing a transgression through the higher afflictions causes one to lose the precepts, it is now said that although all precepts have their respective conditions for release, those are merely categorized divisions and do not match the detailed completeness found here; therefore, this [text] points to them.
The final three phrases employ a light case to illustrate a heavy one.
...up to the point of not seeing yet claiming to see, or seeing yet claiming not to see—this is false speech of body and mind.

[Commentary: To speak directly is called "speech" (*vāk*); to proclaim and relate is called "discourse" (*ukti*). Discourse refers to that which elucidates and clarifies, capable of expressing both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*);
thus it is termed "discourse."

[Note] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*) also states: "Direct speech is called 'discourse,' and deliberative speech is called 'language. The *Zangshu* (Treasury Commentary) says: "Within this, there are three types of karma.
Regarding the first, vocal karma, each of the six consciousnesses and their corresponding six objects can individually constitute false speech.
Here, we discuss only that which arises from [false] views, omitting the rest; therefore it says, 'down to bodily false speech. As for the phrase 'who has obtained it? found in the Vinaya..."
Regarding the fruit of Arhatship: if one picks up or puts down the *saṃghāṭī* robe with a mind of attachment, one is not an Arhat;
it should be said that although no words were spoken, the body has committed false speech. This is as stated in the *Sujāta-sūtra*: "That which is performed by the body is an action of speech.
False speech of the mind refers to a deceitful mind, such as concealing what one has seen, and so forth, as mentioned above. 2. Explaining the Appropriate Response.
Yet the Bodhisattva constantly gives rise to right speech and right view, and also causes all sentient beings to give rise to right speech and right view.
[This] concludes the third section on what is not appropriate;
yet, instead, he further gives rise to wrong speech, wrong views, and wrong actions in all sentient beings.
○ Third, the formal definition of the offense:
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
[Note] Regarding the analogy of the Dharma-gate to the preceding matter, there are four aspects: first, in terms of the object; second, in terms of the dharma; third, in terms of the mind; fourth...

Regarding the gravity of the retribution, there are first three factors: (1) deceiving those who have been kind, such as one's elders and superiors; (2) addressing a great multitude, such as a large assembly; and (3) causing extreme distress to others.
By principle, these constitute a grave offense (*pārājika*). Regarding the nature of the act, there are also three factors:

(1) concerning supramundane dharmas—claiming to have attained superior states and so forth. The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that claiming to be a Buddha does not constitute a grave offense if it is done by oneself [without deceiving others]. (2) [The second factor concerns]... [text fragment]. (3) [The third factor concerns]... [text fragment].

Due to lack of faith, there are three [types of misconduct]: first, regarding pure dharmas, claiming to have attained meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth; second, regarding worldly matters, claiming to see what one has not seen and so forth;

third, regarding the mind, which also consists of three: (1) through false speech, seeking the reputation and profit of a noble person and viewing such things as merit, constantly practicing them without ceasing;
(2) desiring to obtain worldly fame and profit that is vast and immeasurable; and (3) [the third type, as previously described].
Fourth, regarding the retribution: the sin of lying causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of karmic results:
first, they are frequently slandered; second, they are constantly deceived by many people. (From the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, section on Lying)
Speech has many faults: first, one’s breath is foul; second, virtuous people distance themselves from them, and non-human spirits take advantage of them;
third, even when they speak the truth, others do not believe them; fourth, they are never invited to participate in the deliberations of the wise;
and fifth, they are constantly slandered, and their ugly reputation spreads throughout the world. Furthermore, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that for a person who speaks falsely, first—
Deceiving oneself first, one then deceives others; taking the real as false and the false as real, one inverts truth and falsehood and does not receive wholesome dharmas.
This is like an overturned jar into which water cannot enter. The mind of one who speaks falsely lacks shame and remorse, thereby blocking the path to heaven and the gate to *nirvāṇa*.
It is further said that for a person of truthful speech, the benefit is exceedingly vast.
Truly, that which arises from oneself is very easy to obtain and easy to liberate; when the mind is upright and straight, it is easy to escape suffering.
It is like dragging a log out of a dense forest: that which is straight comes out easily. O son of the Buddha, Rāhula, you were once young and ignorant of guarding your speech.
When people came to ask, "Is the World-Honored One here? you would say, "He is not," or "He is not here."
At that time, [Rāhula] spoke deceptively, saying, "There is someone here. The Buddha said to Rāhula, "Take water in this basin and wash my feet.
Having washed them, he said, "Cover this basin. As commanded, he immediately covered it. The Buddha said, "Pour water into it.
Having poured it, he asked, "Does the water enter inside? He replied, "It does not enter. The Buddha told Rāhula, "You have no sense of shame or modesty."
It is likewise with a person whose mind is obscured by false speech; the Way and its Dharma do not enter them. The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"If one gives rise to even a single thought of false speech, one commits a *pārājika* offense.

A Bodhisattva should distance themselves from the four transgressions and abstain from false speech, always speaking what is true, what is factual, and what is timely. Such a Bodhisattva does not [utter false speech] even in their dreams."
If one has abandoned concealment, false views, and malice, and lacks the intention to deceive others, how much more so would this apply to intentional lying?
While lying is indeed placed first [among the verbal misdeeds], in reality, one is free from all four types of speech.

Therefore, except when a Bodhisattva speaks a lie for a beneficial purpose or to save sentient beings from various hardships, they ultimately do not commit an offense. Those who later study the Bodhisattva path...
It is most fitting for a Bodhisattva to keep their mind upright and straightforward, as this makes it easy to enter the Path; therefore, one must be cautious. △ Fifth:
The Precept Against Selling Alcohol.
[Commentary] "Selling" (酤) is a term for trade or commerce, and alcohol is the commodity traded. This alcohol is [the manifestation of] ignorance.
Medicine causes people to fall into a stupor, whereas the body of a Great Being bestows wisdom upon others; to give the medicine of ignorance to people is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that there are thirty-five faults associated with alcohol, which is why it is included among the ten grave precepts (*daśa-guru-dharma*) for Bodhisattvas.

All seven classes of followers commit this offense, and it is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Thus, while the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are identical on this point, they also differ in other respects.
These [cases] are likewise not subject to prohibition; however, because a Bodhisattva acts for the benefit of sentient beings, they differ from a Śrāvaka who is strictly forbidden from such actions.

While violating the third category of offenses constitutes the transgression of the precept against buying and selling, if a Bodhisattva enters a brothel or sells meat, it constitutes a minor offense (*āpatti*).
This is because such actions merely attract and summon people, and do not involve the same degree of intoxication as the sale of alcohol.
[Note] Regarding the thirty-five faults, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* summarizes them in verse as follows: Wealth is empty and invites illness and strife (3);
Nakedness and the manifestation of a shameful name (2); The loss of what was gained by the ignorant (2); Speaking of the hidden and the abandonment of one's work (2); Sorrow upon waking.

Having little physical strength (2), having ruined one's complexion and being arrogant toward one’s parents (2), [disrespecting] śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas (2), as well as paternal uncles, aunts, and elders (2);
not revering the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha (3); aligning with the wicked and distancing oneself from the wise and good (2); violating the precepts and lacking shame and remorse (2);
failing to guard the mind and indulging in sensual desires (2); being loathed by people and abandoned by kinsmen (2); practicing evil and abandoning the wholesome Dharma.

(II) That Which Is Not Trusted by the Wise (I) Being Far from Nirvāṇa Due to Madness and Delusion (II) Falling into Evil Realms at the End of Life (I) If One Obtains Human Form Yet Remains Constantly Stupid (I) Regarding the thirty-five great faults clarified in the *Mahā-śāstra* on the Losses of Alcohol:
the *Śilabhadra-ṭīkā* quotes the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* to explain the ten sins of the oil-pressing house, etc.; the ten sins of the brothel; and the ten sins of the brothel-addict.
The text concerning the offense of running a wine shop is divided into three parts. First, the identification of the person:
"If a Buddha’s disciple.
Second, the sequence of the matter, which has three stages; first, it clarifies that there are three things one should not do. Within this, the first two phrases cite the specific act.
Selling alcohol oneself or teaching others to sell alcohol.
[Commentary]: The wording is the same as the previous section. "Selling" means seeking profit; "teaching others" means causing others to sell wine on one's behalf.
This is likewise a grave offense; teaching others to sell it oneself constitutes a lighter sin.
[Note] The pronunciation of *gù* (酤) is that of "to sell. The dictionary states it refers to selling wine; these three characters are all derived from *yǒu* (wine).
It should properly be read in the departing tone (*qùshēng*). If read in the level tone (*píngshēng*), the entry for "selling wine" (*gùjiǔ*) in the rhyme books also permits its general use.

If read in the entering tone (*shàngshēng*) as *húgǔ* (胡古切), the dictionary states it refers to wine that has fermented for one night. If written as *gū* with the radical for water (*shuǐ*), this is also correct in all three cases.

The character "yīn" (音) is level tone (*ping shēng*) and refers to the name of a river originating from Gāodī; it appears in the *Yúyáng* section under the rising tone (*shǎng shēng*). The rhyme dictionary states that "túgū" (屠沽) also refers to those who sell wine.

Under the departing tone (*qù shēng*), the same dictionary states it is identical [to the preceding entry], while the *Piān* (dictionary) states its pronunciation is "gù" (顧), meaning it is also the name of a river.

Since the entries appear differently in the various dictionaries, although the characters may be used interchangeably, it should properly follow the departing tone (*qù shēng*) with the radical "jiǔ" (酉). [Verse 24: "Forming karma. (二四句成業)
The cause of selling liquor, the condition for selling liquor, the method of selling liquor, and the action of selling liquor.
[Commentary] From "the cause of selling liquor" onwards, the fourfold categorization of the formation of karma is clarified. "Action" refers to the application of the method;
it is the skillful means of the act. "Condition" refers to the fulfillment of five factors: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of a sentient being... [and so forth].

Third, trading for profit; fourth, selling genuine alcohol; fifth, bestowing it upon others. Regarding sentient beings, those who fall into the three aforementioned categories of objects are considered superior;

if they do not become intoxicated or deranged, the offense is light, but if they do become intoxicated or deranged, the offense is heavy. Regarding the middle category of objects, this refers specifically to humans and devas, as they are the primary subjects of the prohibition, and thus the offense is heavy.

Regarding the inferior category of objects, the four realms of existence have a weak capacity for the path of intoxication; therefore, the offense for selling to them is light. As for the assembly, [the same applies].

If one has the perception that it is [already] produced, or expects it to be produced, or harbors doubt, or has a misconception—as previously stated—even if separated by another mind, it constitutes a grave offense.
To sell it for the sake of profit is also grave, because of the desire to sell much. "True wine" refers to that which causes intoxication and confusion;

although medicinal wine may be sold for profit, if it does not cause intoxication, there is no offense in selling it. Second, it is said that at the time of consumption, the offense is determined according to the number of persons.
"If one sells [alcohol] to a child who comes to buy it but ultimately does not drink it, with whom is the heavy [karmic] offense incurred?
[Note: Here, having already cited the topical outline (ko) stating "selling alcohol," this passage now cites the scriptural text (sūtra) to further elaborate upon that outline.

Since the preceding text has already analyzed the matter, the explanation here follows for the sake of convenience; furthermore, because the karma was explained first, these previous instances were all cited as examples.
The *Kēyī xīchāo* (Exegesis on the Meaning of the Vinaya) mistakenly reverses this, taking the present [text] to be erroneous; this is one instance of negligence and error.

Regarding the middle grade of discipline for humans, it may be so, but how could it apply to the heavens? The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that the various devas have wine which is not produced from fermented grain or yeast, but arises from flowers and fruits upon trees;
some say it comes from ponds and streams—this is also "substantial" wine (*vastu-madya*).

Drinking it leads to confusion within the retributions of the heavenly realms; one should likewise exercise restraint and caution, though this confusion differs from that which occurs as a karmic fruit among humans.
When doubts arise regarding exceptional cases, they may be resolved by referring to what precedes them. True alcohol is precisely that which, when drunk, can intoxicate and delude a person.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three types of grain-based alcohol, which is what is produced today, as well as medicinal alcohol.

This does not refer to a person who is confused or intoxicated; it is not the case that children are prohibited from coming here to buy [liquor]—here "buy" (gū, which should be read with a level tone) carries the meaning of purchasing.

Based on this, it appears to be an allowance. However, according to what Jingxi prohibits, even if one commits the offense of a single dewdrop by making food for others at the time prescribed in the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, it is still not permitted;
how much less could such an allowance apply when greed is the cause, as in the case of brewing with malted rice?
To ferment for the purpose of selling is itself the karma of trade. Third, using a light case to illustrate a heavy one:
all types of alcohol must not be sold, for such liquor is the causal condition that gives rise to transgression.
[Note] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are three kinds of liquor: first, grain liquor; second, fruit liquor; and third, liquor made from medicinal herbs, trees, and so forth.
Whether dry or wet, clear or turbid, one must not sell even a single drop the size of a hair-tip;
therefore, it says "all. ○ Second, the explanation of what is appropriate.
Yet a bodhisattva ought to give rise to the wisdom of clear penetration for all sentient beings;
[this is] the third point concerning what is inappropriate,
yet instead they further give rise to the minds of delusion and inversion in all sentient beings.
○ Third, the formal pronouncement of the offense:
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

[Note] Regarding the analogy of the Dharma-gate to the preceding matter, there are three aspects: first, in terms of the dharma; second, in terms of the mind; and third, in terms of the retribution. First:

The reason why selling alcohol is included among the ten grave offenses (*daśa-guruka*) is that while the fault of drinking alcohol oneself—damaging only one’s own person—is not yet profound and thus belongs to the category of minor secondary transgressions (*laghu-āpatti*), selling it harms many people; therefore, it is established as a grave offense.

Furthermore, for a Bodhisattva, between the two benefits of self-benefit and benefiting others, benefiting others is supreme. Since selling alcohol violates the principle of benefiting others, it is considered irrational; how much more so when it actually causes harm to the multitude?

Therefore, as it is inappropriate, the act of drinking has not yet been discussed; first, the giving of alcohol to others is regulated by two factors regarding the mind. As for the mind, it may be of any of the three natures.
If one gives alcohol with a wholesome mind for the sake of reconciling disputes and the like, or out of compassion for their illness, exhaustion, or suffering from cold, the offense is still light.
If it is with an indeterminate mind—meaning the mind is weak while the object is powerful—the offense is of the next degree. If...
To act with a malicious mind to inflict harm is the most grave [offense]. Furthermore, regarding the mind associated with the three poisons, there are two types of greed (*lobha*):
first, when one acts out of a temporary fear for one's own survival due to a lack of self-sufficiency, it should be considered light;

second, when one lacks no material resources yet remains insatiably greedy and attached, it is therefore the most grave. Hatred (*dveṣa*) is also of two types: first, when one bestows [harm] upon another because of existing resentment...

Regarding the delusion that accords with one's own fundamental intent: there are two ways this gives rise to superior-grade anger, causing one to commit evil and obstructing the good in order to gratify that fundamental intent;

this is what makes it grave. Deluded intent is also twofold: first, one considers [the act] not to be grave, thinking to oneself, "Since this is merely produced from water and rice, as long as my mind is not clouded or intoxicated, there should logically be no sin"; therefore, one constantly commits such acts.
Second, regarding the superior merit of abandoning the two views: it is held that by doing so, one will obtain form and power, be able to benefit sentient beings, and cause them great joy;
even if one drinks much [of this], there is gain and no loss. To cling to such an evil view, to act upon it oneself, and to teach others to do so, is logically the most grave offense.
Third, regarding the retribution: as stated in the sutras, there are three types of hells, the first of which is the Hell of the River of Alcohol, where the river consists of fermented liquor.

The second household offense is the Hell of the Liquor Pond, which is the offense of those who sell alcohol; the third is the Hell of Pouring [Liquor] into the Mouth, which is the offense of those who drink alcohol.
Indeed, the faults of drinking alcohol are immeasurable:

it causes others to commit evil karma, leads to stupor and ignorance, and results in the commission of every possible evil, even down to the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*). Such are the faults described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
They form factions with wicked people and distance themselves from the virtuous and good; their wealth is exhausted as they intoxicate their minds, spending without restraint and without limit.
They are shameless in their nakedness, possessing an ugly reputation and ill repute that no one respects.
They disclose all hidden matters to others; though their physical strength is meager, they frequently violate etiquette, opening the door to faults and calamities and giving rise to affliction.
Regarding the affliction [of intoxication], it is as described in the Vinaya concerning the bhikṣu Vālāhaka, who lay drunk upon the ground vomiting; a frog approached his mouth and ate the vomit.
The Buddha said, "This man was able to subdue a venomous dragon, yet now he cannot even subdue a single frog. The faults of alcohol are inexhaustible when explained;
how can a Bodhisattva who upholds the precepts not be cautious? As for the commentary on the Stone Wall (Shibiqi) which says: "If..."
If one brews liquor for one's own benefit but seeks it from others for the sake of profit, it may then be sold. Jingxi cited the teachings stating that "not even a single drop is permitted";
I do not yet know upon what basis Shibi relied to open his argument. A Confucian says: "If a practice is established with frugality, its corruption still leads to greed;
can one not be cautious? △ Sixth: The Precept Against Speaking of the Faults of the Fourfold Assembly.
[Commentary]: This refers to the name for those who speak of the Way (the pronunciation "dào" meaning "to guide").

When the fourfold assembly of followers collectively claims that [a person] has committed the seven heinous offenses or the ten grave transgressions, they suppress and disparage the former individual; because this damages the True Dharma, one incurs sin.

This precept is violated by all seven groups of practitioners and is regulated by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. For a Bodhisattva, whose mind is intent on concealing evil and extolling good, such an offense is particularly grave. Above.

That which is in the second fascicle, that which is in the third fascicle, and that which is at the end of the seventh section concerning the *śrāvaka* dharma—such are the differences between these and those of the bodhisattva. [Note:
First, regarding "yi yimou xigai yi wei suoqi," one character is redundant; following the reading of "Qi" (齊), it is deleted.

Regarding this, it is said that the second article refers to the thirteenth [offense] among the *anāpatti* (rootless) *pārājika* rules, which involves slandering another with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense in order to destroy their purity.
The third article likely refers to the ninety-first [offense] among the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, such as speaking falsely while knowing the truth;
however, I do not yet dare to point to it definitively. All of these are categorized according to the mind to manifest the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior.

To provide further detail: how does this differ from the precept against lying? Ding Shan states: "In the previous case of lying, claiming to have attained the *uttarimanussa-dhamma* (superhuman qualities) for oneself is the primary offense, while slandering others is secondary.
In the present case, speaking ill of others is the primary offense, while self-exaltation is secondary.

The *Xi Chao* states: "Although this is the same as the aforementioned lying in being a vocal karma, this refers specifically to the slander and humiliation of fellow practitioners within the community."
Furthermore, regarding the fault: whether the offense is grave or light, and whether it is true or false, all constitute a violation; thus, they are treated as a separate precept.
However, if one relies on the criterion of "untruth," it is also subsumed under the category of lying (*mṛṣāvāda*). Now, concerning the distinction of the object (*viṣaya*), the faults differ.

It is said that the *Chaoji* (Commentary) does not clarify the distinction between "false speech" (*anṛtavāda*) and "untruth" (*asatya*). The *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states: "Deceiving ordinary people or deceiving sages—there is no actual substance, yet it is a falsehood."
To speak of one’s own excellence is a desire for gain and offerings; to speak of another’s faults is to hear of them and proclaim them so that others may know.
The mind of a Great Being (Mahāsattva) ought to conceal the evil and praise the good of others; how could one possibly hear of a minor fault in another and proclaim it?
Therefore, the Commentary states: "To suppress and obscure another person harms the True Dharma. Thus, this [act] is distinct from false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).

False speech is entirely devoid of factual basis; to report that one has heard of another's faults is not considered false speech because it is based on what was actually heard, and thus the distinction between the real and the unreal is self-evident.
If one were to include both praise and slander in this category, they would be distinct from defamation;

for while one possesses subtle virtues that ought to be cultivated in secrecy, one should not praise oneself, yet if one instead praises their own virtues upon seeing even a slight [virtue] in another...

Because one must provide excessive protection [of others] and refrain from exposing them, yet instead inflicts further humiliation upon them, it is said: "Praise and revile the precepts. The commentary on the *Śāstra* explains:
"To proclaim one's own merits and to deride the faults and evils of others involves two matters; therefore, it is grave.

For a Bodhisattva, who is straightforward toward others and draws in crookedness toward oneself, how could one possibly raise up oneself and revile others? This is clear from the text of the *Śāstra*; this refers to actual facts.
This is not the same as false speech, for it differs from both praising one's own virtues and speaking of others' faults; the distinction is very clear.

If one slanders the Triple Gem, this constitutes a heterodox teaching—claiming that the Dharma of the Triple Gem is no different from the teachings of non-Buddhists, or offering shallow and narrow interpretations of its meaning—and such cases all constitute the slander of the Triple Gem.
Although these are of the same category of vocal karma, the four characteristics must be distinguished, as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
The *Yinlun* (Introduction to the Treatise) states that there are four kinds of speech: first, false speech; second, divisive speech, so called because it causes separation by speaking ill of others;
third, frivolous speech, so called because it praises or reviles without meaning; and fourth, harsh speech, so called because it consists of malicious words of slander and abuse.

However, according to the *Gebi* commentary, these [four] would still result in confusion and overlap. The *Shibi* states: "The first four are identical to the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*) for Śrāvakas in the Vinaya."
The latter four are the same as the four grave offenses of a bodhisattva in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, with the addition of "speaking of the subtle" (*sūkṣma-vāda*) between them;
because speaking of the subtle is more subtle than speaking of the gross (*sthūla*), they are divided into three in successive order. First, the persons are identified.

If you are a Buddha’s disciple: △ Second, the introduction to the matters has three parts, namely: what should not be done, what should be done, and what should be prohibited. ○ Regarding the first, "what should not be done," there are two sections:

first, clarifying the completion of the matter; second, clarifying the completion of the karma. Herein, because the opening provides an illustration by way of contrast, only these two sections are established; those that follow shall be explained below.
As an example, the *Yaoji* (Excerpts) is not clear on this point. First, regarding the accomplishment of the act:
to personally speak of the transgressions of lay or ordained bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, or bhikṣuṇīs, or to instruct others to speak of their transgressions.
II. Explaining the Completion of the Karma. [The factors for the completion of the offense are:
the cause of the offense, the condition of the offense, the dharma of the offense, and the karma of the offense.

[Commentary]: This precept is completed as a grave offense when six conditions are present: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of a sentient being; third, speech; [fourth, the intent to speak]; fifth, the act of speaking; and sixth, the completion of the act.
First, the sinful mind; second, the offense as described; third, the person to whom it is confessed; fourth, the other person’s understanding; fifth, the object being a sentient being;
sixth, the object being of superior or middling capacity—only when one possesses the Bodhisattva precepts is the offense grave, because it obstructs their superior practice.
If one lacks the Bodhisattva precepts and possesses only the Śrāvaka precepts, or if the object is of inferior capacity—whether they possess the precepts or not—the offense is light.
This precept, which purifies [the mind], also serves as a restraint against hindering the conditions for spiritual practice.

The text states that lay bodhisattvas are the *śraddhā-viśuddha* (pure-faith) men and women, while monastic bodhisattvas are those who possess the ten precepts and the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*). Furthermore, it says they are bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
one interpretation holds that these are simply monastic bodhisattvas possessing the full precepts, while another maintains they are śrāvaka monks and nuns.
If one says that this person has committed a grave offense and thus violates a heavy rule, this is because even those who excel in the practice of the Dharma will thereby damage the profound Dharma;

thus, regarding the perception of sentient beings, there are three cases—certainty, doubt, and perversion—the general meaning of which is the same as the three mentioned previously. As for the speaker of the fault, there are two types of intent:
first, the mind of submergence, desiring to cause the other person to lose their reputation and profit; second, the mind of disciplinary punishment, desiring to...
If one causes another person to be bound, these two states of mind are both the primary factors (*karmādhipati*) for violating this precept;
however, if one speaks with the intent to encourage [the offender] or speaks because one has been appointed [to do so], there is no offense.

Regarding the four types of speech mentioned—namely, the seven heinous acts (*ānantarya*) and the ten grave offenses (*daśa-guru-dharma*)—if one refers to the name of the offender, it constitutes a formal violation of this precept. If, however, the intent is to administer punishment, it falls within the four [permissible cases].

Regarding the eighteen cases of violating the prohibitions on the Dharma and the precepts: if one speaks of shedding the Buddha’s blood or causing a schism in the Saṃgha, according to the original Vinaya texts, one must state this before the Saṃgha.
To say such things is to slander the Saṃgha; because events such as shedding blood are rare, this precept is considered light.

However, if one speaks of these matters to someone who lacks the precepts, it constitutes a grave offense. Therefore, when a grave crime is committed, it receives a grave name; this matter should be understood according to its true meaning.

Regarding "light" offenses, this means that if one misinterprets what is appropriate as inappropriate, it constitutes a grave offense; likewise, if one causes the mind to be heavy or the matter to be grave, both are equally grave offenses.

This is called a deviation of perspective (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). As for a deviation regarding the matter itself: if one regards what is actually light as grave, one commits a grave offense; if one regards what is actually grave as light, the offense is light.

This is because the gravity or lightness of the offense depends on the mind's perception of lightness or gravity. If one composes a letter or dispatches a messenger, it is said in one sense to be equally grave.
One interpretation holds that although the offense is light, if one violates the seven heinous acts or the ten grave precepts, one loses the precepts previously received;

it is only said to be a "light defilement" (āpatti) when explained subsequently. Regarding confession to others, this refers to confessing before those of the upper or middle levels who do not possess the Bodhisattva precepts;

because such an act deeply damages the Dharma, it constitutes a grave offense. For those of the lower level, all [confessions] are light, as the damage does not exceed what is profound. As the text states: "The Bodhisattva..."

When one hears the teachings of non-Buddhists or those of the Two Vehicles that contain faults regarding the Buddha-Dharma, one ought to teach and transform them with compassion; yet, instead, one speaks of [the Buddha-Dharma] as being identical [to their errors].
This is to speak of disparagement toward those people to an extreme degree. When the six persons before one believe and understand what has been said, the matter of verbal karma is established;
at this time, the offense is determined. Regarding the quantity of the offense: first, it is said to follow the number of persons; second, it is said to follow the number of utterances.
This refers to karma.

[Note] Regarding the "Ten Precepts" and the "Complete Precepts": the Ten Precepts refer to the reception of the ten major precepts (*daśa-śīla*), while the Complete Precepts refer to the full set of precepts (*upasampadā-śīla*), which are the precepts of the Hīnayāna.
These may involve first taking the Mahāyāna and later the Hīnayāna, or first taking the Hīnayāna and later the Mahāyāna; thus, the meaning encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.

The phrase "two groups" (*dvi-saṃgha*) refers to this very point. Furthermore, regarding the word "etcetera" (*ādi*): since it has already been stated that they have "left the household life," why is it further said there are "two groups"?
This explanation clarifies that both interpretations are valid. According to the Vinaya sections, both [offenses] are minor. One should doubt and avoid these three meanings;
the current text is extremely detailed, and one should apply this principle throughout all the precepts to explain their meaning.
The *Yexi chao* states: "If such is the case even regarding actual facts, how much more so for those who fabricate right and wrong out of thin air?

To suppress the achievements of predecessors and damage the True Dharma incurs the gravest transgressions. When unworthy individuals spread slander—whether under their own names or anonymously—it matters not whether they possess the precepts or not;
one should simply regret it, for the Confucian classics state: 'Hearing of another's faults is like hearing the name of one's parents.'"
It can be heard with the ears, yet it cannot be spoken with the mouth; how much more so for a Great Being whose heart is set on concealing evil and exalting good?
In the *Daci jing* (Great Compassion Sūtra), Dingshan quotes:

"When a renunciant leaves one tavern and goes to another, embracing a boy with his left hand and a girl with his right, at the time when the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa enter parinirvāṇa, he respectfully entreats the sons of the Buddha [to remain]."
One should explain this further. Second, clarifying the "should":

when a bodhisattva hears non-Buddhists, evil persons, or those of the two vehicles speak what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya within the Buddha-dharma, they should constantly give rise to a heart of compassion and teach these evil people so as to cause them to produce wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna.
Third, it is improper;
yet the Bodhisattva, on the contrary, further speaks of the faults and transgressions within the Buddha-dharma.
Third, this constitutes an offense.
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva. [Commentary:

Following the precedent of the previous dharma-gate, there are likewise four aspects: first, regarding the object; second, regarding the speech; third, regarding the mind; and fourth, regarding the retribution.
Regarding the object, there is the object that is spoken of and the object that is confronted. As for what is spoken of, there are six types: first, those on the stages (*bhūmi*).

A Bodhisattva acts contrary to worldly ways for the sake of sentient beings by speaking of what is not so: first, by speaking of the faults of those with the two views; second, by speaking of the subtle lapses of the Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness and the noble ones of the four fruits;
third, by speaking of the transgressions of one’s own Upādhyāya and Ācārya; fourth, by speaking of the faults of the Dharma-transmitting administrators;
fifth, by speaking of the faults of fellow practitioners who observe pure precepts; and sixth, by speaking of those who have broken their precepts or possess no precepts at all.
Beyond these six, there are five objects corresponding to those where the offense is initially grave and subsequently light:
first, speaking of the transgressions of kings and ministers to cause them to abandon their faith and destroy the Triple Gem;

second, speaking of the faults of non-Buddhists, evil persons, or those seeking out faults together with one, to increase their wrong views and cause them to slander the Buddha-dharma; third, speaking of [one's own] corruption to faithful laypeople.

Regarding these three objects of faith, the first is heavy and the latter two are light. There is no offense in five cases: (1) speaking with a pleasant mind to one's own assembly as a skillful means to obtain [their understanding of] transgressions;
(2) exposing faults and reprimanding within the assembly, or speaking to that teacher to have them provide instruction and so forth;
(2) regarding speech, either using extremely base and evil words or speaking with harsh and cutting severity.
By speaking in general terms, the gravity of the offense can be understood; if one writes such things to others, it may likewise be inferred by analogy.
Third, regarding the mind, there are three poisons: either with a deluded mind, one claims that speaking [of faults] is a virtue and does not fear breaking the precepts;
or with a hateful mind, one retaliates against an enemy’s speech to vent one's own emotions; or with a greedy mind, one craves gain and offerings.
To speak of the faults of others for the sake of fame, or to cause them to turn toward oneself for one's own benefit; furthermore, regarding the three moral natures of the mind:

as for the evil nature, it is as described above; as for the wholesome nature, it means speaking to subdue others so that they may become fearful [of wrongdoing], yet not actually doing so—this constitutes no offense.
As for the neutral nature, it refers to speaking with a casual, frivolous mind or through false recollection; in such cases, an offense cannot be avoided. (4)
Speaking in terms of retribution, the karmic consequences for the transgressions of monks, nuns, and bodhisattvas are extremely grave.
As described in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, they enter the Hell of the Plucked Tongue, where their tongues are plowed, and so forth.

Furthermore, as stated in the *Acintyabodhisattvanirdeśa Sūtra*, because the Bodhisattva Bahudhana spoke of the faults of the Bodhisattva Bhadradatta, he fell into the state of a courtesan for ninety-one kalpas.
Having given birth to them within one’s own belly, one discards them so that they are devoured by foxes and wolves;

the suffering caused by a single lapse of speech is such that it serves as a sufficient mirror for reflection. Therefore, a Bodhisattva should always praise all the virtues possessed by all sentient beings, let alone those of other Bodhisattvas and the internal community of monks and nuns.
As the *Wuxing jing* (Sutra on the Five Practices) says: "If one sees a person who has broken the precepts..."
One should not speak of their faults; rather, one should mindfully reflect that such persons will also attain the wisdom of the Path after a long time.

The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* quotes the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, saying: "If those sentient beings possess no goodness whatsoever that may be praised, one should praise them by reflecting upon the goodness of their Buddha-nature.
One should acknowledge one's own faults to purify one's own mind; with the exception of Bodhisattvas who act out of compassion."
Exposing faults, censuring, or expelling may be done for the sake of subduing another’s evil conduct through verbal instruction, or by employing skillful means such as enlisting the power of a king;
in these cases, there is no offense. Conversely, if one speaks of another's faults even with a single thought of malice, one commits a grave offense.
Be careful! Be careful! △ Seventh: The Precept Against Self-Praising and Slandering Others.
[Commentary: "Self-praise" refers to extolling one's own merits; "slandering others" refers to reviling the faults and evils of others.

Because these two matters are combined, they constitute a grave offense for Bodhisattvas. To draw straightness toward others while bending oneself toward them—how could one raise oneself up and slander others?

Therefore, this constitutes an offense. It is committed by all seven classes of practitioners and is regulated by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. However, for Bodhisattvas, the primary aim is to bring benefit and peace to others.

The offense of praising oneself while disparaging others is grave; the Śrāvaka does not concern himself with others, yet to disparage another constitutes the third category of offense, whereas to praise oneself constitutes the seventh group of offenses.
First, the person is identified:
"If a Buddha’s disciple..."
△ Second, the introductory section, which has three parts: first, what is not appropriate; second, [the actual content]; third, [the conclusion]. ○ First, clarifying the accomplishment of the deed:
praising oneself and disparaging others, as well as teaching others to praise themselves and disparage others.
○ Second, clarifying the formation of karma.
[This constitutes a grave offense] by disparaging another’s causes, disparaging another’s conditions, disparaging another’s dharmas, or disparaging another’s karma.
[Commentary: The wording is the same as before. This precept is completed as a grave offense when five conditions are met: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of that being as such;

third, the intention to praise or disparage; fourth, the expression of the means of praise or disparagement; fifth, the understanding of the meaning by the person addressed. First, it must be a sentient being.

Regarding this, one interpretation states that if one destroys an object of the superior or middle [categories], it constitutes a grave offense; if one destroys an object of the inferior category, it is a light offense.

A second interpretation holds that it is grave only when the object of the superior or middle categories is someone who possesses the Bodhisattva precepts, because such a person is deeply afflicted and the obstruction caused is profound; whereas if the object lacks the precepts or is of the inferior category even if they possess the precepts, the affliction and obstruction are shallow, and thus the offense is light.

Regarding the perception of sentient beings, there are three cases: perceiving them as such, having doubt about it, or having a distorted perception. Furthermore, there are three degrees of magnitude: great, medium, and small.
The meaning is the same as the three [previous cases] regarding the mind of praise and disparagement: that is, to exalt oneself and suppress others with the desire to cause them distress.
If this is done for the purpose of subduing [the other], there is no offense. As for the case where one's own mind is not the primary factor but one instructs another, there are two interpretations:

the first says it is equally grave; the second says the offense is light. Regarding the fourth point, concerning those who possess both praise and disparagement: this sutra speaks generally of "others" receiving humiliation, whereas according to the Vinaya...

Regarding the eight matters [of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses], it is said that when the five [factors] are fulfilled and the other person understands, that person understands the words of praise or censure;
for each word spoken, a heavy offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is incurred. Having already lost the precept through this, it is subsequently a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

The previous precept was established to prohibit speaking of another's faults; among the eight matters, the specific offense here is heavy because one speaks to a person who no longer possesses the precepts.
[Note] Regarding "not oneself" (*ji-hi-shin*), Tōzan says: "It refers to the mind that praises oneself and disparages others; this is precisely the karmic lord. "Self" (*ji*) means praising oneself;
it does not mean disparaging others. Regarding "in vain" (*banshu*), the meaning generally refers to other people. The *Kishō* states:
"If one borrows the meaning of 'overflowing water ruining things,' then the karma of praising oneself and disparaging others is like water ruining [the vessel]."

This destroys the roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna nature-precepts. On what basis is this interpretation made? The commentary merely states in general terms that "the karmic characteristics of others receiving humiliation are very extensive;
the eight matters are found in the Vinaya and should be consulted by those who require them.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore" (*zēngshàng*) appearing later, which refers only to natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), Tingshan says: "If one follows the preceding text, the character 'later' (*hòu*) should be changed to the character 'again' (*fù*); thus, it is a restatement."
The preceding precept refers to the aforementioned transgressions. II. Clarifying the Response:
A Bodhisattva should respond by taking upon himself all the suffering, insults, and evil deeds of all sentient beings, while giving his own good fortune to others.

[Note] The *Zangshu* states: "Because the dharmas of the Bodhisattvas consist of taking upon oneself the abuse and injury inflicted upon others—if one does not take them upon oneself, it is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva;
how much more so when one further inflicts abuse and injury? The violation and harm are indeed profound. Thus, the meaning of the concluding text on the gravity [of the offense] is as follows:
to transgress and deceive is called "abuse" (*hui*); to cause another to feel shame and humiliation is called "insult" (*ru*). ○ Third, the conclusion regarding what is improper.
If one extols one's own virtues while concealing the good deeds of others, thereby causing those others to suffer defamation—
this constitutes the third summary of the offense:
it is a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the preceding matters by way of analogy through the Dharma-gates, there are five further points: first, regarding the Dharma; second, regarding the object;

third, regarding speech; fourth, regarding the mind; and fifth, regarding retribution. As for the first: when a Bodhisattva manifests what is appropriate while secretly practicing internal cultivation, they may praise the virtues of others and disparage themselves.
However, this further incurs sinful karma. The previous precept concerned speaking of another’s faults based on those very faults; yet even that [was already a violation].

Now, to enter further into the details: whereas in the previous case the fault was already grave, here the fault is even more serious because one not only recounts past transgressions but adds further insults.

While "recounting faults" and "insulting others" may appear similar and overlap, they differ in that the former involves speaking based on actual faults, whereas this case involves adding insults where no fault exists.
Second, regarding the object (*viṣaya*), it is the same as before; however, in this context, the object includes self-praise. Third, regarding the speech itself, it is as previously described.

To say that another lacks virtue, that their virtues are excessive, or that their virtues are few; to say that they have no faults when they have some, or that their faults are many when they are few—all such acts are skillful means for disparaging others in order to make them believe [one's own superiority].

As for words of self-praise, such as claiming to have attained sainthood (*āryatva*), or asserting that one possesses the precepts when one does not, or that one possesses the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) when one does not—such claims regarding the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) are instances where one speaks of possessing them or other such qualities out of a desire for excellence.
In the *Dṛṣṭivāda*, five types of great thieves are described. The first is one who violates the seven classes of offenses (*saptanikāya*) yet claims to be pure.
Although this case should be distinguished from false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), it is nonetheless included here because of the intent of self-praise;
however, while false speech is also an un-Aryan statement, it differs from this case in that it involves praising oneself by means of disparaging others. (4)
Regarding the first point: if one praises oneself and disparages others for the purpose of inspiring faith in another, there is no offense.
Second, if an offense is committed through negligence or an indeterminate state of mind, or if it is committed out of affection or hatred toward another, these do not yet fall within this category.
Third, if one acts out of a desire for fame, reputation, gain, or offerings, wishing to cause others to show them respect and so forth, this is what is prohibited herein.
This is grave; as stated in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, to disparage those who transmit the Dharma so that the Buddha-dharma cannot prevail in a region is the most serious offense.

Nevertheless, the various sūtras and śāstras caution against this in great detail, clarifying that all offenses committed by those within the Buddhist community arise from a mind of greed and delusion.
In total, there are four types, namely the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).
Furthermore, within the training of the single precept practiced in combination with other practices, there are two types: first, those who affect eccentricity;

such as a bhikṣu who, though not having broken the precepts, is by nature not upright, yet relying on false deliberations manifests extraordinary deportment to dazzle the world and seek fame and profit.
Second, those of shallow understanding; being devoid of deep wisdom, they rely on their own observance of the precepts to overstep and disparage those of superior capacity.
Those who hear of emptiness and become terrified—all such individuals are thieves of the *āraṇya*. Second, regarding the training in vows (*śikṣāpada*), there are also two types:
first, those characterized by greed and deception, meaning those whose nature delights in fame and profit;

though they have long resided in the mountains, their minds have little realization of stillness, yet they manifest signs of meditative concentration to dazzle worldly people, seeking great renown and universally suppressing others who lack such signs.
All such [practitioners] consider themselves to be non-[monastics]; they are also "araṇya-thieves" as described in the *Huashou jing*. Furthermore, another sutra states:

"Wearing patched robes in secluded places, they claim for themselves to be 'āraṇyakas'. These two types refer to those who are characterized by false pride (*mithyāmāna*): their nature is not one of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), yet they rely on the mountains to practice meditation.
Ghosts and spirits empower them, causing them to believe they truly possess meditative concentration and to perceive the unwholesome thoughts of others.
Relying on this, they give rise to pride and great fame, looking down upon others and regarding all else as wrong;

they harm the Buddha-dharma and are great thieves who belong to the faction of Māra. As stated in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra*, the training in the three types of wisdom (*tri-prajñā*) is also twofold:
first, concerning those of shallow capacity, meaning those whose nature is not particularly sharp and who study without sequential order—this is termed "fame-seeking" (*nāma-lābha*).

Driven by impulsive haste, they prematurely proclaim their own views, making arbitrary judgments and slandering the teachings of both past and present; seeking only fame and profit, they lack any intention for spiritual liberation.

Relying on their own lack of practice, they also treat the precepts and meditative concentration with contempt. These are thieves who sell the Buddha-Dharma and shall surely encounter great suffering.
This particular offense appears among the demonic activities described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; in recent times, many practitioners have fallen into this kind of transgression.
Regarding the Buddha-dharma, those who covet fame and profit should reflect upon this to examine their own minds; can they not admonish themselves? Second, concerning those of deep [insight]:

this refers to those whose natures possess some degree of clarity and discernment, and who, though somewhat proficient in the texts and meanings of the Two Vehicles and the Tripiṭaka, have not yet grasped the intent of the Buddha.

Since they are now entrusted with the transmission of the Dharma, they merely praise fame and profit to encourage later students, while disparaging both the ancients and the present. Manifesting... [the truth].

To rely exclusively on this as a virtue and give rise to pride that towers above others—merely reciting the medicine of the Dharma while failing to extinguish one's own afflictions—is already a grave transgression;
how much more so to further give rise to affliction within the Buddha-dharma, which is utterly impermissible!
It is like fire emerging from water; by what means could it be extinguished? This is a thief who harms the Buddha-dharma. (From the *Buddhapiṭaka-daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*)
Among these four, within the context of mixed conduct (*miśra-caryā*), there are also two types: first, regarding meritorious conduct (*puṇya-caryā*).
This refers to those who are not upright by nature but instead employ deceitful schemes to collectively pursue extraordinary merits, dazzling the world and attracting heavy offerings.

Their intent is to call for much by giving little, thereby securing their livelihood. Once they have achieved what they sought, they rely on this to give rise to pride, looking down upon and suppressing others.
When others receive no offerings or gain, they all consider it a lack of profit; since this is so regarding material gain, it is the same regarding fame.
This is also the thief who sells the Buddha-dharma, as stated in the *Kāśyapa Sūtra*. Second, regarding other practices:

those who do not possess the wisdom of intrinsic nature, upon learning even a single teaching, immediately become attached to it and become deluded by what they have studied, using it to attract fame and profit, while they disparage and reject other practices they have cultivated.
None of these are ultimate; they are likewise foolish people who act as vermin and thieves to the Buddha-dharma.
I exhort all later students to constantly examine themselves, ensuring that their own minds do not fall into the grasp of these various thieves who damage the aspiration for Bodhi.

I urge you to read such sutras as the *Ratnakūṭa*, the *Ratnarāśi*, and the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* to take them deeply as a warning. Therefore, in this commentary on the *Tripiṭaka*, I clarify the practice of cultivation.
A bodhisattva should not harbor even a single thought of concealment regarding their own transgressions—
fearing that they might increase and being mindful that they are difficult to extinguish— and should never speak of their own virtues, nor give rise to even a single thought of self-glorification—
fearing that they might be depleted and being mindful that they do not increase. Furthermore, a bodhisattva should always [behave] toward other sentient beings...
To see only their faults and to see only their virtues—for this reason, one endures their faults and draws upon oneself while projecting virtue onto others;
thus the mind remains purely clear, and this constitutes constant practice. He further distinguishes by asking:

"If one endures faults when one has none oneself, and projects virtue when another has none, is this not flattery and false speech? He answers: "How could one who dwells in self-insufficiency be without faults?"

"Loss" refers to the absence of loss; only the Buddha alone is thus, because his defilements have been exhausted. Furthermore, others possess no further goodness than that which arises from the buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*);
this is itself true goodness. If one intends this and practices patience and investigation, it is not merely free from flattery, but also free from falsehood.
As stated in the section on *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, and patience: "Be humble as the ocean and the rivers; though turbid and foul things flow into them, they remain submissive."

Just as a bridge must endure the toil of being trampled by people and horses, and just as a target for archery must receive a multitude of arrows without resentment or malice, so too one who practices such patience should never praise themselves or disparage others.
Therefore, a bodhisattva bhikṣu should constantly examine the sources of his reputation; he should not dwell in places where there is much gain and honor.
Because it causes harm, the *Vyavahāra-śāstra* states: "Gain and offerings are like frost and hail; they can damage the sprouts of merit.

Since one must avoid them even when obtained in accordance with the Dharma, how much more so when various faults arise from them? How could one not exercise self-restraint? Fifth, regarding retribution:
as mentioned above, there is no fault in [avoiding] disparaging others, but it is improper to praise oneself and greedily seek fame and profit through wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Those who dwell within the Buddha-dharma as its thieves will surely fall into hell and undergo all manner of suffering, as explained in detail in the treatises.
Furthermore, the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that there are four ways in which a bodhisattva falls: first, lack of respect for others; second, ingratitude and deceitful crookedness;
third, excessive seeking of gain, offerings, fame, and reputation; and fourth, feigning goodness and proclaiming one's own virtues. These are the four.
They will fall into hell. To speak specifically regarding the retribution for disparaging [the Dharma]:
as recorded in the *Buddha-bhāṣita-śāstra-dūṣaka-sūtra*, there were ten people who slandered the Dharma Master Jibian; consequently, the Buddha-dharma in that region declined and fell into ruin.
These ten people later fell into hell and, for immeasurable kalpas, underwent sufferings such as having their tongues torn out. Subsequently, they were reborn many times blind and without ears.
Later, he encountered Śākyamuni Buddha and left the household life; after practicing asceticism for a long time, however, he attained nothing at all.
He was then made to return to secular life, as is explained in detail in the sūtras. To speak of his self-praise specifically:

when the five men, including Śreṇika, were sitting in the forest with four of them while one remained in the village, he proclaimed, "There is an Arhat in the forest," and consequently received great offerings.
After being raised, he fell into hell and underwent all manner of suffering.

Upon emerging, he was reborn as a human, yet again became a carrier for his original benefactor, serving as a bearer of palanquins and a holder of vessels for filth, as described in detail in the Vinaya texts. Thus we know that self-praise and disparaging others result in even greater transgression.
△ Eighth: The Precept Against Stinginess and Further Disparagement.
[Commentary]: "Miserliness" (*mātsarya*) is a term for the stinginess of craving; "adding insult" refers to physically or verbally humiliating another person.

When someone seeks wealth or requests the Dharma, to be miserly and refuse to give while further adding humiliation is a complete violation of the path of transformation; therefore, one incurs an offense.

Regarding this precept, all seven classes of followers commit the same offense, though its application differs between the Mahayana and Hinayana. For a Bodhisattva, there is no distinction made between those who are close or distant; whatever seekers come, they must bestow [gifts].

If one does not bestow [instruction] but instead insults [the recipient], it constitutes an offense against the original vow because of the commitment to benefit all beings; thus, for a Śrāvaka, this is an offense against the seventh category (*saptama-varga*) as a failure to teach disciples.

If one does not bestow material goods, it does not constitute an offense for the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha within two years [of ordination]; however, regarding the failure to bestow material goods or the Dharma, it constitutes an offense against the third category.
Beyond two years, failing to bestow [these] constitutes an offense against the seventh category. If insult is added, each specific act shall be separately adjudicated.
This is not considered a grave offense.

[Commentary] Not accepting an apology violates the way of engaging with others; therefore, one incurs an offense. This precept is committed by all seven classes of practitioners.

While the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not entirely agree on this, for a Bodhisattva, whose fundamental nature is to embrace sentient beings, to become angry and create a barrier constitutes a grave offense (pārājika); for a Śrāvaka, it does not.
