Therefore, one must not engage in the buying and selling of free persons, slaves, or livestock, nor trade in coffins, timber, or other implements used for containing the dead.
[Commentary]: As for "buying and selling," this refers to those who breed livestock by mouth or those who traffic in free persons, causing much suffering through the dispersal of their kin.
If one trades in coffins, it is due to a malicious intent to seek profit; therefore, both monastics and laypeople alike must refrain from such practices.
II. Providing an illustration by way of comparison:
One should not even do it oneself, much less teach others to do it (some versions omit the character "yìng").
III. Pointing out the fault and concluding that it is wrong.
If one intentionally performs [the act] oneself or instructs another to perform it, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
[Commentary: Whether one performs it oneself, instructs another to do it for oneself, or instructs another to perform it themselves, all constitute a minor offense.
If one steals living beings to sell them as livestock, causes them to be killed, or uses incantations to cause a person's death in order to obtain a coffin for sale—[these are all minor offenses].
This constitutes a separate offense of theft and a separate offense of killing.
△ Thirteenth: The Precept Against Slandering and Defaming.

[Commentary] Because it causes others to fall into ruin and wounds the spirit of compassion, this precept is established. It is regulated in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; all seven classes of practitioners are equally subject to its violation.

Regarding those who take the Bodhisattva precepts together with devas and humans, if one speaks of their seven heinous acts or ten grave offenses— whether they have fallen into ruin or are being punished—
it constitutes a grave offense regardless of whether the basis for the claim exists or not, provided it is spoken toward a person of a different category.

Having already explained the precept against revealing the faults of the fourfold assembly, it is now further ordained that if one speaks toward a fellow practitioner of the same category, it is a grave offense regardless of the status of the recipient.

Regarding those who sink and drown because they either possess or lack the precepts, this offense constitutes a light defilement for both. ○ First, the person is identified: "If a Buddha’s disciple...
△ The introduction to the matter has three parts: first, citing the act of slandering; second, what should be done; third, what should not be done. ○ Now, the first part.
Because of an evil mind, one groundlessly slanders others— such as virtuous people, Dharma masters, teachers, monks, kings, or nobles—
claiming they have committed the seven reversals or the ten grave offenses.
(2) Explaining what should be done.
One should give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience, as well as a mind of compassion and kindness, toward one’s parents, brothers, and the six classes of kinsmen.
[Commentary] Regarding the mention of "parents and brothers," this refers to the mind of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), who constantly regards all beings as his parents and kinsmen,
and should thus give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience, as well as a mind of compassion and kindness.

[Note] The "six relations" refers to father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, wife, and son. Regarding the third [point], "not being worthy of it, yet instead further inflicting injury and harm, one falls into an undesirable state":
this means that although these six relations do not deserve such treatment, one nonetheless commits acts of violence against them and consequently falls into an unfavorable rebirth.
[Commentary: Now, on the contrary, one further incurs the offense of slandering and harming a Śrāvaka who shares the same precepts, views, and conduct;

for those who falsely accuse another of the four grave offenses (*catur-āpattika*) without basis, the penalty is a formal act of suspension (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). The remaining details are explained at length in the Vinaya section. 3. Conclusion of the Offense.
One commits a minor offense of defilement.
△ Fourteenth: The Precept Against Setting Fires.

[Commentary] Because it injures sentient beings with consciousness, this is proscribed for all seven groups of practitioners; it is regulated by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The text is divided into three parts.
○ First, the person is designated:
"If a Buddha’s disciple.
△ The sequence of the matter has three parts: 1. the act of setting fire; 2. the distant presence of burning; 3. the indictment of the fault and the binding of the transgression.
First: Out of an evil mind, one sets a great fire to burn mountains, forests, and wilderness from the fourth month through the ninth month.
[Commentary] Some say that since killing ghosts or animals violates the first grave precept (*pārājika*), this precept was established merely to prohibit burning.

The meaning of "distant harm" is now explained: since killing ghosts or animals does not constitute a grave offense (*pārājika*), the case of burning forest trees where creatures die is governed by the same regulation as that [killing] precept.
From the fourth month to the ninth month, many insects and other life-forms are born;

during this time, both monastics and laypeople are equally prohibited from burning forest trees. This is because there is a significant risk of causing harm to living beings. For a lay bodhisattva, [this constitutes a secondary offense].
Regarding "burning through karma": if a bodhisattva who has renounced the world fails to restrain himself and thereby obstructs the affairs of the community, he should be permitted [to leave];
however, if he does not exercise caution and burns through his transgressions, he incurs a minor offense (light impurity). ○ Second, there is burning from afar.
If one burns the houses, cities, monasteries, fields, or timber of others, as well as the property of spirits, officials,
or any other living beings (in some versions, "kings"), one must not do so intentionally.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "all things that have life," it is an error to say they "have life" when one should instead say they "have an owner.
One should know that if one burns property belonging to an owner, it constitutes the offense of destroying life not only in the fourth and ninth months, but at all times.
[Note] Other editions all read "possessed by a master" (*sāmi-ka*). This section on "forests and mountains" and so forth is divided into two parts:

forests and mountains are objects without a master, while houses and dwellings are objects with a master. However, this interpretation seems somewhat inconvenient, for how could forests and mountains ever be exclusively without a master?
Thus, the Great Master said: "If it were an object possessed by a master, why would [the rule apply] only during the four months? (referring to the nine-day period).
Month. ○ Third, citing the transgression to conclude the offense:
If one intentionally burns [the scriptures], one commits a minor secondary offense (light dust-offense).
△ The Fifteenth Precept on Deviant Teaching.
[Commentary] Because it causes people to lose the right path, [the prohibitions] are established for the seven assemblies, with the same offenses for both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
they are divided into three because of the differences in what each group practices. First, the persons are designated.
If you are a Buddha’s disciple:
△ Section on the Matter, Part Three: First, identifying those who should be taught; second, clarifying what should be done; third, clarifying what should not be done.
○ Now, the first.
[From] the Buddha’s disciples, through non-Buddhists, evil persons, the six types of relatives, and all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

[Commentary: "The Buddha’s disciples" refers to the internal assembly; "non-Buddhists" refers to the external assembly; "the six types of relatives and spiritual friends" encompass both the internal and external assemblies. II. Explaining the Response.

One should instruct each individual to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas; one should instruct them to understand the principles and meanings so that they may give rise to the bodhicitta—
the ten minds of departure, the ten minds of nurturing, and the ten adamantine minds— and understand the sequential methods and applications within these thirty minds.

[Commentary: One should instruct them according to the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas to arouse the ten minds of bodhicitta. These are the ten transcendent minds (*daśa-vyutkrāntika-cittāni*), which give rise to the adamantine mind (*vajra-citta*).
This refers to the ten adamantine minds; the ten nurturing minds are omitted for brevity.
These thirty [minds] must be urgently revealed and explained to practitioners at the beginning of their practice.

[Note] The *Xichao* states: "Briefly omitting what follows" indicates that the older versions of the sutra lacked this section. This makes it clear that the intent regarding the stages of knowledge (*vidyā*) is to cause one to ascend through them;
therefore, it is said that the beginner must act with urgency. ○ Third, [the section on] what is not appropriate.

Yet, if a bodhisattva, out of a malicious mind or a mind of anger, indiscriminately teaches others the precepts, sutras, vinaya, and śāstras of the two vehicles (śrāvakas), or the heterodox and false views of non-Buddhist treatises, [he commits an offense]. [Commentary]:

One should not teach the vehicles of the two [vehicles] or external texts with a malicious mind; however, if one perceives the capacity [of the recipient] and it benefits sentient beings, there is no offense.
These are the three offenses involving forfeiture;
they constitute light secondary offenses.
△ The sixteenth: To preach the precepts perversely for the sake of profit.

[Commentary: Because it violates the way of instruction and transmission, this is established as a transgression common to the seven classes of disciples. While both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna prohibit the preceding precept, that one concealed the Great Vehicle and displayed only the Small;
whereas the present precept, although it speaks of the Great, involves being stingy regarding profit and stubbornly concealing the underlying principles, thus constituting a light defilement.

[Note] *Jin* (靳) is pronounced with the *qie* (切) of *ju* (居) and *xin* (忻); it means "firmly. This refers to being stubbornly attached [to profit], such that one only preaches the *Dharmakara-sūtra* after first securing material gain.
The *Shuchao* (疏鈔) considers this precept to be for the sake of cherishing the Dharma; thus, seeking profit is also virtuous. ○ First, the person is designated.
If you are a Buddha’s disciple:
△ Regarding the three stages of the preliminary practice: first, one should study for oneself; second, one should explain it in full for those who come later;
third, one should not conceal or suppress it for the sake of profit. ○ First, regarding the stage of studying for oneself:

One should, with a sincere heart, first study the Mahāyāna Vinaya-sūtras on majestic deportment to extensively open up and understand their meanings and flavors (some editions read "meanings and principles").
Second, one should explain them in full for those who come later.

[Note] Regarding this precept scripture, the *Tiantai Jieshu* (Tiantai’s Commentary on the Precepts) divides it into only three sections, providing merely a general outline; other commentaries, however, are more detailed.
Here, I shall employ the *Zangshu* (Commentary from the Canon) for a detailed subdivision so that it may be easily understood.
△ Other [commentaries] divide the section beginning with "After seeing" into two parts for the sake of instructing future students. ○ First, the new student comes seeking instruction.
He saw that there were newly initiated bodhisattvas who had come from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas.
△ Second, the actual teaching given to them has two parts: first, he spoke of ascetic practices to strengthen their resolve;
second, he spoke of the true Dharma to increase their wisdom and realization. Regarding the first, there are again two sections. ○ First, the general heading.
One should, in accordance with the Dharma, explain that all such ascetic practices are suffering.
II. Specific Analysis:
Whether one burns the body, the arms, or the fingers, or fails to burn the body, arms, or fingers as an offering to the Buddhas, this is not the way of a renunciant.
A bodhisattva should even give up his own body, flesh, hands, and feet to provide for hungry tigers, wolves, lions,
and all hungry ghosts. Second,
he should preach the True Dharma for them so that their wisdom and awakening may increase.
Thereafter, he explained the True Dharma to them one by one in sequence, causing their minds to open and their intentions to be understood.

[Commentary: This is evident from the text. Some masters say that the ascetic practices listed here were intended to restrain [the Bodhisattva] from saving sentient beings; otherwise, it would be a minor offense.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this is a phrase used for comparison—by citing what is submerged to illustrate what is above water—suggesting that a Great Being ought to sacrifice his own body as an offering to others.
If, after that, he would have fully expounded the Dharma for them, how much more so now, when he merely stops to preach the Dharma—how could he hope for profit while remaining hidden?

[Note] The *Shanbu* (Deletions and Additions) cites the *Zuozhuan*: "He has majesty that is awe-inspiring and decorum that is emulatable. The Sūtras explain the training in concentration (*samādhi*) and the various virtues of majestic decorum;
the Vinaya explains the training in morality (*śīla*) and the standards of ritual decorum. Kuang said: "First, he preached to them regarding suffering."
The intent of this practice lies in valuing the Dharma and disregarding one’s life; it does not mean that one should immediately sacrifice one's body or limbs by burning them.

If one were to immediately sacrifice their body, for whom would they preach the Dharma? This is identical to the second interpretation listed in the Commentary. Three: explaining why [this] is inappropriate.
Yet, for the sake of gain and offerings, a bodhisattva may fail to answer when they ought to, or provide distorted explanations of the words of the Sūtras and Vinaya, lacking proper sequence,
thereby slandering the Triple Gem— such is the speaker.
[Commentary] The characteristics of the three types of texts in the latter stage are shown here and are easy to discern.
[Note] Regarding the three things shown: first, for the sake of gain and offerings; second, failing to respond when one ought to respond; and third, explaining the Sūtras and Vinaya erroneously.
Third, the determination of the offense: one commits a minor secondary offense (light dust-offense).
△ Seventeenth: The Precept Against Begging by Exploiting Power.

[Commentary] Because it causes affliction to others, this is established as a transgression for all seven classes of practitioners; it is regulated by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. ○ First, the identification of the person.
If a Buddha’s disciple:
△ The introduction to the matter has three parts: first, approaching for personal gain; second, making unreasonable requests;
third, exposing faults and assigning blame. ○ Now, the first.
Out of desire for food, drink, wealth, gain, and reputation, one associates with kings, princes, ministers, and officials.
(2) Unjust solicitation.
To rely on the creation of intimidating displays to beg, extort, strike, or drag others away to take money and goods by force;
to seek profit in every way, which is called "evil seeking," "excessive seeking," or "teaching others to seek.
[Note] The *Rongchao* quotes the *Five Hundred Questions*: "In the past, there was a bhikṣu who begged excessively and accumulated wealth, refusing to give it away for the sake of others."
Furthermore, because he did not cultivate the Path while possessing merit, after his life ended, he became a mountain of flesh-camels spanning several tens of *li* in breadth.
During a time of famine and scarcity, the people of the entire country took its flesh daily; as they cut it away, it grew back again.
When people from another country saw this and came to take some, the camel cried out loudly. When asked the reason for this, it replied, "I was originally a practitioner of the Path."
"A person who covets wealth and fails to practice giving incurs a debt to this nation, which must be repaid with their own flesh. I have not incurred a debt to you;

that is why I cried out so loudly. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Covetousness is a great affliction; you should abandon it. (3) This was the third instance of exposing faults by citing transgressions.
They possess neither a heart of compassion nor a heart of filial piety.

[Commentary] Whether one personally relies on power and influence to beg for letters and documents to be placed [in official records], or begs and extorts through beating and flogging—whether acting for oneself or instructing others to do so for one’s sake—one commits this offense.
○ Third, the conclusion regarding the gravity of the offense.
This constitutes the transgression of a minor offense (*āpatti*).
△ The Eighteenth Precept: Prohibiting Teaching Without Understanding.

Yet, having abandoned the seven treasures, they instead study the false views of the two vehicles and external paths, secular classics, the Abhidharma, miscellaneous treatises,
and all manner of written records;

[Note] The *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Store) states: "To learn perversely" means to study in a contrary manner. There are eight [categories]: 1. False views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which is the general heading; 2.

4. Those who practice worldly poetry and literature, which hinders the Path; 5. *Abhidharma*, which here means...
1. *Abhidharma* (Treatise on Phenomena): This refers to the various sectarian disputes of the Hīnayāna schools that contradict one another and undermine the Mahāyāna;
because it is a compendium that intermingles the six Hīnayāna schools, non-Buddhist doctrines, and worldly texts, it is called a "miscellaneous treatise. 2. *Śāstra* (Treatise):

This refers to those who are addicted to the study of calligraphy and calculation, thereby losing their dignified appearance. 3. *Gaṇita* (Calculation): This refers to those who study arithmetic and record the quantity of grain heaps.
If one examines the intent of the sūtras in detail, it may also be that "wrong views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is a general reference to all [views], while "books" (*śāstra*) is a summary of the Piṭakas.
In the commentaries, the absence of the word "all" (*sarva*) regarding the sūtras opens up eight types; this too is unimpeded.

If those of long-standing virtue who are satiated in the Path act as guides for the sake of transforming others, there is no offense even if they study [these things]; the Vinaya also permits these three.

this is severing the Buddha-nature and is a cause and condition for obstructing the Way; it is not practicing the Bodhisattva path. [Commentary]:

"This is severing the Buddha-nature" refers to the third instance of raising a point of what is not [the path] to conclude the fault; practicing the Lesser Vehicle to assist the Great Vehicle does not constitute an offense.

If one studies the scriptures of non-Buddhists, it does not constitute an offense against a bodhisattva; however, if one denies the existence of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), it is called an offense.

[Note] The *Xīchāo* states: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says, "For example, it is like a dog that does not seek food from its master, but instead begs from the laborers.

Citing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it says that the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, in explaining the *Sudurjayā-bhūmi*, stated:
"For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, there are no worldly arts and crafts that the Bodhisattva does not study.
That is to say, he thoroughly masters writing, arithmetic, calligraphy, seals, and various treatises on earth, water, fire, and wind; he is well-versed in medical prescriptions."
He heals all diseases, and is able to completely eliminate insanity and demonic possession.
Regarding literary compositions, praises, and hymns, because they benefit sentient beings, he reveals them all so that they may abide in the Buddha-dharma. ○ Third, the conclusion on offenses.
If one intentionally commits this, one incurs a minor offense (light defilement).
△ The twenty-fifth precept: Not being harmonious with the assembly.

[Commentary] Because it harms oneself and others, it is prescribed for both monastic groups; it is an offense for all three assemblies, and it is regulated as a major or minor offense according to the gravity of the act.
Furthermore, since laypeople have not yet maintained the assembly, they are not subject to these prohibitions. ○ First, the person is designated: "If a Buddha’s disciple.
△ The sequence of the matter has three stages: first, identifying the assembly; second, clarifying what should be done; third, clarifying what should not be done. ○ First, identifying the assembly.

Śāṇakavāsin said: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he shall be the master of preaching the Dharma, the master of practicing the Dharma, the master of the monasteries, the master of transforming others,
the master of seated meditation, and the master of conduct."
[Commentary: There are five types of persons; taking the first phrase as two distinct preparatory stages (upāya), they become six persons.
Within the Vinaya, there are fourteen such persons as described therein; this [text] briefly cites six of them.
[Note] Because the roles of the Master of Dharma-preaching and the Master of Dharma-practice are divided into two, there are six persons.

The *Benjue Xingfa Zhuzang Shu* (The Commentary on the Storehouse of the Essential Methods of Practice by Benjue) lists only five persons; this is because it omits the one person who is the Master of Dharma-practice.

The "Abbot of the Monastery" (*Sengfangzhu*) refers to one who personally assumes the responsibility of administrative leadership and undertakes the arduous tasks for the sake of the community. The "Master of Edification" (*Jiaohua Zhu*) refers to one who guides and leads donors.

The master of seated meditation who oversees the repair and maintenance of stupas and monasteries is so called because he skillfully imparts *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, causing afflictions to be subdued.
The master of travel who leads the assembly on journeys is so called because he ensures that the various faculties are well-restrained and that the prohibitions and precepts are not violated.
○ Second, the explanation of the "correspondence" (*yìng*).
One should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, skillfully reconcile disputes, and properly guard the property of the Triple Gem, not using it recklessly as if it were one's own.

[Commentary] There are three matters to be practiced; the first is a mind of loving-kindness, which means desiring to bestow happiness upon sentient beings. The second is skillfully reconciling strife.

"Sòng" (litigation) refers to the settling of disputes according to the Dharma; there are four types of disputes and seven types of Vinaya rules, which should be resolved according to the Dharma without deviation.
One must properly guard the property of the Triple Gem and employ it for its intended purposes, ensuring that no confusion or misallocation occurs.

[Note] There are four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*): first, disputes over speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*); second, disputes over accusations (*anuvāda-adhikaraṇa*); third, disputes over offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*); and fourth, disputes over legal matters (*vinaya-adhikaraṇa*).

Within the Vinaya, the first three are each divided into nine categories, while the disputes over legal matters are further divided into nine categories, totaling eighteen categories. There are seven methods for settling these disputes (*saptadharmā adhikaraṇa-śamathāḥ*): first, settlement in the presence of the parties (*saṃmukha-vinaya*); second, settlement through recollection (*smṛti-vinaya*);

third, settlement on the grounds of sanity (*amūḍha-vinaya*); fourth, settlement by confession (*pratijñā-kāraka*); and fifth, settlement by the majority (*yadbhūya-sikṣā*); [the remaining two are: settlement by covering over as with grass (*tṛṇaprastāraka*) and settlement by the rule of the majority (*tasya pāpeyasika*)].

Regarding the six offenses and their locations, seven points are as detailed in the *Caturvargika-vinaya* regarding "covering the ground with grass. The present intent concerns the settling of disputes;
matters concerning the property of the Triple Gem are explained in detail as previously discussed under the precept against stealing. ○ Third, what is improper.
On the contrary, they incite disorder among the assembly, engage in strife, and act according to their own whims by misappropriating the property of the Triple Gem.

△ The twenty-sixth precept: Receiving Offerings Exclusively for Oneself.

[Commentary] When the Sangha is invited according to seniority, both newcomers and residents have a share; yet if a resident receives the offerings alone without sharing them with the newcomers, they violate the donor’s intention and harbor greed for profit.
Therefore, this precept was established. Both groups of the ordained community (monks and nuns) commit a grave offense (*mahāpatti*) if they violate it.

The minor *kṣudraka* rules do not apply to the three assemblies [of monastics] or to laypeople who are unaware of monastic affairs; thus they are not prescribed for them. First, the identification of the person: "If a disciple of the Buddha...
The sequence of the matter has three stages: first, there is a guest arriving; second, what should be done; third, what should not be done. Now, the first stage.
Having first resided in a monastic dwelling, one later sees guest bodhisattvas and bhikṣus entering monasteries, houses, cities,
or the residences of kings, even up to places where they observe the summer retreat or great assemblies.
[Commentary] Although the text mentions Bodhisattvas and Bhikṣus, it follows the same principle for Śrāvaka monks when they participate in the distribution of offerings.
[Note] The *Zangshu* states that five locations are briefly cited; first, "the monastic quarters" refers to those who have left home within a monastery (*saṃghārāma*).

Wherever [the Bodhisattva] may be—whether in the two types of residences where a lay Bodhisattva dwells, or in the royal palaces within the city-states of kings, which together constitute the first two positions;
or even in the fourth position, the place of summer retreat (varṣā); or in the fifth position, the midst of a great assembly—[he should be honored].
Second, clarifying what should be done, which has two parts. First, he should be welcomed and received.

The resident monks should welcome him upon his arrival and see him off when he departs; they should provide him with food and drink, dwellings, bedding, rope beds, wooden beds, and every necessary item.

If they lack material goods, they should sell their own bodies or the bodies of their sons and daughters, or even cut the flesh from their own bodies to sell, providing whatever is required and giving it all to him.
2. Regarding the sequence according to the monastic order:

If a donor comes to invite the resident and visiting monks, and there is a portion of offerings to be distributed, the monastery steward should assign the visiting monks to receive the invitation in accordance with their seniority in the monastic order.
[Commentary]: There should be two matters: first, prostrating to welcome [the guest] and providing bedding and other requisites for the Sangha;

second, assigning monks in order of seniority, saying, "I shall sell my own body to provide for you. This is a figurative expression used to emphasize the point. Third, explaining what should not be done.
If the resident monks alone accept the invitation without dispatching visiting monks, the monastery master incurs immeasurable sin;
he is no different from a beast, neither a śramaṇa nor of the Śākya lineage.
[Commentary: It should not be assumed that because the text mentions only the non-sequential selection of monks, it refers solely to the latter case while excluding the former.
If one does not share the property with the monks or fails to receive them, it is governed by the same regulation.

Furthermore, if one knows that the turn has come to a particular person, yet seizes [the property] before they have been selected, this constitutes only a minor offense (light defilement), as at the time of selection, someone might still arrive from outside the boundary and thus the right is not yet exclusive.

Having finished the distribution, one takes [the portion] away and gives it to another person. If that other person knows this, both the one who took it and the one who was appointed are guilty of the preliminary stage of theft (*caurya-prayoga*).

Later, when they receive the alms-food and *dakṣiṇā* from the donor’s household, if five *māṣaka* coins enter their hands, each incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), no different from stealing an animal.

Some say this constitutes the offense of "not appointing according to the monastic order" (*asaṃmata-bhikṣu-paryāya-śīla*). There are six types of appointing according to the monastic order, as described in the Vinaya.
The *Zhong* (Middle) [Agama] states:
[Note] The *Zangshu* says that regarding the offense of rebuking an animal, one first rebukes them by means of three matters: first, because they are foolish, they are the same as animals;
second, because they lack the fruits of holiness, they are not śramaṇas; third, because they lack the causes thereof, they are not Śākyas.
The *Zhongxi chao* states: Regarding the "six types," I have previously inquired of the Vinaya school, yet they were not detailed. The *Rong chao* cites the *Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan*, which says:
When the Buddha was still in the world, visiting bhikṣus would arrive and cry out, "Welcome!

It was the custom of the Western monasteries that whenever a newly arrived bhikṣu was seen—whether he was a visitor, a resident, or a disciple—the senior members of the monastery had to go forward to greet him and cry out [the welcome].
He says, "Svāgata" (this means "Welcome"), and the guest replies, "Susvāgata" (meaning "Most Welcome"). If one does not chant these, first, it violates the monastic regulations;
second, according to the Vinaya, there is an offense. ○ Third, the determination of the offense.
One commits a minor offense (light defilement).
△ The twenty-seventh precept: Accepting Individual Invitations.
[Commentary]: To accept individual invitations separately means that the donor does not invite the Sangha of the ten directions, thereby causing the donor to lose the merit of impartiality.

Because the merit of the mind and the regular offerings to the Sangha of the ten directions were being lost, it was decreed that the five groups of the ordained would equally incur this offense, whereas the two groups of the laity would not.

This regulation had not yet been established for the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, which differ; regarding the Bodhisattva Sangha, one view holds that all offerings at ritual assemblies (*zhāihuì*) must cease if there is an individual invitation (*biéqǐng*).

However, if one is invited to receive the precepts, preach the Dharma, or encounter those ready for instruction (*jiàn jī*), or if it is based on inferential knowledge (*bǐzhì*), [the rule does not apply].
Knowing that this person is without self, one does not cultivate merit; such cases as these are not restricted by the two [rules].

From four people upwards, there is a sequence of monks, and there is no offense; where there are none at all, the meaning of the text of the restriction seems to accord with the former interpretation.
[Note] There are three faults in accepting special invitations (*pṛthag-āmantraṇa*): first, it destroys the sequential dharma of the Tathāgata’s Saṃgha;
second, it diminishes the boundless merit of the donor; third, it burdens oneself by taking what should not be accepted. The *Xīchāo* states: "Alas!
In the Semblance Dharma age, people pursue worldly profit for their own sake and cast aside the teachings as trivial matters, forming many kinds of bonds."

Relying on the morning sun to hasten one’s journey, and furthermore, regarding the distribution of offerings from the faithful, it is necessary to summon the monks of the monastery while also inviting one's own relatives;

this truly deviates from the principle of equality, and the merit and benefit are especially deficient. Since all are equal in their pursuit of goodness, I request that you follow the Buddha’s regulations. First, the identification of the person.
If you are a Buddha’s disciple:

△ This section on the matter has three stages: first, the heading stating what should not be done; second, the explanation of the meaning of why it should not be done; third, the conclusion that it should not be done.
○ Now, the first.
Under no circumstances may one accept special invitations for offerings and take them for oneself.
Second, the explanation of the underlying principle:
these offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions; to accept a special invitation is to take the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself.

[The Master] said: "When a donor cultivates merit through giving, the method should be broad and universal. One must understand that the benefit of such giving fundamentally extends throughout the ten directions. Because you accept it individually, the ten directions cannot be far removed from it; thus, there is the sense of 'seizing' what belongs to the ten directions. Therefore, [accepting it individually] is improper. [Commentary]: When a donor cultivates the dharma of merit, it should be vast and universal. It should be known that the benefit of giving originally pervades the ten directions.

Because you receive it specifically for yourself, the ten directions cannot be distanced from it; this constitutes the principle of "appropriating" what belongs to the ten directions. For this reason, it is not appropriate.

[Note] Regarding the distinction between the Sangha of the ten directions and the present Sangha—as analyzed in the section on the precept against stealing—the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Treasury) poses this question:
"If light property belonging to a deceased bhikṣu also belongs to the Sangha of the ten directions and the present Sangha, how can it be received according to the sequence of the Sangha?
The answer is: "Although it belongs to the ten directions, the established rules differ; for that [deceased property], the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is employed."

Based on this, one should limit [the recipients] to those in the monastic order and receive [offerings] according to their respective original rules without interchanging them. Third, it is improper to offer to the Three Jewels,
as well as to the various Buddhas and Sages among the Eight Fields of Merit, nor to individual teachers, monks, parents, or the sick, using items intended for oneself.
Because of this usage. [Commentary:
All eight fields of merit possess the principle of being entitled to receive offerings in the sequence of the *saṃgha*, just as the Buddha manifests as a member of the *saṃgha* and so forth.

The eight fields of merit are: first, the Buddha; second, holy persons (*ārya*); third, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); fourth, the instructor (*ācārya*); fifth, the *saṃgha*; sixth, the father; seventh... [the mother].
Regarding the mother and the eight sick people: although in the Tripiṭaka the Buddha constantly accepts individual invitations, this is not called a transgression.

First, because the Buddha is the supreme field of merit, he does not diminish the merit of impartiality. Second, in this world there is only one Buddha, and thus there is no principle of one Buddha depriving another of offerings.
○ Third, the formal confession of the offense.
One commits a minor transgression (light impurity offense).
△ The twenty-eighth precept: Prohibiting the Invitation of Monks Individually.

[Commentary: To discriminate between who is a field of merit and who is not—as stated in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, Chapter on King Śrīmālā—one should know that such a mind is narrow and inferior, and it loses the mind of equanimity.
Members of the seven assemblies commit the same offense; the Mahayana and Hinayana do not share the path entirely, nor do the monastics and laity.
When a Bodhisattva requests monks for a vegetarian feast, one interpretation is that they must not invite individuals at all, but should instead invite according to the order of the Sangha.
If a person commits two offenses, it is said: "In the matter of eating together, one need not inquire as to the number of people; it suffices to invite only one monk, and then there is no offense.
If there are none at all, this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*); if everyone is invited, it is even better. The meaning of the text seems to accord with the former interpretation.
[Note] The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, fascicle 24, states: "How does a bodhisattva not observe fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and non-fields of merit?
What constitutes a field of merit? Heretics who maintain the precepts, up to and including the Buddhas—these are called fields of merit.
One should know that such a mind is narrow and inferior. A bodhisattva observes that all sentient beings without exception are fields of merit, even though there are two [types]."
The interpretation of the text’s meaning follows the previous [analysis], specifically relying on the first explanation. ○ First, the designation of the person: "If a Buddha-son. △ Section Three:

The Exposition of the Matter, consisting of: 1. Designating what should be practiced; 2. Explaining the intent of what should be practiced; 3. What should not be practiced. ○ Now, the first: Designating what should be practiced.

When ordained bodhisattvas, lay bodhisattvas, or any donors invite the Sangha as a field of merit to pray for their aspirations, they should enter the monastery and inquire of the administrative official (karmadāna):
"I now wish to invite the Sangha to pray for my aspirations. The official shall reply:
"If you invite them in successive order, you will obtain the Sangha of worthy and holy ones from the ten directions."
[Note] Regarding this precept: whereas the previous regulations concerned those who were invited, the present regulation concerns those who invite. 2. Explanation of the "Appropriate" (yìng):
In the world, it is better to invite one ordinary monk according to the monastic order than to separately invite five hundred arhats or bodhisattva monks.

[Commentary]: This clarifies that although one may have obtained an invitation from ordinary monks (*pṛthagjana-bhikṣu*), it is superior to an invitation from the noble monks (*ārya-bhikṣu*). Others say that five hundred arhats do not equal a single ordinary monk;
this is because [the former] is based on the pervasiveness of the mind and does not take the field (*kṣetra*) into account. 3. What is inappropriate.
If one invites the Saṃgha individually, this is the practice of non-Buddhists; the Seven Buddhas had no such method of individual invitation, as it does not accord with the Way of Filial Piety.
[Commentary]: One should not follow the heterodox methods of non-Buddhists; to fail to comply with the Buddha’s teaching is to deviate from the Way of Filial Piety.
As for the "Seven Buddhas," they all appeared in this land through their manifested traces within the span of a hundred kalpas; those in the Heaven of Longevity have all seen them.
Therefore, many citations from the Seven Buddhas are used to substantiate this meaning, desiring to make it easy for those with faith to understand.
Ninety kalpas ago, at the beginning of time, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin (also known as Vīra).
During the intervening kalpas, there were no Buddhas until the thirty-first kalpa, when two Buddhas appeared: the first named Śikhin and the second named Viśvabhū (also called Suvikrānta).
The ninety-first kalpa is named Bhadrakalpa (the Auspicious Kalpa), during which one thousand Buddhas are destined to appear; four have already passed:
first, Krakucchanda; second, Kanakamuni; third, Kāśyapa; and fourth, Śākyamuni.

[Note] The *Āgama* Sūtras state that when the householder Siṃha invited five hundred arhats separately, the Buddha said it was not as meritorious as [inviting] a single person according to the monastic order;

the merit of the latter is immeasurable. Just as drinking from the great ocean is to drink all its tributary streams, although the number of five hundred arhats is large, they are merely one category of the present Saṃgha, comparable to the waters of a river being but a single [stream].

In this regard, if even a single person in the sequence of the Saṃgha is present, though few, they complete the number of the monks of the ten directions; it is like a single drop of water from the ocean that already contains the essence of all rivers.
As for the difference between fields of merit—whether fertile or barren—the ordinary does not equal the noble. As stated in the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*:
"A hundred generations of filial service to one's parents is not equal to feeding a single Pratyekabuddha; feeding a hundred Pratyekabuddhas is not equal to feeding a single [Arhat]."
The Buddha now takes [the merit] because his mind is impartial; thus it is said that "the field is not considered.
The *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Light) states: "The retribution resides in the six heavens; the longest-lived reaches nine hundred twenty-six billion seven hundred million years.

The *Shangtian beizeng zang shu* (Commentary on the Further Increase of the Upper Heaven Treasury) asks: "If those monks specifically invited are also among the monks of the ten directions, how can they not be the 'ten'?"

In the Fangshe (General Invitation), the response to a specific request involves directing one's attention toward a particular individual; it does not universally encompass the Sangha of the ten directions.

This is not the case with the *sengci* (Invitation by Order of Seniority), for as its intention is free from partiality and encompasses all, it is extensive. ○ Third, citing what is improper to conclude the fault.

Three, citing what is wrong to conclude the transgression—namely, committing an offense because of a lack of compassion. ○ Now, the first part.
Out of an evil mind, for the sake of gain and support:
(1) trafficking in the sexual favors of men and women;
(2) preparing food with one's own hands, grinding it oneself, and pounding it oneself; (3) practicing divination and physiognomy for men and women, and interpreting their characteristics.
(3) Dreams and their auspicious or inauspicious omens; whether [a child] will be male or female; (4) incantations and spells; (5) arts and crafts; (6) methods for training hawks;
(7) compounding a hundred kinds of poisons, a thousand kinds of poisons, snake venom, poisons from living gold and silver, and poisons from insects.

[Commentary]: Regarding the four types of sustenance (*āhāra*) for those of wrong livelihood among the *śrāvakas*—namely, looking upward, looking downward, and so forth—these five matters herein apply to all four types of sustenance:
(1) trafficking in the sexual favors of men and women; (2) making one’s own living; (3) restricting oneself to the monastic path while opening the way for worldly affairs;
(4) interpreting signs of good or bad fortune to sustain oneself like a layperson; and (5) practicing incantations, which is strictly prohibited for those on the Path.
The five arts and crafts and the sixth method of training hawks—these three matters involve no injury to living beings; one may sustain oneself through them in accordance with the Dharma.
For a householder, these are not prohibited; for one who has left the home life, they are entirely forbidden. If one practices medicine purely and without expectation of reward, it is not an offense.
Even for those who have left the home life, the seven types of compounded medicines are permitted; however, administering poison to kill a person constitutes a transgression.
[Note] The explanations provided by other commentaries differ from those of Tiantai. Zang’s commentary states: "Although evil matters are numerous, thirteen are cited briefly: 1.
Selling one's physical form—meaning residing in a brothel to sell female beauty to men or male beauty to women.

According to the teachings regarding the act of adultery itself, this constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*); however, in terms of the act of prostitution itself, it is further classified as a minor defilement (*duṣkṛta*)."
This constitutes two offenses. Second, regarding preparing food with one's own hands: it is personally ignoble and contrary to the Dharma.
The Vinaya states that such actions invite public reproach and obstruct the cultivation of supramundane activities.
If those of noble worldly status sit peacefully while receiving food and do not engage in manual labor, how much more so for a disciple of the Buddha? The Buddha commanded—
1. The disciple manifests the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and causes laymen (*upāsaka*) and laywomen (*upāsikā*) to prepare food and provide offerings;
2. He grinds and husks grain himself three times, which constitutes destroying living beings, improper contact with food, and being subject to worldly reproach; 3.

He practices physiognomy for men and women, divining whether marriages between men and women are auspicious or not, and interpreting their dreams to determine good or bad fortune; 4. He [determines] who is male and who is female.

1. Divination of the womb (*garbha-vidyā*) refers to determining whether a fetus is male or female. 2. The six types of incantations (*ṣaḍ-mantra*) refer to curses and the like, as well as using malevolent spells to curse dragons and other beings.

3. The seven arts (*sapta-kalā*) refer to sorcery, prayers for suppression, talismans, and the like. 4. The eight crafts (*aṣṭa-śilpa*) refer to those who work as artisans or laborers to seek profit. 5. The method of training hawks (*śyena-pāśa-vidyā*) refers to techniques such as blinding them with thread;

once they are trained, one causes them to kill living beings. 6. [The ninth] ... (as above). 7. [The tenth] ... (as above). (Note: The original text lists ten items, but the provided fragment only explicitly names five. The final two items, numbered nine and ten, correspond to the "method of training hawks" and its subsequent application.)
Regarding "harmonizing a hundred kinds of poisonous drugs": this medicine is synthesized from a hundred types of poisons;

the same applies to a thousand poisons, as the principle is that since the number [of ingredients] varies—whether few or many—the potency of the poison should accordingly be mild or acute. Regarding "the venom of eleven snakes": on the fifth day of the fifth month, one collects snakes and combines them with poisonous medicines;
furthermore, one uses poisonous medicines to subdue snakes and so forth. Regarding "producing gold and silver from the twelve [elements]": [this refers to the alchemical process].
To forge counterfeit gold and silver in order to deceive people; as the *Jiùchão* (Old Draft) states, this refers to forging artificial gold and silver to mix with medicines and harm others.
Furthermore, it is said that "raw gold and silver" (*shēng jīnyín*) is a name for poisonous drugs.
Others say it is like placing quicksilver and other medicinal substances into a furnace to transform them into gold and silver for the purpose of poisoning, such as arsenic and the like. (10)
Regarding the three *gū* poisons: these are also snakes, *māo-ghosts* (*māo-kuei*), and so forth, which harm sentient beings.

It is said that if one places a spider on the seventh day of the seventh month, a snake during a clear noon on the fifth day of the fifth month, and a cat in a jar on the twelfth month, and leaves them closed for many days until only one remains, it will then become that poison.
Furthermore, tradition says that one should take a hundred...
Various snakes were placed within a jar; they devoured one another until the strongest became the most poisonous.

Since the commentary (*shu*) preserved only the general outline, it has been supplemented with other commentaries for explanation, making it detailed and easy to understand. ○ Third, citing errors to conclude on the fallacy.
To lack any heart of compassion is to commit a minor offense of defilement.
△ The thirtieth precept: Not respecting auspicious times.
[Commentary]: The three fasting days and six fasting days are all days upon which spirits and deities gain power; on these days, one should cultivate merit and goodness.

Having passed other days, at this present auspicious time, one who has been negligent further commits an offense; according to the specific matter committed and the specific category (*pācittiya*), the offense is established.

At this time and on this day, one should not remain ignorant; furthermore, one precept is added. One interpretation states that all seven classes of followers are equally enjoined and should all show respect during these times.
Another interpretation states that it is only the lay followers who are enjoined for the three long months of the year and the six fast days (*upoṣadha*); the original purpose of these fasts was...
Whether lay or ordained, one should observe the fast for the remainder of one's life, regardless of the specific time of year.
[Note] The "three long months" refer to the second, fifth, and ninth months; these three months begin from the continent of Jambudvīpa.

As for the "six fasting days," these are the six days within each month, as explained in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Zhilun). Regarding the second, third, and fourth months, they correspond to other continents. These follow the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The "six fasting days" are the six days within a month. As for...

The *Changbian piyu jing* (Sutra of Constantly Expounding Parables) states that Śakra, King of Devas, commands the Four Heavenly Kings to traverse the world on the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*) to observe the good and evil deeds committed by humans and report them to the Supreme Sovereign.
Furthermore, the *Jingdu jing* (Pure Salvation Sutra) states that there are six reports per day and four inspections per year. [This concludes the section] marking the person.

Out of an evil mind, they themselves slander the Triple Gem while feigning intimacy;

they speak of emptiness with their mouths yet remain engaged in worldly existence, managing affairs for laypeople and acting as intermediaries between men and women for sexual intercourse, thereby creating all manner of fetters and attachments.
[Commentary]: Whenever there is a transgression, it constitutes a discrepancy between words and deeds; to deviate from and oppose the true reality is to slander the Triple Gem. [Note]:
In the management of laypeople, there is a base text that omits this one sentence: "To feign intimacy while actually slandering the Triple Gem is also a grave offense.

Acting as a matchmaker is surely not the work of one who studies the Way. ○ Second, the time for reverence:
the six days of abstinence (ṣaḍ-upoṣadha) and the three months of long abstinence during the year.
[Commentary] The "time for reverence" refers to the six days of abstinence, the three months of long abstinence, and so forth, all of which have been explained as before. ○ Third.

A householder bodhisattva should practice this matter.

however, for those who unknowingly commit them on the days of the long-month fast (*poṣadha*), this one additional precept is established here. Therefore, the previous commentary states: "At this time, this..."
Day after day, one does not know how to add even a single precept. ○ Third, the summary of offenses:
one incurs a light offense of defilement.

△ The thirty-first precept: Not redeeming [images]. [Commentary]:
To see that the images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are being sold and not to redeem them—this is an extreme form of humiliation and is not the conduct of a Mahāsattva.

One should redeem them according to one's capacity; failure to do so constitutes an offense. Therefore, this is established as a rule for all seven groups of followers, both great and small, without exception.
One should jointly redeem Bodhisattvas, but one does not redeem Śrāvakas who have seen their parents; violating this constitutes an offense of the seventh category.
Regarding scriptures and images, there is no specific prohibition against seeing them. ○ First, identifying the person:

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in this degenerate age, if one should encounter non-Buddhists, various evil people, or bandits—[or] those who sell [images], such as those selling images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or one’s parents;
or those who sell the sūtras and vinaya; or those who trade in bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
If one sells a person who has generated the bodhicitta—a practitioner of the Way—or subjects them to official service as a slave to others;
[Commentary]:
First, regarding the person who is able to sell them, this refers to those sold by bandits, namely images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. This is because...

Sūtra and Vinaya.

△ Thirty-second precept: Refraining from harming sentient beings.

[Commentary] This consists of six matters; because harming others violates compassion, it is strictly prohibited. It is a transgression for all seven classes of practitioners, and is regulated by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

If a Buddha’s disciple:
△ The introductory text enumerates six matters.
One must not sell (other editions say "keep") swords, staves, bows, or arrows; nor keep (other editions say "sell") light scales or small measures; nor exploit government authority.

Using one’s power and influence to seize the wealth and property of others; harboring harmful intent and binding others; destroying successful undertakings; and raising cats, wildcats, pigs, and dogs.

[Commentary] Generally, six matters are enumerated: first, selling instruments of slaughter; second, keeping light scales and small measures, as well as short cubits and feet, following this same principle;
third, seeking money and goods by means of official power and influence; fourth, harboring harmful intent and binding others.
Fifth, destroying success; sixth, raising cats and wildcats—these six things all involve harm and should not be kept as matters that cause injury.
[Note] All versions of the sutra state "keeping knives and staves" (*śastra-dhāraṇa*);
however, since the tenth precept previously mentioned already forbade "selling with light scales," [this repetition is redundant].

Regarding the rule permitting the possession of swords, staves, bows, and arrows: why was this established as a second regulation? According to the *Śāstra*, the section reveals that the wording of the *Sūtra* is erroneous.
The section states: "First, the sale of implements for killing; second, the possession of light scales and small measures.

Therefore, the character "possess" (*chù*) in the first instance should be changed to "sell" (*fàn-mài*), and the character "sell" in the second instance should be changed to "possess"; only then will one see that the former regulation prohibited possession, while the present regulation prohibits selling.
To sell them would be a grave burden; yet, from the beginning, the records have failed to examine this matter, leading to such a state of affairs. III.

therefore, this is established as a transgression for both the Mahayana and Hinayana, though the seven classes of followers do not all incur it equally. ○ First, the identification of the person.

[Commentary]: This regulation applies equally to both the monastic and the lay.

The *Rites of Zhou*, Section on the Summer Official (*Xiaguan*), states: "The King has six armies; a great state has three armies; a secondary state has two armies."
The military force of a small state consists of five types of weapons: the bow, the sword, the *shuo* (a spear one zhang two chi long with two blades), the *ji* (a double-edged halberd with a handle;

Furthermore, one must not listen to the sounds of conchs, drums, horns, lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, pipes, oboes, singing, shouting, or the music of performers.

[Commentary] If for the sake of self-entertainment, neither monastics nor laypeople are permitted to perform or listen to such music. However, if it is for the purpose of making offerings to the Triple Gem, both monastics and laypeople are equally permitted to do so.

the drum refers here to the military drum among musical instruments, following the combined explanation; 3. The *qín* lute; the *Baihu Tong* states: [text continues].
The *qin* is used for restraint; it serves to prohibit licentiousness and depravity, thereby rectifying the mind. Regarding the four *se*:

The five *zheng* resemble the *qin* and have thirteen strings. The six *di* are musical instruments made of bamboo.
Regarding the seven-holed instrument, the *Fengsu Tong* states that it was made by Qiu Zhong during the reign of Emperor Wu, or perhaps by Ling Lun during the time of the Yellow Emperor.
Regarding the seven *sheng* pipes, the *Liji* says they were created by Nüwa; the *Shiming* explains that "sheng" means "to give birth," as they resemble things piercing through the earth to grow.
The eight-holed *hou* is the same as the *konghou*; the *Shiming* says it was created by Shi Yan and is characterized by its seductive melody.
The sounds [of these instruments] emerged from Sangjian and Puchang. The *Continued History of the Han* states that Emperor Ling adopted foreign dress and created the *konghou*.
"The chanting of the Nine Songs" refers to the sound of singing; "chanting" (*jiao*) is sometimes written as "wailing" (*jiao*), both generally signifying the sound of calling out.

In Sanskrit, *pālasa* translates here as "military" (*bing*), which refers to a military game;

that is, the game played today using boards where paths are drawn and divided by rivers, with sixteen pieces—infantry, pawns, cannons, chariots, horses, and elephants—what the common people call "elephant bases.
The Tibetan commentary states this is a military game method from the Western Regions, wherein two players each hold two [boards].
"Ten or more pieces reach the opponent's position, whether as elephants or horses; on the board's paths, one wins by seizing the vital points.
Regarding the phonetic glosses, the *Jiāshì* (釋音) also uses this interpretation. The *Xīchāo* (熙鈔) states: "Bala is a Sanskrit term for a board game;

Regarding the Emperor Wu’s game of *shuanglu* (double-sixes), there have also been those since ancient times who first cast dice to determine the outcome.
As for *si-tanqi* (the four-stone game), the *Rongchao* states that it uses stone for the board and jade for the playing surface, with its four corners raised;
many palace ladies and women of the gentry played this. The *Xichao* states that this originated as a diversion for the decorative caskets in the Wei palace. [From] Ge Hong’s *Xijing ji*.

The *Jing zaji* (Miscellaneous Records of the Capital) states that during the reign of Emperor Cheng of the Han, the ministers presented [this game]. The *Bocang shu* (Catalogue of the Secret Storehouse) says it is the same as *shuanglu* (double-six).

The *Xi chao* (Excerpts from the Xi) quotes the *Chuci* (Songs of Chu): "The *bi* and *bì* are like chess; there is *liùbó* (six-rolls). The *Shuowen jiezi* (Explaining Simple and Analyzing Compound Characters) says:
"A board game played with six *jīn* (pins) and twelve pieces. The *Rong chao* (Excerpts from the Rong) says: "Within the enclosure, lines are drawn on both the left and right sides..."
The "six paths" refers to *shuanglu* (double-sixes). Furthermore, gambling games involving six dice, down to the game of "six clamps," all belong to the category of *liubo* (six-play).
Examining various commentaries now, it is correct to identify *liubo* as *shuanglu*.
As for the mention of a board game with twelve pieces arranged on a diagram of six paths and so forth, these are each [distinct variations].
As for *shuanglu* (double-six), this is a game of dice. Since antiquity, people have used a chessboard to arrange pieces and cast dice, taking them according to the numbers rolled;
this is called "taking the pieces" (*quqi*), and it was used as a form of gambling.

Later gamblers did not use pieces at all, but instead competed solely with the dice to determine the outcome of the game; thus, there are many varieties of *shuanglu*, all of which are fundamentally one and the same.

This is a type of game. The *Guǎng yùn* explains the character 骰 (*tóu*) as "dice for the game of *bó lù*" (six-sided gaming pieces). It further explains the character 博 (*bó*) as "a class of board games such as *liù bó*" (the six-player game).

Therefore, this [interpretation] is taken as correct. According to the *Jìshì* section of the *Táng shū*, Empress Wǔ dreamed that she did not win at *shuānglù* (double-sixes), which was an omen that she would have no children.
The term 六拍毱 (*liù pāi qú*)—where *qú* is pronounced *jú*—is explained in the *Shìyīn* as "kicking a ball" (*ti qíú*). This also applies to the character 毛 (*máo*).
The *mǎnwéi* (ball-shaped object) and the *qù* (leather ball) used for kicking and tossing are both of this category. Seventh is "Tossing Stones" (*zhìshí*) and "Pitch-pot" (*tóuhú*).

These two should properly be combined into one type, as "pitch-pot" is an ancient ritual method from the *Líjì*. The counting-sticks (*chóu*) were twenty-two *cùn* long, representing the twelve months;
they were thrown beyond three steps. Alternatively, the sticks were made entirely of stone, with their tips sharpened; hence it is called "tossing stones."
Regarding *tō-uko* (pitch-pot): as other commentaries state, throwing stones is called *hei-seki* (flying stones);
a twelve-jin stone set in motion by a mechanical device that travels three hundred paces is a siege weapon used in warfare, not a method for games.
Therefore, this interpretation is not employed. Regarding the "eight-by-eight path" (*hachi-hachi-dō-gyō*), the original text contains no characters for "leading path" (*ken-dō*).
Thus, one should know that this is a type of game. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One should not observe any games or jests within the city of the Eightfold Path.
The *Rongchao* says: "The eight strokes constitute the path; moving the chess pieces along them resembles the method of 'walking the city' (*xingcheng*).
The *Xichao* states: "If one follows the *Śrī-samparigraha Sūtra*, the eighth day of the second month is the day of the Four Heavenly Kings."
When [the Prince] held the horse’s hoof as he leaped over the city walls to leave home, this gave rise to the ritual of “walking the city” (xing cheng).

This was performed to follow the tracks of the Prince’s horse, manifesting a sentiment of longing for the Sage. Furthermore, there are those who establish this rite in a confused or excessive manner; it is likely distinct from the original intent.
Within the precepts (*śīla*), many ritual details (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*) may confuse people, so they must be distinguished. **Fourth: Six Matters Regarding Not Divining.**
Divination:
Using fingernails, mirrors, *zhicao* (or *zhizhao*) grass, willow branches, alms bowls, or skulls to perform divination.
[Commentary]: These six matters—performing divination for profit—are prohibited for both monastics and laypeople alike.

[Note] The *Zangshu* states: "Regarding the five matters, the first is the 'mirror of the fingernails. I have heard that in the Western Regions, practitioners of arts apply medicinal substances to their fingernails and recite mantras;
they can then see matters such as good or bad fortune within them. The *Xihao* states: "The sutra mentions only five matters, but according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it says:
'One must never practice divination based on the hands, feet, face, or eyes. It is feared that this [present] sutra may be incomplete in this regard."
Regarding the "one joint," the "two-claw mirror," and so forth, the *Xīchāo* (Commentary on the Rituals) now claims it is improper to supplement these with other scriptures to make six items;
rather, one should divide the "claw mirror" into two: first, the claw, and second, the mirror. Thus, the six things are: 1. the claw, 2. the mirror, 3.

the milfoil stalks (*śi*), 4. the willow twigs, 5. the alms bowl, and 6. the skull. "Claw" refers to applying medicinal substances to the claws, while "mirror" refers to fashioning a mirror using medicinal substances.
The mirror allows one to see matters such as good and bad fortune;

nowadays there are those who use mirrors for divination, or who employ illusory spells upon a polished surface to reflect images on a wall to divine fortune and misfortune—such as the current practice of the "invocation method" (kōshō-hō) or what is called "divination by a youth" (dōji-shō)—all of which belong to this category.
As for the *Qicao* (耆草), it is used for divination by manipulating the stalks (*yeshie*).
Regarding the *shí* (milfoil stalks) and the flourishing branches of the *yáng* (poplar):

the *Mòdìzǐ Wǔxíngchuán* states that on the fifth day of the first month at the hour of *wù*, one should go beneath a willow tree and look upward; if there is a branch that has broken, take it and carve it into the shape of a human figure.
Place it in a quiet room and offer sacrifices of incense, flowers, wine, and dried meat, while reciting a spell (*zhòu*) over it. One will then be able to know the fortunes of others.

Regarding the *jiao* (evil) incantations: according to those traditions, non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) in the Western Regions used incantations for all manner of vessels to have people divine good or bad fortune within them;

the mention here of the "bowl" (*patra*) refers precisely to such a vessel. In this land as well, there are those who use incantations over water-cups to divine matters—all of these belong to this same category.
As for the "skull" (*kapāla*), the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*) cites the example of non-Buddhists listening to a skull.
Regarding "sound," it refers to obtaining a small portion of the conventional *dīpa* (lamp); such matters and characteristics have been sought from various commentaries and are detailed here.
○ Fifth, regarding missions:
one must not undertake missions for thieves or bandits.
[Note] According to the established principles for completing the karma of theft, instructing others to steal and so forth should constitute a grave offense;
however, since these are taken here as "instigators" (*pṛṣṭha*) because they involve what ought not to be done, they are included within this regulation. ○ Third, the summary.
One must not perform each of these individually.
○ Third, regarding the non-binding offense:
if one intentionally performs them, one commits a minor defilement offense (light impurity offense).
△ Thirty-fourth: Briefly considering the precepts of the Hīnayāna.

[Commentary] Because this deviates from what one originally practiced, it is established that the seven classes of practitioners incur the same offense; yet, as the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are not shared, their practices differ.

Desiring to turn away from the Great Vehicle and incline toward the small mind, before one’s mental calculations are complete, one incurs the eighth preceding offense: the precept against turning away from the Great Vehicle and inclining toward the small.

The failure to fulfill this precept is explained within the tenth grave precept. This precept is established because one does not wish to turn away from the Great Righteous Word, considering the Small Vehicle an easy practice;
rather, one desires to sever the fetters first and subsequently attain birth through transformation. ○ First, the person is identified.
If you are a Buddha’s disciple:
△ Regarding the sequence of matters, there are two parts: first, what should be done; second, what should not be done. Within the first, "what should be done," there are again three:
first, guarding the Mahāyāna precepts; second, generating Mahāyāna faith; third, giving rise to the Mahāyāna mind. ○ Now, the first.
Upholding the prohibitive precepts while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one should recite these precepts during the six periods of day and night as if they were a vajra;
like one wearing a life-preserving float while wishing to cross the great ocean, or like a bhikṣu bound by a cord of grass.
[Commentary] One should keep in mind that the Mahāyāna briefly enumerates three matters: first, guarding the Mahāyāna precepts. This is illustrated by two metaphors:

first, the *vajra*, which signifies firmness; second, the "raft" (*phalaka*), as explained in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Crossing [the Ocean]* regarding the binding with grass.
[Note]: Holding the Vajra-vidyā with a firm mind is like a life-preserving float; not transgressing even by a hair’s breadth is the purity of holding the mind.

Regarding the causal story of binding a bhikṣu with grass, one should compare it to those who uphold the precepts today: they should be like the one bound with grass, remaining free from transgression.
The account of the life-preserving float appears in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. As for "binding with grass," the *Vyavahāra-viniścaya-śāstra* states: "There were certain bhikṣus... [text fragment].
In a vast wilderness, a man was traveling when he was plundered and stripped of his clothes by bandits who further intended to kill him.
One among the bandits had previously been a monk; he said to his companions, "We need not kill them all. According to the Dharma of a bhikṣu, one is forbidden from harming even a blade of grass.
He tied the man with grass. Fearing that he might harm the grass, the man was ultimately unable to rise. He looked in the four directions and cried out for help.
The bandits relied upon this [method], and the bhikṣus were bound with grass. Fearing they might violate their prohibitions, they did not dare to pull the bonds apart;
having no clothing, they were scorched by the sun and bitten by mosquitoes, insects, flies, and fleas.
From dawn until dusk, they had to run about as various nocturnal creatures and beasts roamed crosswise, which was truly terrifying. An elder bhikṣu spoke thus:
The verse of admonition says: "If there are those with wisdom who can steadfastly uphold the prohibitive precepts, they will obtain human or celestial rebirths and nirvana according to their wishes.
Because the Naga King Elapatra violated the prohibitive precepts and harmed the lives of various insects, he has now fallen into the state of a dragon.
These bhikṣus, being oppressed by suffering, dared not [trample] for fear of harming the lives of grasses."
As he moved about, he spoke these verses: "In the past, I have committed various evil deeds;
though I may now be born among humans, I have stolen and violated the wives of others, and by the laws of kings I have suffered execution—its count cannot be calculated.
Furthermore, I have endured the sufferings of the hells, which are likewise difficult to reckon. Even if this sunlight were to scorch me until my life-force was dried up..."

"I must uphold the Buddha's precepts and never violate them midway; even if I were to encounter a fierce beast that tears apart my body and head, I would never dare to violate the prohibitions of the Lion of the Śākyas.
I would rather die upholding the precepts than live in violation of them.
At that time, the bhikṣus each rectified their own bodies, remaining unmoving and unshaken. Then, as the king was out hunting in the distance, he [beheld]...
Seeing him, the King suspected he was a naked Nirgrantha ascetic and sent a messenger to investigate;

upon learning he was a bhikṣu, the King was filled with doubt and wonder and went in person to question him, saying: "When I saw you, you appeared to be free of illness, robust, and possessed of great strength;
how is it that you have been bound by grass for days and nights without turning over? The bhikṣu replied: "This grass is extremely fragile; when it is cut, how could it—"

When faced with this difficulty, he was restrained by the Vajra Precepts of the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Hearing this, Yuwen rejoiced; he immediately untied the grass and spoke a verse, saying: "Excellent!
You are able to maintain firmly that which was spoken by the Lion of the Śākyas. Rather than sacrificing your own body and life, you protect the Dharma and do not violate it.
I now likewise take refuge in such a manifestation of the Great Dharma; I take refuge in the One who is Free from Defilement."
"I now take refuge in the Muni, the Honored One of Liberation who endures the heat of affliction and firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts;
if even one who observes minor precepts is thus, how much more so for one who maintains the prohibitive precepts of the Mahāyāna! (2) Second, generating faith in the Mahāyāna.
Constantly giving rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna, one knows for oneself: "I am a Buddha-to-be, while all Buddhas are Buddhas already accomplished.
Third, the arousal of the bodhicitta.
One should give rise to the bodhicitta, never allowing it to depart from the mind for even a single thought-moment.
Second, what is improper:
if one gives rise to even a single thought of the two vehicles or of non-Buddhist paths.
[Commentary: One should not give rise to the thought of self-deliverance in a single moment. As for the term "externalists," this refers to those of the Two Vehicles;
however, if one enters these paths through skillful means for the sake of transformation, such cases are not subject to restriction. 3. Conclusion on the offense.
One commits a minor offense.
△ The Thirty-fifth Precept: Not Making Vows.
[Commentary] A Bodhisattva should constantly vow to seek superior matters; by directing the mind toward wholesome objects, these goals will eventually be accomplished through such causes.
Therefore, it is established that while the seven groups of followers are the same in their status as both great and small, they differ in what they practice.

one should always bring forth all vows to be filial and obedient toward one’s parents, teachers, and the Sangha (some versions include the two characters "Three Jewels").

May I obtain a good teacher.

Fellow students and spiritual friends:

may they constantly teach me the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya.

The ten stages of departure.

Ten Nourishments.
○ Seven Vows and Explanations of the Ten Vajras.
The Ten Vajras.
8. The vow to understand the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The ten stages.

May I attain understanding and practice the Dharma according to the teachings.

to firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
