One should rather sacrifice body and life, never letting [the thought] depart from the mind for even a single moment.
III. Clarifying what should not be done: [Omitted].
"If all bodhisattvas did not make this vow... [Commentary]:

"寧捨" (nìng shě) refers to the second point, which states that one ought to generate this mind; "若一切" (ruò yīqiè) refers to the third point, which states that one ought not to fail to generate this mind.

[Note] The *Zangshu* (Tibetan Commentary) establishes five vows as the structural divisions of the sutra: first, the vow to perfect filial conduct, namely “to be filially obedient toward one’s parents”;

second, the vow regarding superior teachers and friends, namely “to obtain a good teacher”; third, the vow to hear the Great Dharma, namely “to constantly teach the Mahāyāna up to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*)”;
fourth, the vow to give rise to practice based on understanding, namely “may I attain awakening and comprehension.”
Regarding the interpretation that "firmly upholding the five vows and practices" means firmly upholding the Buddha’s precepts and so forth, such an explanation is flawed;

it fails to account for where the ten vows already undertaken are located in the subsequent text on the precepts, and it further loses sight of the fact that the *Rongchao* (Commentary by Zhiyi) refers to the ten grave offenses as the "ten.
Therefore, the classification provided by Tiantai should be regarded as superior. ○ Third, the conclusion regarding the offense.
One commits a minor offense (light defilement).
△ The thirty-sixth precept: Not making a vow.

[Commentary] A vow is a firm and resolute heart; it is the courageous and fierce inception of the will within one's aspirations. If the mind at the start of practice is weak, one must [strengthen it].
If one does not generate the intention to maintain [the precepts], a transgression will arise; therefore, it is prescribed that all seven classes of followers commit the same offense.
However, their application need not be identical, as the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are not shared, and the two vehicles do not prescribe this. It is easy to guard against such a lapse of mind.
○ First, the identification of the person.
If you are a disciple of the Buddha:
△ The introduction to the matter has three parts: first, the exhortation; second, what should be done; third, what should not be done. ○ First, the exhortation:
Having made these ten great vows, one should uphold the prohibitive precepts of the Buddha.
[Commentary]: The first phrase indicates the exhortation to give rise to a single vow; what follows is the response that one should resolve to maintain the precepts.
The final phrase concludes that failing to do so constitutes a transgression. The thirteen subsequent sections correctly clarify the substance of the vows.
△ Second, it clarifies that there should be thirteen great vows; now, following the *Zangshu*, each vow is individually identified. ○ First, in relation to the precepts violated:
He made a vow before a pit of fire and a mountain of blades,

declaring: "I would rather cast this body into a blazing, fierce pit of fire or onto a mountain of blades than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods by engaging in impure conduct with any woman."

[Note] Tiantai merely provides a general outline, whereas other commentaries are extremely detailed; however, they fail to specifically point out the text of the "Ten Great Vows," which is considered a deficiency.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states that because the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* sets forth the ten great vows and thirteen oaths, this [Tiantai] interpretation is necessary.
As for the "fire pit," it destroys only the physical body (*rūpakāya*), whereas female desire can destroy the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); therefore, this analogy is employed.

The *Śīlakośa-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Treasury of Vows) cited below establishes that the twelve great vows are founded upon the precept against sexual misconduct, with the other precepts understood by analogy;

this is not without reason. Since the scriptural text first restrains one from female form in the initial vow, and subsequently states in all the various vows, "I shall never, with this body of broken precepts," and so forth, it is clear that the precept against sexual misconduct is the basis.

The same principle may be applied to cases such as beginning with killing and stealing. Second, regarding the robe offered out of faith, one establishes a vow that hot iron shall wrap around one's body, further making this aspiration:
"I would rather have my body wrapped all around by a thousand layers of hot iron mesh than [accept this robe]."
A person who has broken the precepts receives all kinds of clothing from faithful donors.
[Note] The *Zangshu* states that these various vows are established for three reasons: first, such offerings of faith are received by those of pure precepts;
if one now violates the precepts, it constitutes receiving them as theft. Second, the various donors believe in the words of the Buddha.
Therefore, one renounces wife, children, and provisions to bestow them as a meritorious gift. If one now violates the prohibitions, it constitutes deception;
having misled the donor, one further brings reproach upon the Tathāgata. How can one consume the Buddha’s merit while violating the Buddha’s precepts? (The third [point]:

The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, bestowed even a fraction of his marks of excellence upon his disciples of the bequeathed Dharma so that they might obtain the four requisites. How can one eat the Buddha’s blessings while violating the Buddha’s precepts? (Omitted below)
All are likewise so. Third, regarding the food offered by faithful donors, he establishes the vow of the "Iron Ball and Fierce Fire":

He further makes this aspiration: "I would rather swallow glowing iron balls and great streams of fierce fire with this mouth for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever use this mouth of broken precepts to eat the food of a hundred flavors provided by faithful donors."
Fourth, regarding the vow concerning beds offered out of faith: one stands or lies upon a bed of hot iron and makes this aspiration:

"I would rather let this body lie upon a great flowing river of fierce fire, upon a net of hot iron, than ever again receive even a hundred kinds of beds and seats from a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts."
Fifth, he established a vow of three hundred spears against the medicinal offerings of faithful donors.

He further made this aspiration: "I would rather endure three hundred spears piercing my body for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever again receive the hundred-flavored medicines and tonics from faithful donors with a body that has broken the precepts."
Sixth, regarding the vow to cast oneself into a cauldron of molten iron in exchange for a dwelling provided by faithful offerings:

He further made this aspiration: "I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron and endure it for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever receive even a thousand kinds of dwellings, houses, gardens, or fields from a donor of faithful confidence while possessing a body of broken precepts."
Seventh, he stood before those with faith and made a solemn vow, striking his body with an iron hammer:

"I further make this aspiration: 'I would rather have this body of mine, from head to foot, shattered by an iron hammer until it is like fine dust, than ever receive the respectful prostrations of faithful donors with this precept-violating body.'"
Eighth, regarding the vow to gaze upon beautiful forms: one stands before hot iron and makes a vow to have one's eyes gouged out with it.

One further makes this aspiration: "I would rather have my two eyes gouged out by hundreds of thousands of hot iron knives and spears than ever look upon the beautiful forms of others with a mind that violates the precepts."
Ninth, in response to hearing pleasant sounds, he made a vow to have his ears pierced by a thousand awls.

He further made this aspiration: "I would rather have my entire body pierced by hundreds of thousands of iron awls and endure it for one or two kalpas than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, listen to pleasant sounds."
Tenth, he made a vow regarding the smelling of various fragrances:
"I swear that even if ten thousand blades were used to cut off my nose, I would rather have my nose severed by hundreds of thousands of blades than ever again,
with a mind of broken precepts, greedily smell various fragrances."
Eleventh: In the presence of food and flavors, he made a vow to cut out his tongue with a thousand blades, further vowing:
"I would rather have my tongue sliced by a hundred thousand blades than ever consume the hundred-flavored pure foods of others with a mind that violates the precepts."

[Note] The preceding text has already cautioned against this; the reason it is mentioned again here as "eating" is that while the former was based on the three karmas, this is based on the six sense faculties.
Although the prohibitions are the same, the specific transgressions differ slightly: the former concerns false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), while the latter concerns the tongue’s craving for flavors.
Regarding the twelve types of pleasant tactile sensations, he made a vow like one being struck by a sharp axe that severs the body:
"I further make this aspiration: rather than having my body cut and shattered by a sharp axe, I would never, with a mind of broken precepts, become greedily attached to pleasant tactile sensations."
13. One should constantly vow that sentient beings attain Buddhahood before oneself, and further make this vow that all sentient beings shall all attain Buddhahood. 14.
It should be understood that the final phrase of the third [section] concludes by identifying the failure to generate [the aspiration] as a transgression.
If a bodhisattva does not give rise to these vows—[Note:
These various vows do not exceed the Four Great Vows: that all sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood is the first vow; never to break the prohibitions and precepts is the second vow;
and to study the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, such as the Ten Stages of Departure (daśa-niryāṇa), and so forth, is the third vow.
The vow "I shall personally know myself to be a Buddha-to-be" is the fourth vow, as is clearly evident in the text. III.
Conclusion on the Offense:
One commits a minor offense (light defilement).
△ The thirty-seventh precept: Traveling while disregarding dangers.

[Commentary] When first undertaking the bodhisattva path, one’s progress is often uncertain. Furthermore, a human body is difficult to obtain and is a vessel capable of serving as a support for the Way;

yet, by failing to exercise caution during travel, one may meet with untimely death. To harbor thoughts of danger while living is a grave loss, brought about precisely through a lack of circumspection.
The regulation is established such that the seven groups of followers are equally subject to both the major and minor precepts. ○ First, the persons are identified:
"If a Buddha’s disciple.
△ Second, the matters are introduced in two parts.

[Commentary]: First, it clarifies that the proper conduct regarding one's dwelling and movement constitutes the preliminary conditions for the formulation of the precepts; furthermore, there are three initial points:
first, regarding dwelling and movement; second, regarding the eighteen items that must be carried at all times.

[Note] Regarding the "three sections," these refer to what is appropriate and inappropriate for binding [the precepts], with the first being the appropriate. The commentary’s sub-sectioning here is extremely brief;

I shall now provide a more detailed sub-sectioning. Within the commentary, there are three major divisions: first, clarifying the two periods of movement and rest; second, distinguishing the eighteen items;

and third, clarifying the self-following [of the precepts]. The first [section on movement and rest] is divided into two private parts: first, traveling; second, staying. Therefore, the commentary states:
Wandering and dwelling. ○ Now, first, regarding wandering:
one should always practice the *dhūta* [ascetic practices] during two seasons.
【Commentary】The "two seasons for *dhūta*" refers to the time of wandering; during the two seasons of spring and autumn, one wanders at a moderate pace to transform [beings].
There is no harm or damage to things. Regarding the twelve dhūta practices, they are explained in detail; concerning food, there are five: (1) not accepting special invitations;
(2) always eating one meal a day; (3) not drinking liquids after midday; (4) eating in a single sitting; (5) moderation in the amount of food.
Regarding the dwelling place, there are five: (1) a forest hermitage; (2) always sitting without lying down; (3) staying among tombs.
Dwelling under the four types of trees, sitting in the five kinds of open spaces, and maintaining the two forms of clothing-restraint: first, possessing only the three robes;
second, constantly wearing the patched robe (*kaṣāya*).
[Note: The *Vinaya-śū* states: "Formerly called *dhūta*, now called *duṭṭha*. This is translated as 'washing away,' and also as 'cleansing.'"
He also vigorously shook off [delusions], and although the terminology used for the practices of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differs slightly, their essential substance is no different.

The *Bai lu* states: "I was afflicted by diligent toil from my youth," continuing until it says: "I wore only a single hempen robe for over thirty years, never removing it from my body in either winter or summer.
Thus we know that our Patriarch was truly worthy of being a teacher and model; those who transmit the Way today rely only on—
Is it not shameful in one’s own heart to make the accumulation of robes and alms bowls one’s primary concern? ○ Second, regarding residence:
practicing *zazen* during winter and summer, and observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

[Commentary: Because wandering about during the cold of winter and the heat of summer causes much hindrance and harm, this rule was established. If one does not comply with this regulation, one commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
[Note] The Sanskrit term *dhyāna* is here translated as "grove of merit" (*gōngdé cónglín*) or "cultivation through contemplation" (*sīwéi xiū*).
The *Bǎilù* states: "Sitting in meditation within the hall is one's constant duty. I entrust this to future students: you should always regard this as an urgent priority.
If you are distracted and lack stillness, it is truly what is called "vainly losing the spiritual radiance of one's own nature. [End of] Summer Retreat.
The mountain clouds take shape; the mind is gathered in stillness, which is called "peace" (an). To set a specific period for remaining in this state is called "dwelling" (ju).

The ritual procedures for the *varṣā* retreat are fully contained within the Vinaya texts and must be known. This concludes the first section, "Wandering and Dwelling," among the three topics of this commentary.
△ Twenty-eight Items. ○ First Item.
One should habitually use the *yāśchi* (tooth-stick).
[Note] The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that when chewing the *yāśchi* in the early morning, the Buddha said there are five benefits: first, it can eliminate jaundice and fever;
second, it can eliminate saliva and phlegm; third, it ensures the mouth is free of foul breath; fourth, it aids the digestion of food; and fifth, it clarifies the eyesight.

The *Jingjiguizhuan* (Biographies of Those Who Entrusted Their Relics) states: "The tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) should be twelve finger-widths long, no shorter than eight, and as thick as the little finger.
One end should be made supple; chew it thoroughly for a long while and clean the teeth and gums well. This can strengthen the teeth, perfume the mouth, and remove phlegm.
If used for half a month, bad breath will suddenly vanish; if used for thirty days, painful and decayed teeth will be cured. **II. Two Substances**
Soap powder for bathing.
[Note] The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that it may be made from large and small beans, *kaṭibha* grass, and so forth; furthermore, there are eight kinds of beans:

namely, chickpeas (*mudga*), black beans (*māṣa*), *kṛṣṇa* beans, small beans (*caṇaka*), peas (*makuṣṭha*), mountain beans (*kulattha*), *sālu* beans, and *kāka* beans. These are used to purify the body.
To purify the mouth, one must not place incense inside [the mouth]. The *Mahāvinaya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"If one does not wash one's hands with soap powder and water before handling a sūtra scroll or an incense burner, upon death one will fall into the Impure Hell.
In the past, there was the bhikṣu Jiandian who maintained the fast for sixty years, yet he obtained the merit of only a single day. The Buddha said to him: "It is because of you..."

It is commonly said that rinsing the mouth with ash-water yields immeasurable merit; on one occasion, the merit obtained from rinsing the mouth with water mixed with bathing beans was likewise infinite.
○ Third, the three substances.
The three robes. [Note:
Their general name is *kāṣāya*, which will be explained in the subsequent text. ○ The four items:
the water flask.
[Note] The *Shō* (Commentary) quotes the *Jìguī zhǎn* (Record of Returning to the West): "Generally, there are two types of water vessels for pure and impure use;

the pure one is made of earthenware or porcelain, while the impure one may be made of copper or iron. To remove impurity, one uses impure water to wash it, and to bring it into purity, one uses pure water.
The *Śrāmaṇera Sūtra* states: "If pure water is unavailable, washing the hands with pure grass is also permissible. ○ Five Items.
Alms bowl.
[Note] The Sanskrit term *pātra* is translated here as "proper vessel" (*yingqi*). The Vinaya states that it should be made of clay or iron, as described in the Vinaya texts.
○ The six requisites.
Sitting mat.
[Note] The Vinaya states that it was prescribed for the sake of protecting the body, protecting the robes, and protecting the monastic bedding. In Sanskrit it is called *niṣīdana*;
here it is translated as "cloth for sitting upon. ○ Seven items.
The Tin Staff (Khaṭvāṅga).
[Note] As for "staff" (daṇḍa), it means reliance; one relies upon this staff to eliminate evil and advance toward good. As for "tin" (khaṭvā), it means clarity, binding, and non-retrogression;
because one seeks liberation without turning back. ○ The Eight Articles.
Incense Burner and Coffer.
[Note] A vessel for holding incense; some say that the burner and the coffer are two separate items, or that the character "coffer" (lián) may be omitted from the original text. Nine items.

Water Strainer. [Note] Also called the water-filtering cloth (*pūraka*). In India, it is made of white cotton cloth; in this land [China], it is made of boiled silk. It is used to filter water and remove insects.

When returning to one's original pond, one should carry them nearby; for distant locations, one should place them separately in a release basin (*fangsheng pen*). One should filter the water through three layers.
If there are still those who do not leave, one should abandon [the water] and depart. Day after day, one must inspect it closely; if no insects are found, it may be used.

One must never use water without a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*). If one travels on a road without a companion, even if the entire community would incur an offense, it is better to die of thirst than to drink water containing insects, as explained at length in the Vinaya. ○ Ten Items.
Hand towel.
[Note] In the Vinaya, it is permitted to possess hand-wiping towels, foot-wiping towels, sweat towels, face towels, tear-wiping towels, and so forth.
(11 items).
The Knife.

[Note] It is traditionally referred to as the "Precept-Protecting Knife. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that for the purpose of cutting one's *kāṣāya*, it is permitted to keep a knife four inches long with a blade shaped like a crescent moon. These are the twelve articles.
Fire-starter.
[Note] A tool for producing fire, such as wood, a mirror, or a gem.
○ Thirteen items. Tongs.
[Note] The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that because the hair in a bhikṣu’s nostrils was a source of public derision, the Buddha permitted them to keep [hair-removers] made of copper or iron.
The *Rongchao* states that in India, many walk barefoot; it is suggested that these [tools] were used to extract thorns, though its source is unknown.
(14 items).
Rope Bed.
[Note] According to the Vinaya regulations, beds with curved legs, straight legs, and so forth, may be used for practicing meditation or preaching the Dharma in various locations. ○ Fifteen Items.
Sūtra.
○ Sixteen items.
Vinaya.
○ Seventeen items.
Buddha image.
○ Eighteen articles.
Bodhisattva image.

[Note] Since the Sūtras and Vinayas reveal that the practice of cultivation relies on the dharmas of concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā), an image of the Buddha serves as a reminder not to forget one’s original teacher, and an image of a Bodhisattva serves as a constant contemplation of virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra).
The preceding fourteen items are the conditions for the path of cultivation, while the latter four types are the bases upon which one relies;
it is by means of these that one cultivates the path. The above constitutes the first major section of the Commentary.
Twenty-eight items. △ Third, the personal requisites (*pārihārika*) also have two parts: first, those for traveling; second, those for staying.
Regarding the first, there are again two parts: first, the formal explanation of the *dhūta* practices; second, an incidental clarification of the *poṣadha*. ○ Now, the first part.
When a bodhisattva practices *dhūta* austerities or travels from place to place, even when traveling a hundred or a thousand *li*, these eighteen items always accompany his person.
As for the practitioner of *dhūta*, during these two periods— from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month,
and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month— these eighteen items [are required].
Objects always follow one's person like the two wings of a bird.
[Note] The former refers to the spring season, and the latter refers to the autumn season; during these two seasons, it is neither cold nor hot, making them most suitable for traveling.
○ Second, an explanation of the *poṣadha* (confession and purification) ceremony.

If, on the day of the *poṣadha*, a newly practicing bodhisattva recites the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts during the fortnightly *poṣadha* ceremony, he should recite them before images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Whether there is one person performing the *poṣadha*, or two, three, or even up to a hundred thousand people, they shall all recite together as one. Thus he should recite.
The preceptor shall sit on the high seat and the listeners on the lower seats; each shall don the nine-strip, seven-strip, or five-strip *kāṣāya*.
[Note: *Poṣadha* is translated here as "Pure Abiding" (*jìngzhù*). Disciples of the Buddha, whether ordained or lay, should regularly perform the *poṣadha* every half-month.

Regarding the ritual procedures for the *poṣadha*, such as the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā*) and the proclamation of matters, these have been recorded separately at the end of this volume; they must be consulted.
Regarding the phrase "wearing the nine-strip *kāṣāya* and so forth," there are three types of robes. First is the *saṃghāṭī*, which has nine varieties ranging from nine strips to twenty-five strips.
This name was established according to its meaning; some call it the "robe for subduing the assembly" because it subdues the assemblies of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Others call it the "heavy robe" or the "patchwork robe. It may also be named according to its function, such as when one enters [the village].
The two types of robes for the royal palace and the village are the *uttarāsaṅga*.
Its meaning is translated as "upper garment," because it is worn over the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṇṭhaka*), or as "middle-priced garment"; nowadays it is used as the robe for entering the assembly.
Third is the *antarvāsaka* (or *antavāsaka*), which refers to the "walking robe" or the "work robe"; this is the robe that fits closest to the body. The *uttara*... [is the upper garment].
The *saṃghāṭī* consists of seven strips, and the *antarvāsaka* consists of five strips; thus, these three robes must not be lacking even one.

In their manufacture, they should be made of cloth; however, while the top [of the robe] must be rounded, the lower garment (*cīvara*) must be square—this is the physical form of a monk and a construction according to the Dharma.
Recently, there have been two kinds of people who have never given this a thought, as the Sūtras state that one whose body does not wear [the robes] is not a monk.

Regarding those who possess only the three robes: ghosts follow in their tracks while devas do not protect them; when the noble ones see them, they designate them as "those without the Dharma" and "those without shame.
First, there are those who claim to have attained mastery of the Great Way and thus disregard minor details.

They argue that adhering strictly to the regulations for robes is the practice of the Lesser Vehicle, and so they indulge their extravagant desires, using gauze, brocade, and flowery ornaments. Second, there are those who lack understanding.
Those who observe the precepts among the ignorant of the village know only that the head is round and the robes are square;
they do not understand what the so-called "robes" truly are as a Dharma. They use silk and gauze at will, desiring only to complete the garment—this is truly pitiable.
Though they wish to shield their eyes from others and drape these over their bodies, when the devas and sages behold them in the empty void, they see nothing but a bald head.
If you are merely a layperson, ghosts and spirits will be able to treat you with contempt. I urge all monks to manufacture the three robes (tricīvara) and maintain them without fail;
not only will you be rebuked by the sages, but you will also invite calamity upon yourselves. Question:
Since the *poṣadha* ceremony includes both the laity and the ordained, meeting together as one assembly, how can it be said that those who are laypeople also "wear the *kāṣāya*"?
The *Śāyadharvinaya* states that single-layered (unsewn) robes are specifically for the laity;

however, the Vaipulya Sūtras say that those who cultivate pure conduct according to the bhikṣu dharma and enter the *maṇḍala* while possessing the three dharma-robes must wear single-layered triple robes (*tricīvara*).
Jingxi says that "single-layered" means back-stitching is not permitted, lest it be confused with the robes maintained by the Great Sangha; as for "back-stitching," it refers to...

The "bird-foot" stitch refers to a single running stitch; whether folded or pasted, both methods are applicable to the three robes (*tricīvara*), as their long and short strips are similar, differing only in that the *saṃghāṭī* consists of three layers and so forth, while the color remains the same.
Furthermore, although the three robes are prescribed, they are not the attire of the laity; our ancestor, the Dharma Master Zhi, offered a gourd-bark *kaṣāya* to the Prince of Jin.
It is said that when performing the *poṣadha*, one should wear this very robe;

this signifies that the sovereign’s honored teachings have roughly formed a monastic garb, thereby causing [the people] to follow the Vaipulya sutras. ○ Second, regarding dwelling and personal conduct:
When entering the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one should likewise observe each requirement according to the Dharma.

[Commentary: Some say that when a Bodhisattva makes his vow for the five-month retreat from the second half of the fifth month to the first half of the eighth month, the text states that at this time he no longer practices *dhūta* (ascetic) practices; this constitutes the limit of the retreat.
[Note] This explains the previous section on the period of staying put; it is an abridgment regarding those who practice seated meditation without speaking.
△ Second, "What Should Not Be Done Privately" is divided into two parts: first, what should not be done while traveling; second, what should not be done while staying put. ○ Now, the first part.
When practicing the dhūta austerities, one must not enter dangerous places. Whether it be a wicked realm, the territory of a wicked king,
terrain with steep elevations and depressions, dense vegetation, or dangers from lions, tigers, wolves, water, fire, wind, bandits on the road, or venomous snakes—
one must by no means enter any such perilous places while practicing the dhūta path.
[Commentary] To travel while braving hardships is entirely a matter of restriction.

[Note] The *Zangshu* states: "Regarding the twelve difficult places: first, the difficulty of a 'bad king'—if the king of that country does not believe in the Triple Gem, a dhūta practitioner may not enter his realm;
second, the difficulty of uneven terrain; third, the difficulty of deep grass and dense forests."
The secret [text] lists fourteen [perils]: first, black lions that devour men; second, tigers; third, wolves; fourth, water; fifth, fire; sixth, wind; seventh, bandits; eighth, venomous snakes;
ninth, the paths they traverse; tenth, a summary of all difficult places; eleventh, national calamities—meaning floods, droughts, and warfare; twelfth, as the *Xīchāo* states: "Question:
Regarding the sixteen minor [offenses] mentioned previously, it says 'even [encountering] a starving tiger.'"

Question: If one should give away one's own body, flesh, hands, and feet to the wolf, how does this not contradict [the previous teaching]? Answer: The preceding passage clarifies the giving of material things (*vastu-dāna*);

it was feared that those on the stages from the *gotrabhūmi* upward would already be fully capable of practicing it. This present case, however, refers to a beginner who must be cautious regarding difficult circumstances;
for the karma of ordinary beings and bodhisattvas is largely indeterminate. (2) It is improper to dwell there.
Up until the time of the summer retreat (varṣā), one must not enter any of these dangerous places.
[Note] Since one should also speak of sitting in meditation (dhyāna) here, the phrase "up until" is used to include it as well. 3. Raising the fault to conclude the refutation.
If one enters [the hall] intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
△ The thirty-eighth precept: Regarding the violation of the order of seniority between the honored and the lowly. [Commentary:

Because such disorder violates proper decorum, this rule is established for all seven assemblies; it is prescribed for both the great and the small. ○ First, the identification of the person [who violates].
If you are a Buddha’s disciple:
△ Section One: The Sequence of Affairs, consisting of (1) what is appropriate, (2) what is inappropriate, and (3) a summary of the appropriate and inappropriate. ○ Now, the first:
One should sit according to the proper sequence; those who received the precepts earlier sit in front, and those who received the precepts later sit behind.
Regardless of whether they are old or young, monks or nuns, nobles or kings and princes, or even eunuchs and slaves,
those who have received the precepts first should sit in front, while those who have received the precepts later should sit in order behind them.
Second, it is improper:
do not act like the foolish outsiders, whether old or young, who sit without precedence or sequence,
following the manner of soldiers or slaves.
[Commentary: One must not disrupt the order. Third, the summary:
In my Buddha-dharma, those who come first sit first and those who come later sit later; yet these bodhisattvas each sat in a manner that did not accord with the proper sequence.

[Commentary] To summarize the principles of what is appropriate and inappropriate: the sequence of the Śrāvakas as it appears in the Vinaya section concerning the rules for bedding and requisites proceeds by way of the precepts.
This extends from the "Great Muhūrta" (the time unit) down to those designated as *upādhyāya* (senior elders), who include both monastics and laypeople across nine groups:
1. Bhikṣus; 2. Bhikṣuṇīs; 3. Ṣaṣṭidharmikās; 4. Śrāmaṇeras; 5. Śrāmaṇerīs; 6. Those who have left the household life.
Seventh, the bhikṣuṇī; eighth, the upāsaka; ninth, the upāsikā. These nine assemblies follow a sequential order and must not be disordered, as explained in the Vinaya-piṭaka.
[Note] Regarding "a muhūrta," the Abhidharmakośa states that thirty muhūrtas constitute a day and night; the Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya states that one first receives [the precepts].
From the full precepts down to a mere moment, such a person should first receive water and first receive food and drink.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "If one first [observes] the minor [precepts] and later the major, then the minor summer retreat is opened up to constitute the major summer retreat.

If one first receives the major [precepts] and later receives the disciplinary rules (*vinaya*), then if they are minor, one follows the minor; if they are major, one follows the major. Although this is the principle, it depends on the local customs of the region.
Unlike the monastic community of this land, where there is no distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, in the West they are strictly and eternally separated.

Nevertheless, when the four reliances appear in the world, both the Great and Small Vehicles must be propagated together; it is only according to the capacity and conditions of sentient beings that their scope is either universal or limited.
Regarding the six dharmas for nuns—that is, the *śikṣamāṇā* training in the six dharmas—this has already been explained above. Furthermore, it says: "Leaving home, leaving home."
“Nī” means “nī,” which refers to women; it denotes those men and women who have first left the household life. ○ Third, the determination of the offense:
one commits a minor secondary offense (light dust-offense).
△ The thirty-ninth precept: not cultivating merit and wisdom.
[Commentary]: The two adornments of merit and wisdom are like the two wings of a bird; they must be cultivated, for without them one deviates from the path of liberation.

Therefore, it is ordained that the seven classes of followers—both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna—should cultivate them together. While not exclusively encompassed by the Bodhisattva vehicle, all wholesome practices should be cultivated.

Specifically, during the summer retreat, Śrāvakas should undertake a vow to cultivate meritorious deeds; at other times, no such restriction is imposed. First, the persons [to whom this applies] are identified.
If you are a disciple of the Buddha:
△ The preface to the matter has three stages: first, cultivating merit; second, cultivating wisdom; third, concluding with the faults. ○ Now, for the first:
one should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings, establishing monasteries, mountain forests, gardens, and fields, and constructing Buddha-stūpas.
One should establish [these] in all places for sitting in meditation during the winter and summer retreats, as well as in all places for practicing the Path.
[Commentary: Regarding the seven matters briefly enumerated in the text—namely, first, monasteries; second, mountain forests; third, gardens; fourth, fields; fifth, stupas;
sixth, places for winter and summer meditation retreats; and seventh, all places for practicing the Path—one should personally undertake them or instruct others to do so.
All such categories should be established as powers; if one is unable to do so, there is no offense. [Note]:

In the task of cultivating merit, the essential for a student of the Buddha lies in daily practice and never forgetting what has been heard; thus, the two adornments are complete. Regarding the four lines from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"An elephant’s body adorned with a net of seven treasures—this is a case of having merit but lacking wisdom"; an Arhat should apply this.

If one makes offerings while being thin [in merit], there is the phrase "having compassion but lacking merit," and the rest should be understood accordingly. Thus, one knows that the two adornments of merit and wisdom are like the two wings of a bird.

Regarding the seven matters, one should avoid wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) for one's own sustenance, as the *Śāsanānuśāsanī-sūtra* (Teaching of the Last Instructions) does not permit the acquisition of fields and houses or the raising of people;

[Note] The phrase "extinguishing offenses" contains profound meaning. There are two methods of repentance: *zuo-fa chan* (repentance through ritual procedure) and *jian-xiang chan* (repentance by perceiving signs).
The character for "extinguishing" (*mie*) refers to *wusheng chan* (repentance of non-arising). If it were not for this wondrous principle, offenses...

What is the principle of cessation? It is the manifestation through which transgressions vanish and views become quiescent, reaching the state of *nirvāṇa*. As it is said, "By the cessation of causes, one realizes true unity": first, the term "cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the purification of all things;
second, it refers to the absolute stillness and severance [of delusions]. Because it encompasses these two meanings, it accords with the non-arising of phenomena.

This passage reveals virtue by means of its faults: if one does not possess the auspicious signs, one cannot obtain the precepts; conversely, this demonstrates that as soon as one obtains the auspicious signs, [the precepts are attained].
When one abides in the principle of quiescence, all precepts are restored. (2) Regarding the attainment through augmentation:
one attains the augmentation of receiving the precepts.

[Note] Some versions lack the character "yi" (benefit). Based on what was previously seen, the auspicious signs indicate that the old precepts are fully restored; this refers to the restoration of the precepts upon seeing auspicious signs.

It is said that once one has obtained the precepts, they need not be received again. However, if one does not obtain a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*) despite such diligent practice of repentance, what then?
For this person, the "augmentative reception" (*vṛddhi-upasaṃpadā*) is opened;

that is, it is permitted to receive them again before a teacher in accordance with the ritual for receiving the precepts—this is called the augmentative reception. If this is so, then since the transgression of a grave offense (*pārājika*) applies universally...
What harm is there in receiving [the precepts] again after having transgressed them at will? Nevertheless, one must perform repentance according to the Dharma for a period of up to one year.
If no auspicious signs are seen, one may then obtain the increased precepts (*viśeṣa-śīla*). If one does not undergo such diligent and arduous repentance, it cannot be called obtaining the precepts;
how could one allow oneself to receive them again after having committed an offense, thereby opening the gate of negligence? Question: Now...

This opening for repentance is established for those who have committed the ten grave offenses. Why is there no such repentance for those who previously committed the seven heinous crimes (*saptānantarya*)? Furthermore, the preceding precept states that one must not confer the present-life ordination upon those who have committed the seven heinous crimes; does this mean that those who have committed the seven heinous crimes are never permitted to receive ordination? Answer: Mount Ding (Dingshan) distinguishes the seven heinous crimes from the ten grave offenses by means of five points. First, regarding the nature of the offense: the seven heinous crimes are transgressions against the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), whereas the ten grave offenses are transgressions against the Buddha’s person. Second, regarding the gravity of the retribution:

the seven heinous crimes result in immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), while the ten grave offenses involve retribution that may be deferred. Third, regarding the possibility of remediation: the seven heinous crimes are so severe that they cannot be remedied even through the power of the Three Jewels, whereas the ten grave offenses can be remedied through the power of the Three Jewels. Fourth, regarding the capacity for transformation: those who have committed the seven heinous crimes lack the capacity for transformation, while those who have committed the ten grave offenses possess the capacity for transformation. Fifth, regarding the scope of the precepts: the seven heinous crimes pertain to the prohibitions against killing, while the ten grave offenses pertain to the prohibitions against stealing and other acts. Thus, although the ten grave offenses are similar to the seven heinous crimes in their severity, they differ in these five respects. Therefore, the opening for repentance is provided for those who have committed the ten grave offenses. As for the prohibition on conferring ordination upon those who have committed the seven heinous crimes, it refers specifically to the present life; it does not preclude their eventual attainment of the Way through future cultivation. Thus, while the seven heinous crimes are extremely grave, the ten grave offenses allow for the possibility of repentance and restoration.

The differences are as follows: first, regarding the three faculties—whereas the previous passage stated that if one sees the seven heinous offenses or the eight difficulties, one should teach them to repent, and that for those who have committed the seven heinous offenses, this sutra should be preached;

the former was spoken in reference to those of superior faculties who are easily purified, while the latter is spoken in reference to those of middling or inferior faculties who are difficult to transform.
Second, regarding the gravity of repentance. Third, regarding the mutual clarification through partial inclusion (śāyala). Fourth, regarding the difference in names but identity in meaning.

The textual passages concerning the five categories of granting and withholding [karmic results] and so forth are merely prolix and lack definitive judgment; those who require them may read them and see the meaning for themselves.
Now, regarding grave offenses (*ānantarya*), they must be distinguished and cannot be conflated.

As previously explained in the commentary, within the three grades of the precept against killing, the highest grade constitutes an offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) when committed against the Buddhas, sages, one’s parents, or teachers and monks.

When humans and devas commit grave offenses, they belong to the lower grade; those in the four realms of existence may be either light or grave. Because they are not suitable vessels for the Dharma, they are categorized as belonging to the light or neutral grades.

These three grades are extremely clear and distinct. Furthermore, the previous commentary clarifies the three obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), distinguishing between what constitutes an obstruction and what does not.

It states: regarding the seven heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), first, it says that if they are extinguished through repentance, they do not constitute an obstruction; second, it says that whether one commits one such offense and repents it or does not repent it, [the nature of the obstruction remains the same].

Regarding these obstructions to the ten grave offenses (*daśa-ānantarya*), there are three interpretations. The third states: "If one has not yet repented, they completely obstruct [the path]; once repented, they are no longer an obstruction.

Although the seven reversals (*sapta-viparyaya*) and the ten grave offenses each have many interpretations, and while there is no definitive selection among them, the latter interpretation is taken as correct.

According to these texts, both repentance and non-repentance of the seven reversals constitute obstructions; furthermore, they are distinguished from the grave offenses themselves. Based on such passages, the grave offenses and the reversals must be differentiated. As for...
Why name them differently if their meaning is the same? To categorically refuse [to allow] this is certainly not permissible.

Thus we know that when receiving the precepts, the inquiry regarding obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) includes both the primary and secondary obstacles; while the former may still be purified through repentance, the latter truly cannot be.

Since the text explicitly states, "One must not confer the precepts upon those who have committed the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) in their present life," and the regulation is so clear, how can one stubbornly remain deluded and claim that those who have committed grave offenses are eligible for repentance?

One who has attained the extinction of offenses may receive the precepts; however, for one who has committed an offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), there is no scriptural text permitting its reception in the present body.

If it is argued that even those who have committed the seven offenses of immediate retribution can universally obtain the precepts, why then is their reception restricted to the present body? Or, it may be asked:

since the previous section on the precepts permitted repentance and this sutra should be expounded, why is the reception of the precepts categorically denied here? The answer is that this requires a precise discernment regarding repentance.
Repentance and the attainment of precepts are not the same; it was because people of old were confused about this that they threw ethical relations into disorder.

The previous commentary explained that for those who have attained the three fruits [of the path], one must not arbitrarily alter the text of the commentary. This is because it is understood that even for a person who has committed a heinous offense (*ānantarya-karma*), since their transgression is profound, repentance is permitted.
Therefore, the preceding passage states: "One should instruct them to repent so that they may gradually attain purification and avoid falling into hell."

Regarding this very present body, one cannot receive the precepts; since there is no scriptural text to support the contrary view, how could it be permissible to privately accommodate such a sentiment?
The commentaries and records merely multiply their lists of categories, yet they openly violate the [Vinaya] and run counter to the Sūtras—how could this be acceptable?

In the *Xizhi Chao* (Commentary on the Vinaya), there are many omissions and deficiencies, all of which are generally of this nature; I am unable to provide a full refutation here. ○ Regarding the minor impediments for the three assemblies [of novices].

This is a summary of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Each of these is not clearly understood, and their meaning is not grasped.

Generally, those who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts are called "evil persons. If one were to preach them prematurely, they would be unable to receive them with earnest gravity once they do so later;

△ The forty-third precept: Receiving Offerings Without a Sense of Shame.

[Commentary]: Having committed an offense within one's own category, if one does not reflect upon it with shame and remorse, yet brazenly accepts offerings without feeling any sense of guilt, the Buddha established this precept for the five classes of monastics—both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna—together, because such individuals are unworthy of being fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). As the text states:

"Regarding those who have left home with faith but violate the true precepts: since householders have not yet attained the status of a field of merit, they were not subject to this regulation. This is the initial heading.
People. If a Buddha’s disciple:
△ Section on the Threefold Matters: 1. Not receiving offerings; 2. Being reviled by humans and ghosts; 3. Exposing faults and drawing conclusions.
[This is] an error. Now, first:

because one has left the household life with faith and received the Buddha’s true precepts, anyone who conceives the intent to violate these holy precepts shall not receive the offerings of any donor, nor shall they walk upon the ground of the king, nor drink the water of the king.
[Commentary]: First, those who possess offenses and lack a sense of shame are unworthy of receiving offerings;
for kings originally grant land and water to those of virtuous conduct, and those without virtue may not enjoy them. Second, they are reviled by humans and spirits.
Five thousand great ghosts constantly block his path ahead, saying, "Great thief! When he enters houses, cities, or dwellings, the ghosts further sweep away his footprints.
All people in the world revile him, saying, "A thief within the Buddha-dharma!

This is the general [classification].

[Note] In the *Xīchāo* (Commentary on the Splendor), fascicle six, the first six are termed "specific," meaning that the six phrases following "the Lotus Treasury World" all state that they "encompass and include the inexhaustible.
Thus, the scripture says, "In this way, all Buddhas... [An alternate version of the text reads, "As suchness, all Buddhas..."].

Alternatively, it may be read as "or as all Buddhas. Since this text states that among the dharmas taught, the preceding six are specific and this one is general, it should correctly be read as "or as all Buddhas. Dingshan said:

"The former are specific and the latter is general" means that within these seven phrases, the first six are specific and the last one is general; this is because he takes the Buddha of cause and effect [as the referent].
The nature permeates the preceding six phrases and does not transcend this treasury; the lotus is that upon which it relies, and the atom serves as its metaphor.
These all reveal that the *dharmamukha* (dharma-gate) of inclusion and containment is simply another name for this sutra.

Regarding the phrase "the heart of all Buddhas" and so forth, this is likely a collective enumeration of the headings of the present chapter. "Heart-treasury" (*cittagarbha*) and "Earth-treasury" (*bhūmigarbha*) are precisely the two characters of "Heart-ground" (*cittabhūmi*).
The "Treasury of Precepts" (*śīlaskandha*) is itself the Dharma-gate; "immeasurable practices" and so forth refer to the fruition and the person who attains it.
That individuals receive this category and cultivate their vows encompasses both cause and effect, as well as Buddha-nature, from beginning to end.

Phrases such as "all these" and so on further summarize the preceding sentences. Regarding the explanations of the general and specific phrases in the *Chaoji* (Commentary), each differs; if one follows...
Dingshan takes the phrase "the Buddha-nature of cause and effect" as the general principle and treats the subsequent phrase, "seeing the suchness of all Buddhas," as superfluous;
he then claims that the following summary of the preceding phrase is entirely contrary to the meaning of the text, and thus it cannot be used.
Now, taking the *Xihui-chao* (Xi’s Commentary) to explain the text is more convenient. △ From "In the worlds of a thousand billion... onwards is the fourth major section.
The assembly’s practice is also twofold: first, the hundreds of billions of assemblies; second, pointing to other locations. Now, for the first:
throughout the worlds of the hundreds of billions, all sentient beings receive, uphold, and joyfully practice it.
[The second point] concerns other locations.

If one wishes to expand upon the characteristics of the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*), they are as explained in the "Seventh Chapter on the King of Lotus Radiance" (*Buddhāvatamsaka-rāja-saptama-parivarta*).
[Commentary]: The preceding section clarified that within the worlds of the thousands of millions of buddha-fields, sentient beings each speak and each practice accordingly.
The second finger [indicates] that other sections are explained extensively in the "Chapter on the King of Flower Radiance," which should be among the Great Texts.
The "Three Thousand" refers to the three thousand modes of deportment that a bodhisattva should study. The "three years" refers to five years for śrāvakas and three years for bodhisattvas.
The "three matters" are precept, concentration, and wisdom. Thus it is.
[Note] In ancient editions of the scripture, there are instances where it is written as "three years" (sān nián) and others where it is written as "three matters" (sān shì); these are scribal errors.
The current edition should read "three thousand" (sān qiān), as explained previously. Regarding the verse that follows, neither the *Shū* nor the *Cāo* commentaries provide an explanation.

Examining this verse in detail, I suspect it was excerpted from other passages of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* by Kumārajīva for inclusion here, rather than being part of the original text of this chapter.

My ancestors did not understand the old scriptures, and there are those that remain and those that do not. Since these are scriptural texts, what harm is there in recording them for others to study and recite?
Now that they are currently circulating, I have therefore provided a private commentary to assist those seeking understanding, dividing the whole into three sections:
△ First, praising the merit and function of the precepts; second, refuting errors to reveal the truth; third, admonishing and exhorting to conclude by returning to the source.
The first section consists of three parts: first, the introductory praise; second, the formal praise; and third, the concluding praise. Now, for the first: the introductory praise.
A person of wisdom whose patience and insight are strong Is able to uphold such a Dharma as this. Until they attain the Way of Buddhahood, They will securely obtain five kinds of benefits.

[Note] Only those of lofty intelligence and virtue can practice patience and wisdom, maintaining them firmly without transgression; though they have not yet attained Buddhahood, they securely obtain benefit.
○ Second, the formal praise:
First, the Buddhas of the ten directions take pity on them and constantly protect them; second, at the time of the end of life...
1. With right view, the mind is joyful; 2. In every successive birth, one dwells in [favorable] places; 3. One becomes a friend to all bodhisattvas; 4.
One is a mass of merit, with the perfection of ethical discipline fully accomplished; 5. In this and future lives, one is perfected in natural virtue, merit, and wisdom.
[Note] Regarding the five kinds of benefits, various corresponding explanations could be provided without exception; however, here they are discussed solely in terms of cause and effect:
the first four praise the cause, while the last one praises the fruit. Whether categorized or taken as the ultimate, all arise from this.
3. Conclusion and Praise.
This is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity; the wise should contemplate it well. △ Part Two:
Refuting the False and Revealing the True, which has two sections: first, refuting the false; second, revealing the true. ○ Now, the first section.
Those who calculate by means of a self and cling to signs cannot give birth to this Dharma; nor is one who has extinguished all grasping and attained realization a place where seeds can be sown.
[Note] Refuting two kinds of non-conditions:
first, those in the stage of ordinary beings—the six kinds of ordinary beings—take this as an object of grasping and attachment, and thus possess a self.

First, the refutation: "The marks of persons cannot produce the dharma of the true mark. This means that those of the Two Vehicles dwell in the realm of partial realization through sinking into emptiness;
they extinguish the life-span of the wisdom of the Dharma-body, and thus are not fields for the seed of Buddhahood—all such cases are rejected.
Second, the manifestation of what is [the true field], which has three parts: first, showing the light of the true mark; second, clarifying the fruit of the eight negations; third, manifesting...
The Causes of Practice. First:
To cause the sprout of bodhi to grow, and for its radiance to illuminate the world, one should calmly observe the true nature of all phenomena.

[Note] In the preceding text, the Buddha immediately emitted light from his mouth; because of this emission of light, the sutra explains it as having causes and conditions that are neither form nor mind.

Now, since this light contemplates the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is identical to the interpretation in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), which holds that the emission of light symbolizes the preaching of the true reality.
For this reason, the preceding note once cited this as evidence. ○ Second, the clarification.
The eight negations:
neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, neither identical nor different,
neither coming nor going.
[Note] The six classes of ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-pṛthagjana*) are attached to the realm of arising and ceasing; the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) give rise to views of permanence and annihilation;

the three vehicles (*triyāna*) possess practices of identity and difference; and the partial Buddhas manifest the characteristics of coming and going. Now, the wondrous precepts of the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*), which constitute the essence of the Buddha-fruit, are free from these eight faults;
therefore, the first two lines of the eight [verses] speak of them in terms of the six classes of ordinary beings and the non-Buddhists. This is the meaning.
Thus, the latter two phrases are easy to understand. How is this clarified? First, "like" (rú) means suchness.

The two vehicles perceive the three realms as suchness; the Bodhisattva perceives the three realms as both suchness and different. When emerging from the provisional to dwell in the ultimate, they reside in difference.

Furthermore, this is cited from one perspective; therefore, we know that this phrase is intended to refute the three vehicles, stating that they are "neither identical nor different. This concludes the explanation.
The Master’s palace departs; he comes to achieve perfect enlightenment. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) distinguishes between the vertical and horizontal [dimensions]:

even the Tathāgata does not accord with the present meaning, let alone the partial fruits of the *Āgama* and *Abhidharma* vehicles. Furthermore, the verses of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the emergence of the stupa in the *Lotus Sutra* both rely upon the "Eight Negations" to manifest the perfect and eternal.
Because there is no arising, there is no difference; because there is no permanence, there is no coming; and because there is no cessation, there is no departing.

Therefore, it is neither one, nor severed, nor departed. This explanation is provided to establish the first two [stages] by listing the remaining six, and to establish the gate of non-arising through the union of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
△ Third, revealing the causes of practice, which has three parts:
(1) the root of the Bodhisattvas, (2) the root of the Buddha-sons, and (3) the source of all Buddhas; these are all brought into accord with the practices previously explained in the commentary.
This consists of three phrases. First, regarding the fundamental basis of the bodhisattva:
Within this single mind, through skillful means and diligent adornment, one should train in the successive stages of what a bodhisattva ought to do.
[Note] This refers to what the preceding sutra calls "the root of practicing the path of the bodhisattva. ○ Second, the root of the Buddha-sons:
Regarding those in training and those beyond training, do not give rise to discriminatory thoughts.
[Note] This refers to what the preceding [text] calls "the root of the great assembly of all Buddha-sons. ○ Third, the source of all Buddhas.
This is called the foremost path, And it is also called the Mahāyāna. All conceptual proliferations and evils are extinguished from this place;
The sarvajñā (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas All emerge from this very source. [Note]:
This is an exegetical commentary on the aforementioned "Original Source of All Buddhas. It is provided here for comparison and verification against the preceding text of the sub-commentary (*shu*).

The general meaning is highly consistent. △ Third, the conclusion consisting of admonition and exhortation, which has two parts: first, the admonition and exhortation; second, the concluding dedication.
○ Now, the first part: the admonition and exhortation.
Therefore, O sons of the Buddha, you should rouse great courage and vigor regarding the pure precepts of all Buddhas.
Guarding and upholding it like a bright pearl, as all bodhisattvas of the past have already studied within this,
those of the future shall study it, and those of the present are now studying it.
(2) The conclusion and dedication.
This is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity, praised by the Holy Lord.
Having followed this in my teaching, may the immeasurable mass of merit be dedicated to all sentient beings, so that together we may proceed toward omniscience.
May all who hear this Dharma attain the path of Buddhahood.
[Note]: Regarding the phrase "returning to the Buddha-way of the three virtues of Nirvāṇa," there are two interpretations as to who spoke this verse.
First, based on my own interpretation that it was spoken in accordance with [the Buddha's intent], one knows it is the Buddha’s teaching.

Second, it is argued that since the first line contains the phrase "praised by the Holy Lord," the Buddha would not have referred to himself in such a manner; thus, it was likely composed by Master Kumārajīva at the time of his recitation and translation.
The verse is uttered as an exaltation of the precepts; when it says "I," Master Kumārajīva is referring to himself.
Since these precepts are those praised by the Holy Lord, I now rely upon the Buddha to recite these precepts every half-month.
To say "reciting in accordance" means to follow what was taught by the Holy Lord, the World-Honored One. Now, [the opponent] raises the objection that the original text of the sutra has not arrived.
To verify this, I request that you examine it further: the commentaries on the *Prajñāpāramitā* stop their explanation at the preceding section, which concludes with the "Circulation" (流通) passage;
they do not explain the long prose and the verses beginning from "At that time, Śākyamuni... onwards. The *Rongchao* states:
"According to other versions of the scripture, there are ten additional lines of long prose and fourteen lines of verse; these are present in all editions of the scripture."
As for why these are not explained here: it is because this passage is a narrative by the *sūtra-compilers* (*sūtrakāra*) extolling the praises of ancient masters;
since its meaning is not urgent, they have omitted it without explanation. Now, I say that Master Rong’s lack of discernment is extreme.
If the "sūtra-compilers" were indeed the compilers (*saṃgītikāra*), then in the preceding text there would have been at least some instances of the compiler’s own phrasing as an example.
If you do not [accept] this as the work of the compilers of the sutras, how could it be categorized alongside the praises of the ancient masters?
Why have you not investigated this so thoroughly?
[End of] Fascicle Lower of the Commentary on the Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra.

Those who recite and study the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* are numerous, and its commentaries are likewise many; yet, as the various commentaries run counter to one another, there are passages where no commentary exists.
Regarding those points that are difficult to understand, there is no means by which to resolve them through consultation.

Xian has constantly desired to integrate the commentaries into the sūtra for annotation, seeking out and examining the various masters' sub-commentaries and digests, even though the commentaries preserved at Shibi Cave are each...

There exists a commentary that, while failing to enter the threshold of the Tiantai school, nevertheless provides a complete account of the ritual facts (*shixiang*) yet lacks clarity regarding the underlying principles (*liyi*).
Now, taking the Master Zhiyi’s sub-commentary as the structural framework, I have inserted it beneath the scriptural text;

furthermore, I have selectively incorporated the various family commentaries (*caojì*) and the *Shibiqizang shu*, recording those instances where the ritual facts are applicable or where the doctrinal interpretations are particularly superior.

Furthermore, the value of recitation and study lies in this: when one encounters a point of doubt or obstruction upon unrolling the scroll, understanding dawns instantly within the space of a fixed gaze, without waiting for a later time.
The *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* ordains that the *poṣadha* be observed every half-month;
yet those who study Buddhism often neglect it, failing to uphold it and thereby losing its excellent instructions—this is truly lamentable. Now, having obtained an ancient manuscript...
The protocols for the *poṣadha* ceremony have been compiled here by collating the practices found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

I humbly entreat all great beings of power throughout the various quarters not to forget the Buddha’s instructions, but to proclaim the *zongmen* (the school of our lineage) and to respectfully adopt and practice them.

In this way, may the sublime teachings and pure regulations be revitalized in these final times, so that all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu* may together traverse the *Huazang* (Flower Treasury) world-realm.

This is the method for the fortnightly *poṣadha* ceremony (the fifteenth day of the waxing moon and the fifteenth day of the waning moon—that is, the thirtieth day; in months with fewer days, the fourteenth day—that is, the twenty-ninth day), by which one directly reaches the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
First, strike the bell to assemble the assembly (once the assembly has gathered, they recite the verse for hearing the bell in unison):
Subduing the enemy of Māra’s power, Exhausting all fetters without remainder, The *ghanṭā* is struck upon the open ground;
Monks who hear it should assemble. All you who wish to hear the Dharma, Cross over the flood of the ocean of birth and death.
Hearing this wondrous sound, all shall gather here like clouds.
(Upon the conclusion of this verse, enter the hall in succession and stand with palms joined before your respective seats.)

Second, performing prostrations and reciting the *Poṣadha* verses (standing firmly, each unfolding their sitting mat, performing three prostrations, kneeling with lowered right knee, and reciting the verses):
"Your observance of the precepts is pure like the full moon; Body and speech are bright and stainless, free from blemish.
The great assembly is harmonious and free from dispute; Only then may you together perform the *Poṣadha*."
(At the conclusion of the verse, they fold their sitting cloths, rise, and each takes their seat in the full-lotus posture).
Third, the ritual for the Sangha: the assembly emerges, and one person—the *karmadāna*—announces the proceedings (*jñapti*). Four persons perform the ritual;

incense water, pure water, and two hand towels are prepared and arranged before the prostration seats. The *karmadāna* kneels in the center, and the four persons proceed in succession to emerge and recite verses.
The Verse on Pure Water says:
"The water of eight virtues purifies all dust; Washing the palms removes grime, leaving the mind unstained.
Holding the prohibitive precepts without omission or transgression— All sentient beings are likewise so."
The Verse on Fragrant Bathing Water says:
Bathed and perfumed with fragrant waters, all defilements are cleansed;
The Dharma-body is complete, the five parts are full, Prajñā shines perfectly, and liberation is fulfilled; All sentient beings together enter the expanse of the Dharmadhātu.
The four [monks] rise, each taking a pure water vessel and a hand towel, and proceed through the assembly. The Rector (Vina) rises and strikes the wooden mallet.
The four Rectors sound the mallets, saying: "The assembly, be mindful and make vows" (this is spoken in the level tone; chanting is not used).
I respectfully address all sons of the Buddha: join your palms and listen with a sincere mind. Each of you should recite this according to the sound:

"In such-and-such a state, in such-and-such a village, in such-and-such a monastery within this Jambudvīpa, I, a disciple of the legacy teachings of our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha—whether an ordained or lay bodhisattva—reflect upon myself that throughout the long kalpas of birth and death, it has been due to..."
Having encountered the Unsurpassed Compassionate Honored One, if one does not now give rise to the mind of renunciation, there is fear that one will again wander through saṃsāra;
therefore, on this day, we together revere the Triple Gem, and those who thirst for and look up to the Mahāyāna shall collectively proclaim the treasury of the Bodhisattva precepts.
By means of this merit, may the eight classes of devas, including the nāgas, be enriched and their majestic power become sovereign.
May the Sage Transformation of Your Majesty, the Emperor, be inexhaustible; may the blessings of the Crown Prince and the various princes extend for ten thousand generations;

may the preceptors, monks, parents, and kin always remain secure and at peace. May those who rejoice in this, as well as all who see or hear it, have their past obstructions melt away like ice and the karmic offenses of the three miserable realms and four modes of birth be cleansed and eliminated.
We, [names], vow to depart from this Sahā world and, together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). (End of recitation)
(Strike the mallet once).
Five: Those who have not yet generated the bodhicitta, come forth! (Chant:
"O Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! This treasury of Bodhisattva precepts is the assembly of fellow students of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time."
Those who have not yet resolved to attain Bodhicitta and have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts should leave (after the third proclamation has finished, strike the bell once).
Fifth, the inquiry regarding observance (proclaim as follows):
"Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! Among those present here, have you who have not yet resolved or received [the vows] now emerged?

From this body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, throughout the interval between them, are you able to abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox, resolve upon Bodhicitta, sever evil and cultivate good, uphold the Bodhisattva precepts, and practice the Bodhisattva path? [The assembly replied, "We are able to practice."]
Sixth, the Questioning of the Junior Protectors (chant as follows):
"All sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! Who among this assembly is the youngest? Let them come forward to receive protection" (chant three times, strike once).
The Seventh Inquiry on Entering Purity (Chant):
"All Buddha-sons, listen attentively! There is a Pure Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva entering" (Chant three times; strike once).
The Eightfold Inquiry and the Distribution of Voting Slips (*śalākā*).

First, the distribution of the voting slips for ordination: "O sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! Among the assembly, those who are junior have already been gathered and protected. Outside, there are pure Mahāsattvas who have entered;
both internally and externally they are tranquil, free from all obstacles, and fit to receive the distribution of voting slips. We shall extensively perform the Poṣadha ceremony."

The *bodhisattva-bhikṣu* [Name] shall distribute counting sticks (*śalākā*) for the sake of the community to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony. The assembly should be single-minded in mindfulness and resolve to perform the *poṣadha*.
May the senior, middle, and junior seats each receive their sticks in due order according to the Dharma. (After the three proclamations from "May the senior, middle, and junior seats...
down to "...strike once," distribute the sticks. As the great assembly receives the sticks, each should recite the following verse:
Vajra Unimpeded Liberation Counting-stick— Hard to obtain, hard to encounter, like a golden fruit;
I now receive it with joy upon my crown, And all sentient beings shall do likewise.
(Recite these nine lines for the Householder Counting-stick.)

"O sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! Next, the tally-sticks for lay bodhisattvas are being distributed. (Chant three times; strike the gong once; distribute the tally-sticks. The verse for receiving the tally-stick is as before.
Chant the count of the tally-sticks ten times (chanting as follows):

"O Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! In this single dwelling place, at this single *poṣadha* assembly, there are such-and-such numbers of ordained bodhisattvas and such-and-such numbers of lay bodhisattvas, totaling such-and-such individuals.
Each of you, upholding the purity of the Buddha-dharma, shall gather in harmony for the *poṣadha*.
Above, you shall accord with the Buddha’s teachings to repay the four debts of gratitude; below, for the sake of all sentient beings, each of you shall recite the name of Amitābha Buddha."
11. Requesting the Elder to Recite the Precepts (The *Vina* performs three prostrations before the Elder and says in a level tone):

"May the Elder, out of compassion, recite the precepts for the sake of the assembly. (If the Elder recites them himself, he silently grants permission; if another monk is appointed, the *Vina* says in a level tone: "Please recite the precepts for the sake of the assembly."

When it is one’s turn to preside over the *poṣadha* ceremony during the half-month, if one’s speech is muddled and dull and fears troubling the assembly, there may be a certain Bodhisattva within the assembly who is able to recite the precepts;

one should go to him and inform him, saying: "Please recite the precepts for the sake of the assembly. (The *karmadāna* shall then go before that monk, join his palms, and inquire after his well-being, saying:)

The Elder announced, "Recite the precepts for the sake of the assembly" (if there was someone with a resonant voice in the assembly, they were requested to serve as the *brahmadanda* *karmadāna*; he would go before that person, inquire after their well-being, and request them).
12. Requesting the Proclamation of the Precepts (Ring once and chant):
"O Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! The Saṃgha has appointed the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu [Name] to proclaim the precepts for the assembly;
the Dharma Master [Name], in the Brahma-voice, shall ascend the high seat."

13. The Preceptor Ascends the Seat (The monk reciting the precepts leaves the assembly; prior to this, he prepares his ritual implements, burns incense, spreads his sitting mat, performs three prostrations with kneeling and speech).

"I, Bhikṣu [Name], bow my head in salutation and respectfully address the great assembly: The assembly has appointed me to recite the precepts, yet as my three karmas have not been diligent, I fear there may be omissions or errors.
I pray that those who would join in the recitation will instruct me. (Having finished speaking, he rises and ascends the seat.)
14. Brahma-like Chanting (Once the precept-reciting monks have ascended the seat and are seated, the mallet is struck once, and the Brahma-like chanting monks intone).
15. Burning Incense and Scattering Flowers (The monks performing the ritual rise and proceed to scatter flowers, reciting the verse as follows).
Scattering flowers as adornment throughout the ten directions, Scattering various precious flowers to form a canopy,
Scattering various precious flowers throughout the ten directions, Making offerings to all the Tathāgatas. (The Venerable Leader,
holding an incense burner before the assembly, kneels and chants, raising his voice:)

The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, and the fragrance of liberation—clouds of radiant light pervading the entire Dharma-realm, making offerings to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions. All who see or hear are universally perfumed, realizing tranquil extinction.
(Recite this sixteen times; when the Sanskrit chanting ceases, strike the bell once.)
Recitation of the Precepts.
Seventeenth, upon completion of the recitation, the *brahmaghoṣa* (the monastic chant in Sanskrit) is performed:
"Dwelling in the world like empty space, like a lotus flower unsoiled by water, with a pure mind, one transcends to the other shore. Bow.
First, prostrate to the Unsurpassed Honored One (or it is also permissible to recite the *pañcābhijñā* verse).
The eighteen precept masters perform their bows of thanks (the monk who recited the precepts descends from his seat, performs three prostrations before the assembly, kneels, and speaks as follows):

I, the bhikṣu [Name], prostrate with my head at the feet of the assembly and respectfully offer my thanks. As the assembly was appointed to recite the Prātimokṣa, there were many instances that did not accord with the Dharma, thereby troubling the assembly.
May the assembly, out of compassion, grant me their joy and forbearance.
19. The Three Refuges (The assembly rises, spreads their sitting cloths, and performs three prostrations; the *vinaya-dhara* strikes the mallet and chants):
"I take refuge in the Buddha; may all sentient beings realize and understand the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed resolve."
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all sentient beings govern and lead the great assembly, free from all obstacles.
Having thus spoken of the merit of the precepts, may it be scattered and moisten the entire Dharma-realm; I pay homage to the noble assembly.
The Twentyfold Great Assembly Celebrates Joy (*Bai ji gui shuo jie yun*).
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is the foremost joy; Hearing the Dharma and practicing it brings the joy of peace and stability;
The harmony of the great assembly and the bliss of *nirvāṇa*— Sentient beings being freed from suffering is the joy of liberation.
When the verses were finished, they each dispersed.
